questions.stem: Which phase of the cell cycle is when a cell duplicates its DNA?

rationales.whyCorrect: The S (synthesis) phase of interphase is when DNA replication occurs, producing an identical copy of each chromosome so that the cell can later divide its genetic material equally. G1 and G2 are growth and preparation gaps, and M phase (mitosis plus cytokinesis) is when the already-duplicated material is physically separated. Correctly placing DNA synthesis in S phase is essential for understanding why each daughter cell ends up with a complete genome.
rationales.eli10: Think of the cell cycle as getting ready to share a recipe book with a new roommate. Before you can split up, you first have to photocopy the whole book so there are two complete copies. That photocopying step is the 'S' phase (S for synthesis, meaning 'making a copy'). The other phases are for growing and double-checking, but the actual copying of the DNA instructions only happens in S phase.

questions.stem: Which term describes two identical copies of a chromosome joined together at the centromere after DNA replication?

rationales.whyCorrect: After S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical DNA copies called sister chromatids held together at the centromere. Homologous chromosomes are the maternal and paternal versions of the same chromosome (similar but not identical), a tetrad is the four-chromatid structure formed by paired homologs in meiosis I, and chromatin is the uncondensed complex of DNA and protein. Distinguishing sister chromatids from these other terms is fundamental to tracking chromosome behavior in mitosis and meiosis.
rationales.eli10: When the cell photocopies a chromosome, it doesn't let the copy float away. Instead the original and the copy stay stuck together in the middle, like two socks pinned together at their toes. Because they are exact copies of each other, we call them 'sister' chromatids. They stay attached until it's time to pull them apart into two new cells.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the four main phases of mitosis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mitosis proceeds as prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes align at the cell's equator), anaphase (sister chromatids separate to opposite poles), and telophase (nuclear envelopes reform). This ordered sequence ensures accurate segregation of duplicated chromosomes into two genetically identical nuclei. Knowing the order lets you predict what a cell should look like at each stage.
rationales.eli10: A memory trick is 'PMAT.' First things Prepare (Prophase), then they line up in the Middle (Metaphase), then they get pulled Apart (Anaphase), and finally Two new nuclei form (Telophase). Picture kids lining up in the middle of a gym, then being split into two teams pulled to opposite walls, then settling into two separate rooms.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the checkpoints found throughout the cell cycle?

options.text: To speed up DNA replication whenever the cell is growing quickly
To confirm that conditions and DNA are sound before division proceeds
To double the cell's chromosome number just before mitosis begins
To physically attach sister chromatids to one another at the centromere

rationales.whyCorrect: Cell cycle checkpoints (notably at G1, G2, and the spindle/M checkpoint) act as quality-control stops that verify cell size, nutrient availability, DNA integrity, and proper spindle attachment before allowing progression. This surveillance prevents the propagation of damaged or incompletely replicated DNA, which is why checkpoint failure is closely linked to cancer. Checkpoints govern the timing and quality of division; they do not accelerate replication, add chromosomes, or physically link sister chromatids, which is the job of cohesin proteins.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a factory line where an inspector stops the belt to check each product before it moves on. If something is broken, the inspector halts everything until it's fixed. Cell cycle checkpoints are those inspectors: they make sure the DNA isn't damaged and everything is ready before the cell is allowed to keep dividing. When these inspectors quit, bad cells slip through, and that's how cancer can start.

questions.stem: Which comparison between mitosis and meiosis is accurate?

options.text: Mitosis produces two identical diploid cells, while meiosis produces four genetically varied haploid cells
Mitosis involves two divisions, while meiosis involves only one division
Mitosis produces four genetically varied cells, while meiosis produces two identical cells
Both mitosis and meiosis reduce the chromosome number by half

rationales.whyCorrect: Mitosis is a single division yielding two diploid cells genetically identical to the parent, supporting growth and repair. Meiosis is two consecutive divisions yielding four haploid gametes with genetic variation introduced by crossing over and independent assortment. Only meiosis halves the chromosome number, which is what keeps the chromosome count constant across generations after fertilization.
rationales.eli10: Mitosis is like a copy machine: put one page in, get two identical pages out, still full-length. Meiosis is more like shuffling a deck and dealing it into four hands, where each hand has only half the cards and no two hands are the same. That's why your body cells are all identical copies (mitosis), but your egg or sperm cells are unique and carry only half your chromosomes (meiosis).

questions.stem: Which event during meiosis I is the main source of new combinations of alleles on a single chromosome?

options.text: Alignment of tetrads at the metaphase plate in metaphase I
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I
Condensation of chromatin in prophase I
Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I

rationales.whyCorrect: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange corresponding segments at chiasmata in a process called crossing over (recombination), producing chromosomes with new allele combinations. Condensation of chromatin only packages the DNA, while metaphase I alignment and the anaphase I separation of homologs shuffle whole chromosomes (independent assortment) rather than rearranging alleles along a single chromosome. Crossing over, along with independent assortment, is a key driver of genetic diversity in offspring.
rationales.eli10: Picture two friends each holding a string of colored beads that represent the same genes from mom and dad. During crossing over, they swap matching sections of their strings, so each string ends up with a brand-new mix of colors. This bead-swapping happens early in meiosis and is why you can get a combination of traits neither parent's single chromosome had.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely cause a cell to divide uncontrollably?

options.text: An increase in the number of functioning cell cycle checkpoints
An increase in the time the cell spends in G0 (resting)
A slowdown of DNA replication during S phase
A mutation that disables the proteins that stop the cycle when DNA is damaged

rationales.whyCorrect: Regulatory proteins such as tumor suppressors (for example, p53) normally halt the cycle so damage can be repaired or the cell can be eliminated. If mutations disable these brakes, cells with damaged DNA continue dividing, accumulating further mutations and forming tumors. More functioning checkpoints, slower replication, or more time in G0 would all restrain rather than promote division.
rationales.eli10: A car needs both a gas pedal and brakes. The cell's brakes are proteins that stop division when something is wrong. If those brakes break, the car can't slow down even when there's danger ahead, so it keeps going and going. A cell with broken brakes keeps dividing when it shouldn't, and that runaway dividing is what a tumor is.

questions.stem: A body cell of a certain organism normally contains 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will be in each daughter cell produced by mitosis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell, so each retains the full diploid number of 12 chromosomes. The DNA is duplicated in S phase and then evenly distributed, keeping the count constant. Halving to 6 would occur only in meiosis, which produces haploid gametes.
rationales.eli10: Mitosis is the copy-machine kind of division, so the two cells you get are exact copies of the original. If the starting cell has 12 chromosomes, each new cell also has 12, not fewer. The count only gets cut in half when the cell is making eggs or sperm, and that's a different process called meiosis.

questions.stem: A scientist observes a dividing cell in which sister chromatids are being pulled toward opposite poles of the cell. Which phase is the cell most likely in?

rationales.whyCorrect: Anaphase is defined by the separation of sister chromatids, which are pulled by shortening spindle microtubules toward opposite poles. In metaphase the chromosomes are still aligned at the equator, in prophase they are condensing, and G2 is part of interphase before division. Recognizing chromatid movement as the anaphase signature lets an observer identify the phase from a single snapshot.
rationales.eli10: The clue is 'pulled apart toward opposite ends.' That tug-of-war, where the two stuck-together copies finally get yanked to opposite sides of the cell, only happens in anaphase (think 'A' for 'Apart'). In metaphase they're just lined up in the middle waiting, and in prophase they're still getting ready.

questions.stem: Which example correctly matches a body process with the type of cell division that carries it out?

options.text: Replacing old cells lining the intestine is accomplished by mitosis
Producing sperm and egg cells is accomplished by mitosis
Healing a cut on the skin is accomplished by meiosis
Growing from a single fertilized cell into an embryo is accomplished by meiosis

rationales.whyCorrect: Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells and is responsible for growth, tissue repair, and the routine replacement of cells such as the intestinal lining. Meiosis is reserved for producing haploid gametes (sperm and eggs). Wound healing and embryonic growth also rely on mitosis, so only the intestinal replacement option is matched correctly.
rationales.eli10: Remember the simple rule: mitosis is for building and fixing your body (growth and repair), and meiosis is only for making eggs and sperm. Your intestine wears out cells every day and replaces them with identical new ones, which is a repair job, so that's mitosis. Healing a cut is also mitosis; only baby-making cells come from meiosis.

questions.stem: What would happen if homologous chromosomes failed to separate during anaphase I of meiosis?

options.text: All four resulting gametes would have the normal number of chromosomes
Some gametes would have an extra chromosome and others would be missing one
The cell would produce two identical diploid cells instead of gametes
Crossing over would be prevented in the following division

rationales.whyCorrect: Failure of homologous chromosomes to separate, called nondisjunction, causes chromosomes to be distributed unequally, so some gametes receive an extra copy and others lack a copy. After fertilization this leads to aneuploidy, such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome). This illustrates why precise segregation in anaphase I is critical for producing chromosomally balanced gametes.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two people are supposed to each take one of a matching pair of shoes, but instead one grabs both and the other gets none. Now one ends up with too many and the other with too few. When chromosomes fail to split up properly (nondisjunction), the egg or sperm ends up with an extra chromosome or a missing one, which can cause conditions like Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains why offspring produced by sexual reproduction show genetic variation while a cell's mitotic descendants do not?

options.text: Mitosis includes crossing over and independent assortment, while meiosis only copies the parent genome
Mitosis produces haploid cells that later fuse at fertilization, generating new allele combinations
Meiosis shuffles alleles by crossing over and independent assortment, and fertilization joins unlike gametes
Both processes randomly rearrange chromosomes, but only the products of mitosis are later joined at fertilization

rationales.whyCorrect: Genetic variation in sexual reproduction arises from three sources: crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis, plus the random union of two genetically distinct gametes at fertilization. Mitosis has none of these shuffling mechanisms, yields diploid rather than haploid cells, and its products never fuse at fertilization; it simply copies the genome faithfully, producing clones. Understanding this contrast explains why siblings differ from one another while a person's body cells are genetically identical.
rationales.eli10: Mitosis is a plain photocopy, so every copy looks the same. Meiosis is like shuffling a deck (crossing over) and dealing hands in a random way (independent assortment), and then fertilization mixes one shuffled hand from mom with a different shuffled hand from dad. All that shuffling and mixing is why brothers and sisters aren't identical, but your own body cells are all copies of each other.

questions.stem: Which term refers to a segment of DNA that codes for a specific protein or functional product?

rationales.whyCorrect: A gene is the basic physical and functional unit of heredity, consisting of a segment of DNA that provides the instructions for making a specific protein or functional RNA. A chromosome is a much larger structure that packages many genes, a nucleotide is a single building block of DNA, and the genome is the organism's entire set of genetic material. Distinguishing these levels of organization is fundamental to all of genetics.
rationales.eli10: Think of your DNA as a giant cookbook. One single recipe in that book is a gene. It tells the cell how to make one particular thing, like a protein that helps make the pigment in your eyes. The whole book is the genome, and a chromosome is like one big chapter holding many recipes.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines an allele?

options.text: A structure made of tightly coiled DNA and protein
The physical appearance produced by a genotype
One of the alternative versions of a gene at a given location
A cell containing two complete sets of chromosomes

rationales.whyCorrect: An allele is one of two or more alternative forms of a gene that occupy the same locus (position) on a chromosome and produce variation in a trait. The other options describe a chromosome, a phenotype, and a diploid cell, respectively. Understanding alleles is essential because differences between alleles explain why individuals inherit different versions of the same trait.
rationales.eli10: A gene is like a slot for blood type. An allele is the actual card you slide into that slot, and the cards come in versions: an A version, a B version, and an O version. Everyone has the blood-type slot, but which card versions they carry is their alleles.

questions.stem: What is the primary difference between an organism's genotype and its phenotype?

options.text: Genotype is the genetic makeup; phenotype is the observable trait
Genotype is the observable trait; phenotype is the genetic makeup
Genotype applies to dominant genes; phenotype applies to recessive genes
Genotype is inherited; phenotype is never inherited

rationales.whyCorrect: The genotype is the specific set of alleles an organism carries for a trait, while the phenotype is the physical, observable expression of those alleles (and their interaction with the environment). Both dominant and recessive alleles contribute to the genotype, so option C is incorrect. This distinction underlies how hidden genetic information can produce visible characteristics.
rationales.eli10: Your genotype is the secret code written inside your cells, like the ingredients list you cannot see. Your phenotype is the finished cake you can actually look at and taste. The hidden recipe (genotype) shapes how the visible cake (phenotype) turns out, though things like the oven and the baking time, the surroundings, change the final cake too.

questions.stem: An individual is heterozygous for a trait with one dominant and one recessive allele. Why does the dominant phenotype appear rather than the recessive one?

options.text: The recessive allele is physically destroyed during development
Dominant alleles are always more numerous than recessive alleles
The dominant allele's product masks the effect of the recessive allele
The recessive allele can only be inherited from the father

rationales.whyCorrect: In a heterozygote, both alleles are present, but the dominant allele produces a product (often a functional protein) that determines the phenotype, masking the recessive allele's effect. The recessive allele is not destroyed and is still passed to offspring; it simply is not expressed in the phenotype when a dominant allele is present. This explains how recessive traits can skip generations.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two kids shouting different answers, but one has a microphone (the dominant allele) and the other only whispers (the recessive allele). You hear the microphone. The whisper is still there and can be passed on, but for now the loud voice covers it up.

questions.stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that the two alleles for a trait separate during gamete formation. What is the direct consequence of this law?

options.text: Each gamete receives only one allele for each trait
Alleles for different traits are always inherited together
Offspring always resemble only one parent
Each gamete receives both alleles for every trait

rationales.whyCorrect: The law of segregation holds that the paired alleles of a gene separate during meiosis so that each gamete carries only one allele for each trait. Fertilization then restores the paired condition in the offspring. This ensures offspring inherit one allele from each parent, which is the foundation of predictable Mendelian ratios.
rationales.eli10: You have two socks of a gene, but when you make an egg or sperm cell, you can only pack one sock into each. Later, when egg and sperm meet, the baby gets one sock from mom and one from dad, making a new pair.

questions.stem: Which comparison between homozygous and heterozygous genotypes is accurate?

options.text: Homozygous individuals cannot pass alleles to offspring
Homozygous has two different alleles; heterozygous has two identical alleles
Homozygous only occurs for dominant traits; heterozygous only for recessive
Homozygous has two identical alleles; heterozygous has two different alleles

rationales.whyCorrect: A homozygous genotype contains two copies of the same allele (for example, both dominant or both recessive), while a heterozygous genotype contains two different alleles for that gene. Homozygosity can occur for either dominant or recessive alleles, so option C is wrong. This distinction determines whether a recessive trait can be expressed and how alleles are transmitted.
rationales.eli10: Homo means same and hetero means different. If both of your gene socks match, you are homozygous. If they are two different socks, you are heterozygous. Simple as checking whether your socks are a matching pair or a mismatched one.

questions.stem: Which change to a DNA sequence would most likely alter the protein a gene produces?

options.text: Coiling the DNA more tightly around histone proteins
Increasing the total number of chromosomes in a body cell temporarily
Moving the chromosome to a different region of the nucleus
A mutation that changes the order of the nucleotide bases

rationales.whyCorrect: Because the sequence of nucleotide bases specifies the order of amino acids in a protein, a mutation that changes that base sequence can change the resulting protein. Coiling DNA around histones affects how accessible the DNA is but does not rewrite the code, and simply relocating a chromosome does not change its sequence. This is why mutations in the coding sequence are a key source of genetic variation and genetic disorders.
rationales.eli10: The letters in a gene spell out instructions, like a sentence. If you swap or scramble the letters (a mutation), the sentence can mean something different, so the cell builds a different protein. Just folding up the paper or moving it to another drawer does not change the words on it.

questions.stem: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) for a simple dominant trait, which phenotypic ratio is expected in the offspring?

rationales.whyCorrect: A Bb x Bb cross yields genotypes in a 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb ratio. Because BB and Bb both show the dominant phenotype and only bb shows the recessive phenotype, the phenotypic ratio is 3 dominant to 1 recessive. This classic 3:1 ratio is the hallmark result Mendel observed and demonstrates how a recessive trait can reappear from two carrier parents.
rationales.eli10: Each parent can give a big B or a little b. The possible combos are BB, Bb, Bb, and bb, so three out of four show the dominant look and only one shows the recessive look. That is where the famous 3-to-1 pattern comes from.

questions.stem: A couple, both unaffected, have a child with a recessive genetic condition. Which example best explains how this happened?

options.text: Both parents are homozygous dominant carriers
One parent has a brand-new mutation in every body cell
The condition was caused only by the child's environment
Both parents are heterozygous carriers of the recessive allele

rationales.whyCorrect: For a child to inherit a recessive condition from two unaffected parents, each parent must carry one copy of the recessive allele while showing the dominant (unaffected) phenotype, making them heterozygous carriers. When both pass the recessive allele, the child becomes homozygous recessive and expresses the condition. Homozygous dominant individuals carry no recessive allele to pass on, so option A cannot produce an affected child.
rationales.eli10: Both parents secretly carry one hidden recessive card but look normal because their other card is dominant. If they each happen to hand the hidden card to their baby, the baby gets two hidden cards and the trait finally shows up. That is why healthy parents can have a child with a recessive condition.

questions.stem: A geneticist is analyzing a trait and finds that offspring inherit two genes independently of each other, so the alleles of one gene do not affect which alleles of the other are inherited. Which of Mendel's principles does this illustrate?

rationales.whyCorrect: The law of independent assortment states that alleles of different genes are distributed to gametes independently of one another (for genes on separate chromosomes), so inheriting one gene's allele does not influence which allele of another gene is inherited. The law of segregation concerns the separation of the two alleles of a single gene, and the law of dominance concerns which allele is expressed. Independent assortment is a major source of genetic variation among offspring.
rationales.eli10: Imagine packing two separate lunch items, a fruit and a drink. What fruit you grab does not decide which drink you grab; each choice is made on its own. In the same way, the gene for one trait gets sorted into a cell independently of the gene for another trait.

questions.stem: In snapdragons, a red-flowered plant crossed with a white-flowered plant produces all pink offspring. What would happen if this same inheritance pattern applied and two pink offspring were then crossed with each other?

options.text: All offspring would be pink, matching their parents exactly
Offspring would appear in a ratio of 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
Offspring would appear in a ratio of 3 red : 1 white
All offspring would be either red or white, with none pink

rationales.whyCorrect: The pink flowers result from incomplete dominance, in which the heterozygote shows an intermediate (blended) phenotype rather than one allele masking the other. Crossing two heterozygous pink plants gives a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio that here equals the phenotypic ratio: 1 red (homozygous) : 2 pink (heterozygous) : 1 white (homozygous). Unlike complete dominance, each genotype produces a distinct visible phenotype.
rationales.eli10: When red and white mix into pink, no allele is bossing the other around, they blend. So when two pinks have babies, some get two red cards (red), some get one of each (pink again), and some get two white cards (white), giving one red, two pink, one white. The blend reveals every genotype as its own color.

questions.stem: Identical twins raised in very different environments can end up with noticeably different heights and health outcomes despite sharing the same DNA. Which concept best explains this observation?

options.text: The twins must actually have different genotypes
Phenotype results from the interaction of genotype and environment
Genotype has no influence on traits like height
DNA sequence changes rapidly to match each environment

rationales.whyCorrect: Identical twins share the same genotype, so differences between them must arise from environmental influences such as nutrition, activity, and exposures interacting with that shared genetic blueprint. Phenotype is the product of both genotype and environment, not genotype alone, which is why genetically identical individuals can differ. This also shows that DNA sequence does not simply rewrite itself to match surroundings.
rationales.eli10: Two seeds from the same plant have the same instructions, but if one gets lots of sun and water and the other gets little, they grow into different-sized plants. The instructions (genotype) are identical, yet the surroundings shape the final result (phenotype). Nature and environment work together.

questions.stem: Which term describes the specific pair of alleles an organism carries for a particular trait?

rationales.whyCorrect: Genotype refers to the genetic makeup of an organism, specifically the combination of alleles present for a given gene (for example, Bb or bb). It is distinct from phenotype, which is the observable expression of that genotype. Understanding this distinction is foundational to predicting and interpreting inheritance patterns.
rationales.eli10: Think of a gene like a recipe you inherit two copies of, one from each parent. The genotype is the exact pair of recipe cards you are holding (say, one 'brown' card and one 'blue' card), while the phenotype is the cake that actually comes out. Genotype = the cards; phenotype = the cake.

questions.stem: In Mendel's pea experiments, a plant that consistently produced offspring showing the same version of a trait as itself when self-pollinated is described by which term?

rationales.whyCorrect: A true-breeding (purebred) line is homozygous for the trait in question, so self-pollination yields offspring with that same trait generation after generation. Mendel relied on true-breeding parental lines to establish a known starting point before making his crosses. A heterozygote would not breed true, a hybrid is the offspring of two differing lines, and dihybrid refers to a cross tracking two traits at once.
rationales.eli10: True-breeding means 'copies itself every time.' If a tall pea plant is true-breeding, planting its own seeds always gives tall plants, never a surprise short one. Mendel needed that reliability first, because you can only tell what a cross did if you knew exactly what you started with.

questions.stem: An organism with two identical alleles for a trait, such as TT or tt, is best described as which of the following?

rationales.whyCorrect: Homozygous means an organism carries two copies of the same allele for a gene, either two dominant (TT) or two recessive (tt). This contrasts with heterozygous, where the two alleles differ (Tt). The term is central to predicting which offspring will breed true for a trait.
rationales.eli10: Homo means 'same.' If both of your inherited cards for a trait are exactly the same, like two 'tall' cards, you are homozygous. If they are different, like one 'tall' and one 'short,' that is heterozygous, where hetero means 'different.'

questions.stem: Why does a heterozygous individual (Bb) for a trait with complete dominance show the same phenotype as a homozygous dominant individual (BB)?

options.text: The recessive allele is destroyed during fertilization
The dominant allele masks the effect of the recessive allele
The two alleles blend to form an intermediate trait
The recessive allele is never inherited by offspring

rationales.whyCorrect: In complete dominance, a single copy of the dominant allele produces enough functional product to fully express the dominant phenotype, masking the recessive allele's contribution. The recessive allele is still present and can be passed to offspring; it is simply not expressed. This is why heterozygotes are indistinguishable in appearance from homozygous dominants.
rationales.eli10: Imagine the dominant allele shouts and the recessive allele whispers. Even if a whisper is there, all you hear is the shout, so the person looks 'dominant.' The whisper is not gone though, it can still be passed down to a child who might have two whispers and finally be heard.

questions.stem: Mendel's law of segregation is best explained by which cellular event?

options.text: DNA replicating twice in a row before a single round of cell division
Sister chromatids fusing together with their copies during the process of fertilization
Genes located on the same chromosome always being inherited together as one unit
Homologous chromosomes separating during meiosis so each gamete receives one allele

rationales.whyCorrect: The law of segregation states that the two alleles for a trait separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele. This corresponds to the physical separation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I. This mechanism ensures offspring receive one allele from each parent, restoring the paired condition at fertilization.
rationales.eli10: You have two copies of each trait card, but when your body makes egg or sperm cells, it deals out just one card per cell, like splitting a pair of socks so each bag gets only one sock. That splitting is segregation, and it happens when the matching chromosomes pull apart during meiosis.

questions.stem: Which comparison between Mendel's law of segregation and his law of independent assortment is accurate?

options.text: Segregation involves alleles of two different genes, while independent assortment involves the two alleles of a single gene
Both laws describe how two alleles blend together to create new intermediate traits in offspring
Segregation involves the two alleles of one gene, while independent assortment involves how alleles of different genes sort into gametes
Both laws apply only to sex-linked traits carried on the X chromosome in males

rationales.whyCorrect: The law of segregation addresses the separation of the two alleles of a single gene into different gametes. The law of independent assortment describes how alleles of different genes (on different chromosome pairs) sort into gametes independently of one another. Neither law involves blending, and both apply generally, not only to sex-linked genes.
rationales.eli10: Segregation is about one trait: your two cards for eye color get split up. Independent assortment is about two different traits at once: the way your eye-color card gets dealt does not affect how your hair-color card gets dealt, they shuffle separately. One is about splitting a pair, the other is about pairs not influencing each other.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to the predicted offspring ratios if two genes Mendel studied were located very close together on the same chromosome?

options.text: The alleles would tend to be inherited together instead of assorting freely
The genes would still assort independently, giving the usual 9:3:3:1 ratio
One gene would block the other entirely, keeping it out of every gamete
Both genes would become recessive, so only recessive phenotypes would appear

rationales.whyCorrect: Genes located close together on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited as a unit because they are less likely to be separated by crossing over. Observed offspring ratios therefore deviate from independent assortment, with parental allele combinations overrepresented instead of the usual 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio. Linkage only skews these proportions; it does not stop either gene from being inherited or turn dominant alleles into recessive ones, and Mendel's law of independent assortment holds most reliably for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on the same chromosome.
rationales.eli10: Independent assortment works because trait cards are shuffled separately. But if two cards are glued close together on the same strip, they tend to travel as a pair instead of shuffling apart. That stickiness is called linkage, and it bends the usual ratios.

questions.stem: In pea plants, tall (T) is completely dominant to short (t). A cross between two heterozygous tall plants (Tt x Tt) is performed. Which phenotypic ratio is expected in the offspring?

rationales.whyCorrect: A monohybrid cross of Tt x Tt yields genotypes in a 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt ratio. Because T is completely dominant, TT and Tt both appear tall, giving three tall for every one short. This classic 3:1 phenotypic ratio is a hallmark result of a heterozygous monohybrid cross.
rationales.eli10: Each parent can give a T or a t, so the four equally likely combos are TT, Tt, Tt, and tt. Three of those four have at least one 'tall' shout, so they are tall, and only the tt one is short. That is where 3 tall to 1 short comes from.

questions.stem: A geneticist wants to determine whether a purple-flowered plant is homozygous dominant (PP) or heterozygous (Pp). What is the primary purpose of crossing it with a homozygous recessive (pp) plant?

options.text: To reveal the unknown genotype based on whether any recessive offspring appear
To force the unknown plant to become homozygous
To create offspring that are all heterozygous regardless of the parent
To increase the number of dominant alleles in the population

rationales.whyCorrect: This procedure is a test cross. If the purple parent is PP, all offspring are purple; if it is Pp, roughly half the offspring will be white (pp). The appearance of any recessive-phenotype offspring exposes a hidden recessive allele in the unknown parent, revealing its genotype.
rationales.eli10: You cannot tell by looking whether a purple plant secretly carries a hidden white card. So you mate it with a plant that is all white cards. If any white babies pop up, the purple parent must have been hiding a white card. This detective trick is called a test cross.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates incomplete dominance rather than complete dominance?

options.text: A Tt pea plant is just as tall as a TT pea plant
A brown-eyed parent and blue-eyed parent produce a brown-eyed child
A person with type AB blood expresses both A and B antigens on red cells
A red-flowered and a white-flowered parent produce pink-flowered offspring

rationales.whyCorrect: In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype that blends the two homozygous phenotypes, as in pink offspring from red and white parents. This differs from codominance (AB blood, where both alleles are fully and separately expressed) and from complete dominance (the tall pea and brown-eye examples). The intermediate blend is the defining feature.
rationales.eli10: With incomplete dominance, neither allele fully wins, so the result is a mix, like pouring red and white paint together to get pink. That is different from codominance, where you would see distinct red and white spots side by side instead of a blend.

questions.stem: Two parents who both have normal pigmentation have a child with albinism, an autosomal recessive condition. Which conclusion about the parents' genotypes is best supported?

options.text: Both parents must be homozygous recessive for the albinism allele
One parent must be homozygous dominant and the other homozygous recessive
Both parents must be heterozygous carriers of the albinism allele
Neither parent can carry the albinism allele

rationales.whyCorrect: Because this form of albinism is autosomal recessive, an affected child must have inherited a recessive allele from each parent. Since both parents have normal pigmentation, neither can be homozygous recessive, so each must carry one recessive allele hidden by a dominant one, making them heterozygous carriers. Two carriers have a one in four chance of producing an affected child in each pregnancy.
rationales.eli10: For a child to show a hidden recessive trait, they need two copies of the recessive card, one from each parent. The parents look normal, so each must be secretly carrying just one recessive card that stayed hidden. Both parents quietly passing their hidden card is the only way this works.

questions.stem: A single gene affects both fur color and lifespan in a group of mice, and a rare allele produces an unusually pale coat but also shortens survival. Which concept does this scenario best illustrate?

options.text: Epistasis, in which one gene masks the expression of a different gene
Pleiotropy, in which one gene influences multiple distinct traits
Polygenic inheritance, in which many genes contribute to one trait
Independent assortment of two separate genes into gametes

rationales.whyCorrect: Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene affects two or more seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits, here both coat color and lifespan. This differs from epistasis (one gene masking another) and polygenic inheritance (many genes shaping one trait). Recognizing pleiotropy explains why one allele can have wide-ranging, sometimes unexpected effects on an organism.
rationales.eli10: Sometimes one gene is like a single light switch wired to several rooms at once, so flipping it changes more than one thing. Here one gene controls both coat color and how long the mouse lives. One switch, many effects, is called pleiotropy.

questions.stem: A **disaccharide** such as sucrose is broken into its two **monosaccharides** during digestion. Which reaction accomplishes this breakdown?

options.text: Condensation, which forms a new glycosidic bond.
Hydrolysis, which splits the glycosidic bond by adding a water molecule.
Dehydration, which removes water and releases energy.
Oxidation, which adds electrons to the monosaccharides.

rationales.whyCorrect: Hydrolysis means water splitting; the water molecule adds a hydrogen and a hydroxyl across the glycosidic bond, separating the disaccharide into monomers. questions.stem: A student lists the four major classes of macromolecules. Which statement correctly identifies a class that is NOT built from repeating **monomers** joined into a **polymer** chain?

options.text: Proteins are polymers of nucleotide monomers.
Nucleic acids are polymers of amino acid monomers.
Fats and oils are not polymers because they are built from glycerol and fatty acids joined by ester linkages rather than by repeating monomer chains.
Polysaccharides are polymers of fatty acid monomers.

rationales.whyCorrect: True polymers are long chains of repeating monomers, and polysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids all qualify. A, B, and D each mislabel the monomer of a true polymer class.
rationales.eli10: Think of a chain of identical paper links, where each link is one monomer and the chain can be as long as you like. rationales.highYield: Carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids are polymers, but lipids are not built from repeating monomers.

questions.stem: A student claims that humans cannot use **cellulose** as an energy source even though they can digest **starch**. Which explanation best supports the claim?

options.text: Cellulose is a protein that stomach acids denature before absorption.
Starch is made of glucose, while cellulose is made of amino acids.
Humans lack the enzyme that breaks the beta glycosidic linkages in cellulose, though its monomers are glucose just like starch's.
Cellulose is digested but stored as fat before it can be used for energy.

rationales.whyCorrect: Both starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose, and the difference lies in the linkage. Starch uses alpha linkages that human enzymes can cleave, while cellulose uses beta linkages that our digestive enzymes cannot break, which is why cellulose passes through as dietary fiber. A and B state wrong chemistry, and D is the opposite of what happens.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two bracelets made from the same beads but strung in different patterns, one threaded straight through and the other linked sideways. Your mouth has a tool that can only undo the straight-threaded bracelet, which is starch. The sideways bracelet, cellulose, stays locked, so it just passes through your body. Same beads, different stringing, totally different outcome.
rationales.highYield: Starch and cellulose are both glucose polymers that differ only in alpha versus beta linkages, and enzymes are linkage-specific.

questions.stem: During a long run, an athlete's muscles must release glucose rapidly to fuel contraction. Which property of **glycogen** best explains why it can supply glucose so quickly?

options.text: Glycogen is highly branched, so many glucose monomers can be released at once from the chain ends.
Glycogen is a single long unbranched chain that unwinds slowly.
Glycogen dissolves in water as individual glucose molecules.
Glycogen is a lipid that stores more energy per gram than any carbohydrate.

rationales.whyCorrect: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide, and its many branch points create numerous free ends where enzymes can remove glucose simultaneously, speeding release. B describes a less branched structure with fewer release points. C and D misstate what glycogen is, since it is a carbohydrate polymer rather than dissolved monomers or a lipid.
rationales.eli10: Think of glycogen as a ball of yarn with hundreds of loose ends poking out. If a machine pulls one thread at a time, a ball with many ends gives up yarn much faster than a ball with just two ends. That is why the branched ball of glycogen can feed working muscles quickly. A straight, two-ended chain would take far too long.
rationales.highYield: Branching means more chain ends, and more ends mean faster glucose release from glycogen.

questions.stem: Two fats sit at room temperature: butter stays solid while olive oil stays liquid. Which difference between **saturated** and **unsaturated fatty acids** best explains this behavior?

options.text: Butter contains more water molecules than olive oil.
Olive oil contains saturated fatty acids that pack more tightly.
Butter contains saturated fatty acids with no double bonds, allowing the chains to pack tightly and stay solid, while olive oil's unsaturated chains with double bonds kink and stay liquid.
Olive oil contains longer fatty acid chains than butter.

rationales.whyCorrect: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and stay solid at room temperature. rationales.highYield: Double bonds create kinks that keep unsaturated fats liquid, while saturated fats are straight, pack tightly, and stay solid.

questions.stem: When **phospholipids** are placed in water, they spontaneously form a bilayer. Which property of the molecule drives this behavior?

options.text: The entire phospholipid is hydrophobic and repels water.
The phosphate heads repel each other and form separate layers.
The fatty acid tails are hydrophilic and hold water inside the bilayer.
The hydrophilic phosphate heads face the water while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails cluster together away from water.

rationales.whyCorrect: Phospholipids are amphipathic, with hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty acid tails. In water, the tails cluster together away from water while the heads face the aqueous surroundings, producing the bilayer that forms cell membranes. A, B, and C assign the wrong water behavior to the wrong part of the molecule.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two rows of tiny boats floating side by side, with the flags facing outward and the anchors dangling inward. The anchors of the two rows hook together in the middle, and the flags wave in the water on both sides. All the boats line up this way because the anchors hate water and hide from it, while the flags love water and wave at it. That double row of boats is the membrane wrapped around every cell.
rationales.highYield: Phospholipid bilayers form because the heads love water and the tails fear it.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin consists of four folded **polypeptide** chains that assemble into one oxygen-carrying protein. Which level of **protein structure** does the assembly of separate chains into one functional unit represent?

options.text: Primary structure, the linear sequence of amino acids.
Secondary structure, the folds formed by hydrogen bonds in the backbone.
Tertiary structure, the overall shape of a single folded chain.
Quaternary structure, the arrangement of multiple polypeptide chains into one functional unit.

rationales.whyCorrect: Quaternary structure is the level at which two or more polypeptide chains assemble into a single functional protein, and hemoglobin's four globin chains are the classic example. Hemoglobin is a castle made of four towers that must be joined before it can carry oxygen.
rationales.highYield: Quaternary structure is the only level of protein organization that involves more than one polypeptide chain.

questions.stem: A reaction in a cell has a positive change in free energy, so it is **endergonic** and will not proceed on its own. How does the cell use **energy coupling** to drive this reaction forward?

options.text: By lowering the temperature of the cell to slow competing reactions.
By allowing the reaction to run in the opposite direction.
By coupling it to the hydrolysis of ATP, which releases free energy.
By increasing the concentration of the products to push the reaction.

rationales.whyCorrect: Energy coupling joins an endergonic reaction to the exergonic hydrolysis of ATP, so the energy released from ATP drives the reaction that needs it. Lowering temperature (A) slows every reaction instead of supplying energy, and running the reaction backward (B) just reverses the problem. Raising product concentration (D) would increase the free energy needed, making the reaction even harder.
rationales.eli10: Picture a heavy door that will not open when you push it alone. You can hook it to a strong spring that is already loaded and ready to snap. The spring unloads its energy and yanks the door open. The cell does the same thing, spending a loaded energy packet to power jobs that cannot happen on their own.
rationales.highYield: ATP hydrolysis releases the energy that powers endergonic reactions through energy coupling.

The ability to perform substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle.
The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane that powers ATP synthase.
The carbon dioxide released when pyruvate is oxidized.

rationales.highYield: The inner mitochondrial membrane hosts both the electron transport chain and the proton gradient it builds.

### Q06-11 Lactic acid fermentation

During intense exercise, a muscle cell runs low on oxygen and switches to **fermentation**. What does lactic acid fermentation accomplish for the cell, and what is its ATP yield per glucose?

- **A.** It produces about 30 ATP per glucose and removes CO2.
- **B.** It produces ethanol and CO2 in the mitochondria.
- **C.** It regenerates NAD+ in the cytosol, allowing glycolysis to continue at its net 2 ATP per glucose.
- **D.** It regenerates FADH2 while producing 4 ATP per glucose.

**Correct Answer:** **C.** It regenerates NAD+ in the cytosol, allowing glycolysis to continue at its net 2 ATP per glucose.

**Why This Is Correct:** Lactic acid fermentation reduces pyruvate to lactate, which regenerates the NAD+ that glycolysis needs, and the pathway's only ATP comes from glycolysis itself, about 2 per glucose. A reports aerobic yields. B describes alcohol fermentation. D names the wrong coenzyme and ATP count.

> **High-Yield:** Fermentation exists to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can keep producing its 2 ATP per glucose.

**ELI-10:** Think of NAD+ as a delivery bike that must return to the warehouse before the next delivery. When oxygen runs low, the cell quickly changes pyruvate into lactate, which hands the bike back. The cell earns no new coins from this change, but it keeps the small two-coin rhythm of glycolysis going.

questions.stem: Yeast growing without oxygen converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO2 in **alcohol fermentation**. Which statement best describes this pathway?

options.text: It runs in the mitochondria and produces about 30 ATP per glucose.
It requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
It produces lactate as its end product.
It runs in the cytosol, regenerates NAD+, and nets 2 ATP per glucose from glycolysis.

rationales.whyCorrect: Alcohol fermentation runs in the cytosol, where pyruvate loses CO2 to become acetaldehyde and is then reduced to ethanol, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue at its net 2 ATP per glucose. A puts the pathway in the wrong location with aerobic yields. B describes aerobic respiration. C names the end product of lactic acid fermentation.
rationales.eli10: Picture a pizza kitchen where the dough must be kneaded over and over. The kneading enzyme needs a clean towel between batches, and that towel is NAD+. The yeast recycles the towel quickly without oxygen by turning pyruvate into ethanol, so the kneading never stops. The kitchen still earns only two coins per batch, but it stays open.
rationales.highYield: Both fermentations regenerate NAD+ and yield only the 2 ATP from glycolysis, never more.

questions.stem: A researcher compares a plant's **absorption spectrum** (which wavelengths the pigments capture) with its **action spectrum** (which wavelengths drive the most photosynthesis). At a wavelength absorbed strongly by **carotenoids** but weakly by **chlorophyll**, which of the following is most likely true?

options.text: Photosynthesis still runs because carotenoids pass the absorbed energy to chlorophyll.
Photosynthesis stops completely because carotenoids cannot pass energy to chlorophyll.
Photosynthesis runs faster than at any other wavelength because carotenoids outperform chlorophyll at every job.
The action spectrum matches the absorption spectrum exactly at every wavelength, with no exceptions.

rationales.whyCorrect: The action spectrum reflects photosynthesis driven by all pigments, and carotenoids can pass captured energy to chlorophyll, so absorption by carotenoids still supports photosynthesis. B wrongly claims carotenoids are isolated from the reaction centers. C overstates the role of carotenoids, which are accessory pigments rather than the main light harvesters. D ignores that accessory pigments create real differences between the two spectra.
rationales.eli10: Think of a plant leaf like a solar panel that can only use certain colors of sunlight. If you shine a green light on the panel, almost nothing happens because green light bounces off the leaf. The absorption spectrum shows which colors the pigments grab, and the action spectrum shows which colors actually make the plant grow fastest. Green light gets reflected away, which is why leaves look green to your eyes.
rationales.highYield: The action spectrum, not the absorption spectrum, shows which wavelengths actually drive photosynthesis.

questions.stem: In addition to helping harvest light, carotenoids protect the photosynthetic machinery from damage. Which of the following best describes that protective role?

options.text: They convert excess light energy into extra ATP that speeds up the Calvin cycle.
They absorb excess light energy and dissipate it as heat, protecting chlorophyll from damage.
They absorb only green light, which the plant safely discards as waste.
They reflect all incoming light away from the leaf so the pigments stay cool.

rationales.whyCorrect: Carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb excess light energy and harmlessly release it as heat, shielding chlorophyll from photo-oxidative damage. A gets the mechanism backwards, because excess light energy is not converted into useful ATP. C is wrong because carotenoids absorb blue-green light rather than green light. D describes reflection, which would steal energy from photosynthesis instead of protecting it.
rationales.eli10: Carotenoids are like backup singers who catch notes the lead singer misses. Chlorophyll handles red and blue light well, but carotenoids absorb other colors and pass that energy to chlorophyll. They also act like sunscreen, soaking up excess brightness so the leaf does not get scorched. In autumn the green chlorophyll breaks down and the orange carotenoids show through.
rationales.highYield: Carotenoids harvest extra light and shield chlorophyll by absorbing and dissipating excess energy as heat.

questions.stem: When a photon of light strikes a chlorophyll molecule in **photosystem II**, which of the following happens first in the energy conversion chain?

options.text: NADPH is formed directly by the energized chlorophyll.
ATP is pumped out of the thylakoid lumen.
An electron in the chlorophyll is boosted to a higher energy level and captured by the primary electron acceptor.
Carbon dioxide is split to replace the electron the chlorophyll has lost.

rationales.whyCorrect: Light energy excites an electron in the chlorophyll reaction center, and the primary electron acceptor grabs that high-energy electron to start electron transport. A is wrong because NADPH is made later at photosystem I, not directly here. B reverses the direction, since ATP forms in the stroma, not out of the lumen. D misidentifies the electron donor, which is water, not carbon dioxide.
rationales.eli10: Imagine an energy ball bouncing through a row of people. When light hits the chlorophyll in photosystem II, an electron inside jumps up to a higher shelf. The plant replaces the lost electron by splitting a water molecule, like grabbing a spare part. Oxygen is left over and released as a waste gas. That is why plants give off the oxygen we breathe.
rationales.highYield: Light strikes photosystem II and kicks a high-energy electron to the primary electron acceptor, which water then replaces.

- **C.** An electron in the chlorophyll is boosted to a higher energy level and captured by the primary electron acceptor.
- **D.** Carbon dioxide is split to replace the electron the chlorophyll has lost.

**Correct Answer:** **C.** An electron in the chlorophyll is boosted to a higher energy level and captured by the primary electron acceptor.

**Why This Is Correct:** Light energy excites an electron in the chlorophyll reaction center, and the primary electron acceptor grabs that high-energy electron to start electron transport. A is wrong because NADPH is made later at photosystem I, not directly here. B reverses the direction, since ATP forms in the stroma, not out of the lumen. D misidentifies the electron donor, which is water, not carbon dioxide.

> **High-Yield:** Light strikes photosystem II and kicks a high-energy electron to the primary electron acceptor, which water then replaces.

**ELI-10:** Imagine an energy ball bouncing through a row of people. When light hits the chlorophyll in photosystem II, an electron inside jumps up to a higher shelf. The plant replaces the lost electron by splitting a water molecule, like grabbing a spare part. Oxygen is left over and released as a waste gas. That is why plants give off the oxygen we breathe.

questions.stem: The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from which molecule?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, because its carbon is fixed into sugar and its oxygen is released.
Glucose, because sugar breakdown releases oxygen as a byproduct.
ATP, because energy transfer releases oxygen atoms.
Water, because photosystem II splits water molecules to replace electrons lost by chlorophyll.

rationales.whyCorrect: The light reactions replace chlorophyll's lost electrons by splitting water, and the oxygen atoms from those water molecules pair up and are released as oxygen gas. A confuses the fates of carbon and oxygen in carbon dioxide, which supplies the carbon for sugar, not the oxygen. B is wrong because photosynthesis makes glucose rather than breaking it down. C confuses energy carriers with elemental sources of oxygen.
rationales.eli10: Picture a water molecule being pulled apart like a cracker split in two. The oxygen atoms left behind pair up into oxygen gas, and the plant releases it into the air. The electrons from the water step in to replace the ones sunlight knocked loose. No water means no replacement electrons and no oxygen, no matter how bright the sun shines.
rationales.highYield: The oxygen plants release comes from split water molecules, never from carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: As electrons travel from photosystem II to photosystem I along the **electron transport chain**, the energy they release is used to do what?

options.text: Pump protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen, building a gradient used to make ATP.
Pump protons out of the thylakoid lumen into the stroma, building a gradient used to make NADPH.
Fix carbon dioxide into G3P before the Calvin cycle begins.
Split water into oxygen and protons inside the lumen.

rationales.whyCorrect: Electrons lose energy as they move through the transport chain, and that energy pumps protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen to build the gradient for ATP synthesis. B gets the proton direction backwards, and NADPH is made at photosystem I, not by proton flow. C misplaces carbon fixation, which happens later in the Calvin cycle. D misidentifies water splitting, which occurs at photosystem II, not along the chain.
rationales.eli10: The electron transport chain between the photosystems is like a bucket brigade carrying a hot coal downhill. Each carrier hands the coal to the next one and uses the released energy to pump protons into the thylakoid space. That crowded inner space becomes a charged battery. The battery will later spin ATP synthase to make ATP.
rationales.highYield: Electron transport between the photosystems pumps protons into the thylakoid lumen to power ATP synthase.

As electrons travel from photosystem II to photosystem I along the **electron transport chain**, the energy they release is used to do what?

- **A.** Pump protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen, building a gradient used to make ATP.
- **B.** Pump protons out of the thylakoid lumen into the stroma, building a gradient used to make NADPH.
- **C.** Fix carbon dioxide into G3P before the Calvin cycle begins.
- **D.** Split water into oxygen and protons inside the lumen.

**Why This Is Correct:** Electrons lose energy as they move through the transport chain, and that energy pumps protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen to build the gradient for ATP synthesis. B gets the proton direction backwards, and NADPH is made at photosystem I, not by proton flow. C misplaces carbon fixation, which happens later in the Calvin cycle. D misidentifies water splitting, which occurs at photosystem II, not along the chain.

> **High-Yield:** Electron transport between the photosystems pumps protons into the thylakoid lumen to power ATP synthase.

**ELI-10:** The electron transport chain between the photosystems is like a bucket brigade carrying a hot coal downhill. questions.stem: In **photosystem I**, the electron that is excited by light is ultimately passed to which molecule?

options.text: Oxygen, where it is released as a waste gas.
NADP+, where it reduces the carrier to form NADPH.
ATP synthase, where it powers the rotation of the enzyme.
Water, where it is stored until the Calvin cycle needs it.

rationales.whyCorrect: Light re-excites the electron, and photosystem I passes it to NADP+ to make NADPH, the reducing power the Calvin cycle needs. A misidentifies oxygen as the electron acceptor. C confuses electron flow with proton flow, since ATP synthase is spun by protons, not electrons. D is wrong because water is split at photosystem II, not used as an electron sink.
rationales.eli10: Photosystem I is like a second boost station for electrons that have run out of energy. After the first ride, the electron is tired and rolling slowly. Light hits photosystem I and gives the electron a fresh push to a higher shelf. From there the electron hops into NADPH, a delivery box that carries it away to build sugar.
rationales.highYield: Photosystem I hands its re-excited electrons to NADP+ to build the NADPH the Calvin cycle needs.

### Q07-06 Photosystem I and NADPH

In **photosystem I**, the electron that is excited by light is ultimately passed to which molecule?

- **A.** Oxygen, where it is released as a waste gas.
- **B.** NADP+, where it reduces the carrier to form NADPH.
- **C.** ATP synthase, where it powers the rotation of the enzyme.
- **D.** Water, where it is stored until the Calvin cycle needs it.

**Correct Answer:** **B.** NADP+, where it reduces the carrier to form NADPH.

**Why This Is Correct:** Light re-excites the electron, and photosystem I passes it to NADP+ to make NADPH, the reducing power the Calvin cycle needs. A misidentifies oxygen as the electron acceptor. C confuses electron flow with proton flow, since ATP synthase is spun by protons, not electrons. D is wrong because water is split at photosystem II, not used as an electron sink.

> **High-Yield:** Photosystem I hands its re-excited electrons to NADP+ to build the NADPH the Calvin cycle needs.

**ELI-10:** Photosystem I is like a second boost station for electrons that have run out of energy. After the first ride, the electron is tired and rolling slowly. questions.stem: During **chemiosmosis** in the thylakoid membrane, the synthesis of ATP by **ATP synthase** is driven by which of the following?

options.text: The direct transfer of electrons from photosystem II to the enzyme.
The splitting of water, which provides phosphate groups for ADP.
The flow of protons down their concentration gradient from the thylakoid lumen through the enzyme.
The binding of carbon dioxide, which releases energy that powers ATP synthesis.

rationales.whyCorrect: Chemiosmosis couples proton flow to ATP synthesis, and protons flood down their gradient from the lumen through ATP synthase, spinning the enzyme. A is wrong because electrons do not enter ATP synthase. B confuses phosphate sources, since water splitting releases oxygen and protons, not phosphate. D misplaces carbon dioxide, which powers nothing directly in the light reactions.
rationales.eli10: Think of protons as marbles crowded onto one side of a wall. The thylakoid membrane is that wall, and the electron transport chain pumps marbles into the space behind it. The marbles want to push back, and they can only escape through tiny turnstiles called ATP synthase. Each marble that squeezes through spins the turnstile and glues a phosphate onto ADP to make ATP. This turnstile trick is called chemiosmosis.
rationales.highYield: Protons flowing out of the thylakoid lumen through ATP synthase drive ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.

questions.stem: For every three turns of the **Calvin cycle**, which of the following best describes what is consumed and produced?

options.text: Three ATP and three NADPH are consumed, and three G3P molecules are released.
Two G3P molecules are consumed to build glucose, and nine ATP are produced.
Carbon dioxide is consumed and oxygen is released as the main product.
Three CO2 molecules are fixed using nine ATP and six NADPH, yielding one net G3P.

rationales.whyCorrect: Each turn fixes one carbon dioxide and consumes three ATP and two NADPH, so three turns consume nine ATP and six NADPH and release one net G3P. A miscounts the ATP and reports three G3P instead of one net. B reverses consumption and production, since G3P is produced, not consumed, and ATP is consumed, not produced. C describes cellular respiration, while oxygen is released in the light reactions, not the Calvin cycle.
rationales.eli10: The Calvin cycle is like a sugar factory with three repeating stations. At the first station, carbon dioxide is captured and attached to a starter molecule. At the second station, ATP and NADPH pay the energy bill to fix the carbon. At the third station, the factory rebuilds its starter molecule so it can run again. Every few laps the factory keeps one sugar molecule as profit, the G3P the plant uses to grow.
rationales.highYield: Three Calvin cycle turns fix three CO2 using nine ATP and six NADPH to produce one net G3P.

questions.stem: In the Calvin cycle, the enzyme **RuBisCO** performs carbon fixation by attaching carbon dioxide to which molecule?

options.text: **RuBP**, a five-carbon molecule, producing two molecules of 3-PGA.
G3P, a three-carbon sugar, producing glucose directly.
NADPH, producing the energy needed for reduction.
ATP, producing the phosphate needed for regeneration.

rationales.whyCorrect: RuBisCO attaches carbon dioxide to RuBP, a five-carbon sugar, and the unstable six-carbon product splits into two molecules of 3-PGA. questions.stem: On a hot, dry day a **C3 plant**'s stomata close, causing oxygen levels to rise inside the leaf. Which of the following is the direct consequence?

options.text: The Calvin cycle speeds up because more oxygen energizes the reactions.
RuBisCO fixes oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, and photorespiration consumes ATP without producing sugar.
Photosystem II splits oxygen instead of water, doubling oxygen production.
The electron transport chain runs in reverse, pumping protons out of the thylakoid.

rationales.whyCorrect: With stomata closed, oxygen accumulates and RuBisCO fixes oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, starting photorespiration, which burns ATP and releases already-fixed carbon without making sugar. A has the consequence backwards, since oxygen does not energize the Calvin cycle. C invents an impossible reaction, because photosystem II never splits oxygen. D contradicts the one-way flow of electrons in the transport chain.
rationales.eli10: RuBisCO is a picky worker that usually grabs carbon dioxide, but on hot dry days it can grab oxygen instead. When it grabs oxygen, the factory wastes energy and makes no sugar, which is photorespiration. It is like a worker who keeps inserting the wrong part into the machine. C4 plants hide the picky worker in cells where carbon dioxide stays high, so the wrong grab almost never happens.
rationales.highYield: Hot dry conditions push RuBisCO to fix oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, wasting ATP in photorespiration.

questions.stem: A plant captures carbon dioxide at night, stores it as an organic acid, and releases it to the Calvin cycle during the day while its stomata stay closed. This strategy, called **CAM**, differs from the **C4** strategy in what way?

options.text: CAM uses RuBisCO, while C4 uses a completely different carbon-fixing enzyme.

questions.stem: A greenhouse grower measures photosynthesis while slowly raising light intensity at a constant, low carbon dioxide level. The rate of photosynthesis rises and then levels off even though light keeps increasing. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The pigments become permanently damaged by the increasing light.
The Calvin cycle produces so much sugar that it blocks the light reactions.
Photosynthesis always stops at a fixed rate regardless of any conditions.
Carbon dioxide has become the **limiting factor**, so additional light no longer increases the rate.

rationales.whyCorrect: The rate of photosynthesis is set by the least available resource, so once carbon dioxide becomes limiting, extra light cannot push the rate higher. A invents permanent damage, which bright but non-damaging light does not cause. B mischaracterizes product inhibition, which is not how the cycle behaves here. C ignores that the rate rises with light before leveling off, which is not a fixed rate.
rationales.eli10: Photosynthesis is like baking bread that needs flour, heat, and time all at once. If you add more flour but the oven is cold, the bread still rises slowly. The factor that is lowest is the one holding everything back, like the shortest leg of a stool. Raising the shortest leg speeds up the whole process until a different leg becomes the new bottleneck.
rationales.highYield: Photosynthesis is limited by the least available factor, so raising any other factor will not help.

questions.stem: A signaling pathway proceeds when an extracellular signal molecule binds a receptor on the target cell, relay proteins pass the message inward, and the cell finally carries out a response such as turning on a gene. questions.stem: A cell's DNA is packaged as loose **chromatin**, which condenses into visible **chromosomes** when **mitosis** begins. Which sequence lists the stages of mitosis in the correct order from beginning to end?

questions.stem: Under a microscope, a researcher watches chromosomes being pulled toward opposite poles of a cell by fibers of the **mitotic spindle** attached to their **kinetochores**. Which stage of mitosis is this cell in?

questions.stem: An animal cell and a plant cell both complete mitosis and now need to divide their cytoplasm during **cytokinesis**. Which mechanism does each cell type use?

options.text: The animal cell builds a cell plate while the plant cell pinches inward with a cleavage furrow.
Both cells pinch inward with a cleavage furrow, but the plant cell seals the pinch with new wall material.
The plant cell splits in half along its rigid wall without adding any new material.
The animal cell pinches inward with a cleavage furrow, while the plant cell builds a cell plate that forms a new wall.

rationales.whyCorrect: Animal cells divide by pinching in with a contractile ring that forms a cleavage furrow, while plant cells cannot pinch because of their rigid wall, so they assemble a cell plate that becomes the new wall. rationales.highYield: Match the mechanism to the constraint, animal cells pinch because they are flexible, plant cells build a plate because their wall is rigid.

questions.stem: After DNA replication, a human cell about to enter mitosis contains 46 chromosomes, each made of two identical **sister chromatids** joined at a **centromere**. How many sister chromatids does the cell contain at this point?

options.text: 92, because each of the 46 chromosomes consists of two sister chromatids.

rationales.whyCorrect: A replicated chromosome contains two sister chromatids, so 46 chromosomes mean 92 chromatids total. B counts only one chromatid per chromosome, C confuses chromatids with chromosome pairs, and D wrongly doubles the count again, since G2 performs no further replication.

rationales.highYield: Chromosome number counts the centromeres, chromatid number counts the copies, so 46 chromosomes after S phase means 92 chromatids.

questions.stem: A drug blocks assembly of the mitotic spindle by disabling its **microtubules**. Which event of mitosis will be disrupted most directly?

options.text: Attachment of chromosomes to the spindle and their separation in prometaphase and anaphase.

rationales.highYield: The spindle is the motor of mitosis, anything that blocks it halts chromosome alignment and separation, not the copying steps.

questions.stem: In a dividing cell, one chromosome fails to attach to spindle fibers from both poles. The M checkpoint should normally block the next step. If the M checkpoint fails, what is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The cell pauses in metaphase until the attachment improves on its own.
The unattached chromosome is copied again so a spare is available.
The chromosome decondenses and the cell returns to prophase.
The cell enters anaphase anyway, producing daughter cells with the wrong number of chromosomes.

rationales.whyCorrect: The M checkpoint holds anaphase until every kinetochore is attached, and when it fails, cells proceed with misattached chromosomes and produce daughters with missing or extra chromosomes. rationales.eli10: Imagine a bus driver whose rule is to count every passenger before closing the door. If the rule is skipped, the bus leaves with a passenger still standing on the platform. rationales.highYield: The M checkpoint exists to prevent anaphase with unattached chromosomes, and its failure is how chromosome number errors arise.

questions.stem: A scientist tracks the levels of a **cyclin** and its partner **cyclin-dependent kinase** in dividing cells. She finds that the cyclin's concentration rises through interphase, peaks as the cell enters **M phase**, and then falls sharply. Which conclusion is best supported by this pattern?

options.text: The cyclin's rise and fall help time entry into mitosis.
The kinase's concentration changes in the same way and drives the cycle alone.
The cyclin is destroyed because it cannot bind its kinase at M phase.
The cyclin level stays low in cells that are dividing rapidly.

rationales.whyCorrect: Cyclins accumulate through interphase and activate their partner kinase, and the cyclin–kinase complex drives entry into mitosis before the cyclin is destroyed, which resets the timer. The kinase's level is steady rather than oscillating, the partnership works best at M phase, and rapidly dividing cells need repeated cyclin peaks, not a constant low.
rationales.eli10: Think of a cyclin as the timer on a microwave. The timer slowly fills, then it hits full and beeps, and then it resets to zero. The beep only happens when the timer is full, and the reset makes the beep possible again later. Cell division runs on the same rising and falling rhythm.
rationales.highYield: Cyclin levels oscillate while kinase levels stay steady, and the cyclin peak is what fires the cell into mitosis.

questions.stem: A mutation makes a growth-promoting protein permanently active, so the cell divides even when no **growth factor** is present. What is such a mutated gene called?

options.text: A tumor suppressor gene, because it turns off the division brake.
An oncogene, because it drives division without a growth signal.
A checkpoint gene, because it pauses the cell cycle.

rationales.whyCorrect: Oncogenes are mutated forms of growth-promoting genes whose products stay active, freeing the cell from the need for growth factor stimulation. Tumor suppressors restrain division, checkpoint genes pause the cycle, and apoptosis genes promote death rather than division.

questions.stem: Two pea plants that are both **heterozygous** (Pp) for flower color are crossed, and both show the purple **phenotype** produced by the **dominant** allele P. Which **genotypic** ratio is expected among the offspring?

rationales.whyCorrect: The law of segregation ensures that each gamete carries only one allele, so the Pp by Pp cross yields offspring in the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio of PP, Pp, and pp. B gives the 3:1 phenotypic ratio for the same cross, which answers a different question. rationales.highYield: A cross between two heterozygotes always produces a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio and a 3:1 dominant to recessive phenotypic ratio.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant shows the dominant phenotype for stem height, but its genotype is unknown. A **test cross** is used to determine whether the plant is **homozygous** dominant (TT) or heterozygous (Tt). Which cross would accomplish this?

options.text: Crossing it with a tall plant of unknown genotype.
Crossing it with a homozygous dominant (TT) plant.
Crossing it with a homozygous recessive dwarf plant (tt).
Observing the plant's height under a microscope to read its genotype directly.

rationales.whyCorrect: A test cross mates the unknown dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive individual, because any recessive allele hidden in the unknown parent will show up in the offspring. If the plant is TT, all offspring are tall, but if it is Tt, half the offspring are dwarf, revealing the genotype. A and B can never expose a hidden recessive allele, and D is wrong because a phenotype cannot be read directly from cells in this way.
rationales.eli10: A test cross is like finding out what is hidden inside a mystery sandwich by feeding half of it to a friend. The friend's sandwich is plain, so any secret ingredient shows up in what they bite into. If the mystery sandwich had a secret ingredient, the friend would bite into it half the time. That is how breeders expose hidden recessive alleles.
rationales.highYield: A test cross always uses a homozygous recessive partner so the unknown parent's hidden alleles are revealed in the offspring's phenotypes.

questions.stem: A person with type AB blood has both A antigens and B antigens on their red blood cells, and neither antigen is a blend of the two. This full expression of both alleles is an example of **codominance**. Which statement correctly explains how the A and B alleles produce this pattern?

options.text: The A and B alleles are incompletely dominant over each other, producing a blended antigen.
The A and B alleles are expressed together in full in the heterozygote.
Both A and B alleles must be homozygous for the AB phenotype to appear.
The AB phenotype appears only when the O allele is also present.

rationales.whyCorrect: Codominance means both alleles are fully expressed in a heterozygote, and that is exactly what happens when both A and B antigens appear on the red blood cells of a person with type AB blood. A describes incomplete dominance, which would blend the antigens into a single new form. C is wrong because the AB genotype is heterozygous, and D is wrong because the O allele produces no antigen at all.
rationales.eli10: Picture a jacket with one red sleeve and one blue sleeve sewn together without any mixing. The jacket is not purple, because each sleeve keeps its full color. That is how codominance works, both traits appear completely at the same time.
rationales.highYield: In codominance both alleles show up fully at once, exactly like the A and B antigens in AB blood.
