questions.stem: Blood type in humans is controlled by three **multiple alleles**, IA, IB, and i, where IA and IB are each dominant to i. A man with type A blood and genotype IAi has a child with a woman who has type B blood and genotype IBi. Which blood types are possible for their child?

options.text: Types A, B, AB, and O are all possible.

rationales.whyCorrect: Each parent passes either of their two alleles, so the IAi by IBi cross can produce IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B), and ii (O) with equal probability. A, B, and D each omit some of the four possible combinations. This is why two parents with types A and B can have a child with any blood type.
rationales.eli10: Think of the blood type genes as three kinds of candy, one red, one blue, and one plain, and each person holds two of them. One parent holds a red and a plain, and the other holds a blue and a plain. Each parent hands the baby one of their two candies. Every mix is possible, so the baby could end up with any of the four blood types.
rationales.highYield: In the ABO system, a cross of IAi by IBi produces all four blood types, each with a one quarter probability.

questions.stem: Color blindness is a **sex-linked** trait caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome, inherited in the **X-linked** pattern. A color-blind man (XbY) and a woman with normal vision who is a carrier (XBXb) have children. What is the probability that a son they have will be color-blind?

rationales.whyCorrect: A son receives his Y chromosome from his father, so the father's X chromosome never reaches him, and the only X a son gets comes from his mother. The mother passes XB or Xb with equal probability, so half of her sons are XbY and color-blind. The father's own color blindness does not affect his sons at all.
rationales.eli10: Think of the X chromosome as a stamp book and the Y chromosome as a blank page. A boy builds his stamp book from his mother only, because his father gives him the blank page. The mother has two stamps, one good and one bad, and she gives one at random. So the boy gets the bad stamp half the time, which is 50 percent.
rationales.highYield: Males get their single X chromosome from their mother, so an X-linked recessive condition is passed from mother to son, never directly from father to son.

questions.stem: A **pedigree** chart shows a rare disorder in which two unaffected parents have an affected son and an affected daughter, and the trait does not appear in any earlier generation. Which mode of inheritance does this pattern most strongly support?

options.text: Autosomal dominant, because a new case of the trait appeared in this generation.
Autosomal recessive, because both unaffected parents must be carriers of the recessive allele.
X-linked dominant, because the affected children include a son.
Polygenic, because several genes could contribute to the disorder.

rationales.whyCorrect: For a rare recessive trait, affected children are homozygous for the recessive allele, and their unaffected parents must both be carriers, which matches this pedigree. An affected daughter rules out X-linked recessive inheritance because her unaffected father would have to pass her an X chromosome carrying the disease allele, which he does not have. Dominant inheritance would require an affected parent, and polygenic traits show a continuous range of variation rather than clear affected and unaffected categories.
rationales.eli10: A pedigree is like a family tree that tracks who shows a secret trait. When both parents look normal but a child shows the trait, each parent must be hiding one copy of the trait gene. Because a daughter shows the trait too, the gene cannot ride on the father's special male chromosome, since he would have shown the trait himself. So the gene hides on a regular chromosome and needs two copies to appear.
rationales.highYield: Two unaffected parents who have affected children, including daughters, is the signature of autosomal recessive inheritance.

questions.stem: A couple is planning to have two children, and both parents are heterozygous (Aa) for a recessive disorder. Using the **sum rule** of probability, what is the chance that exactly one of their two children will be affected (aa)?

rationales.whyCorrect: The chance that any one child is affected is 1/4, and the chance that a child is unaffected is 3/4. Exactly one affected child can occur in two orders, so the sum rule gives (1/4 x 3/4) plus (3/4 x 1/4), which equals 6/16, or 3/8. A is the chance for a single affected child, B is the chance that both are affected, and C is the chance that at least one is affected.
rationales.eli10: Think of a trick coin that lands on heads only one time out of four, and you flip it exactly twice. You want to see exactly one heads, which can happen two ways, heads first or heads second. Each way has its own small chance, and the sum rule says to add the two chances together. The total chance comes out to three out of eight.
rationales.highYield: For two independent children, the probability that exactly one is affected is 1/4 times 3/4 added to 3/4 times 1/4, which comes to 3/8.

questions.stem: Two pea plants that are both RrYy for seed shape (R round, r wrinkled) and seed color (Y yellow, y green) are crossed. Using the **product rule** of probability, what is the probability that an offspring will be round and green (R_ and yy)?

options.text: Signals the ribosome where to begin translation

Codes for the amino acid sequence of the finished protein
Adds the poly-A tail to the mature messenger RNA

rationales.whyCorrect: The promoter is the DNA sequence where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription, while the terminator marks where transcription stops. rationales.highYield: The promoter is the start signal for RNA polymerase, and the terminator is the stop signal.

questions.stem: A newly transcribed eukaryotic pre-mRNA must be processed before it can direct protein synthesis. Which statement correctly describes **mRNA processing**?

options.text: A 5-prime cap is added, but introns are kept in the mature mRNA
The poly-A tail is added to the DNA template strand before transcription begins
A 5-prime cap and a poly-A tail are added, and introns are removed by splicing
Splicing joins introns together and removes the exons from the mRNA

rationales.whyCorrect: Eukaryotic mRNA processing adds a 5-prime cap and a poly-A tail and removes introns through splicing, so the mature message is stable and ready for translation. rationales.eli10: A freshly printed script for a play still has boring stage notes between the real lines. Before the actors can use it, three things happen. The director staples a cover page, the cap, onto the front. A helper tapes a bow at the end, the poly-A tail. An editor crosses out all the stage notes and glues the real lines together, which is splicing.
rationales.highYield: Capping, polyadenylation, and splicing all happen to the mRNA before it leaves the nucleus.

questions.stem: A **frameshift mutation** inserts a single extra nucleotide into the middle of a gene's coding sequence. What is the most likely consequence for the protein that is produced?

options.text: Only the single amino acid at the insertion site changes
Every amino acid after the insertion point changes, and a premature stop codon may appear
The protein sequence is completely unchanged because the mutation is silent
Only the stop codon is removed, so the protein becomes longer

rationales.highYield: A frameshift mutation changes every codon downstream of the insertion, not just one amino acid.

**Correct Answer:** **B.** Activator proteins bound to the enhancer loop the DNA so they contact and stimulate RNA polymerase at the promoter

**Why This Is Correct:** Activator proteins bound at an enhancer bend the DNA into a loop so the enhancer region physically reaches the promoter, where the activators interact with the transcription machinery and boost transcription. A mischaracterizes enhancers as transcribed sequences, and C confuses transcription with translation. D describes methylation-based silencing, the opposite of enhancer action.

> **High-Yield:** Enhancers work from a distance by looping the DNA to bring activator proteins to the promoter.

**ELI-10:** Picture a stadium where the fans in the cheap seats are far from the stage. They unroll one long banner that reaches all the way down to the stage. At the stage, the banner's end prods the singer to sing louder. An enhancer works the same way, reaching across the DNA to cheer on RNA polymerase.

### Q12-11 DNA methylation and gene silencing

In eukaryotic cells, **DNA methylation** of a gene's promoter region is most closely associated with which effect?

- **A.** Speeding up translation of the gene's messenger RNA
- **B.** Loosening the chromatin so transcription factors bind more easily
- **C.** Repressing transcription by making the promoter less accessible
- **D.** Adding the poly-A tail to the gene's pre-mRNA

**Correct Answer:** **C.** Repressing transcription by making the promoter less accessible

**Why This Is Correct:** Methylation of cytosines in promoter regions attracts proteins that compact the chromatin and block the transcription machinery, so the gene is typically silenced. B describes the opposite effect, which belongs to histone acetylation. A confuses transcription with translation, and D describes mRNA processing, which is unrelated to promoter methylation.

> **High-Yield:** DNA methylation compacts chromatin and silences genes, while acetylation loosens chromatin and activates them.

**ELI-10:** A housekeeper with a roll of sticky tape walks through a library of books, the DNA. Wherever a book should not be read, she tapes the cover shut. Readers cannot open that book no matter how hard they pull. Methylation works that way, taping up a gene so the cell leaves it unread.

questions.stem: **MicroRNAs** are short noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription. Which statement best describes how microRNAs work?

options.text: They bind DNA promoters and block RNA polymerase from transcribing the gene
They carry amino acids to the ribosome during translation
They remove introns from pre-mRNA during splicing
They base-pair with target messenger RNAs and block translation or trigger their degradation

rationales.whyCorrect: Mature microRNAs load into the RISC complex, which uses the microRNA as a guide to base-pair with target messenger RNAs and then block their translation or trigger their degradation. A describes a block at the level of transcription, which is not how microRNAs act. B describes tRNA, and C describes the spliceosome, both different molecules with different jobs.
rationales.eli10: A microRNA is like a tiny note taped over a sentence in a cookbook. When the chef tries to read that page, the note covers the words, so no dish is made from that recipe. Sometimes the note also marks the page for shredding. Either way, the dish from that one recipe never appears.
rationales.highYield: MicroRNAs silence genes after transcription by pairing with messenger RNA and blocking its use.

questions.sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
### Q12-12 How microRNAs regulate genes

**MicroRNAs** are short noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription. Which statement best describes how microRNAs work?

- **A.** They bind DNA promoters and block RNA polymerase from transcribing the gene
- **B.** They carry amino acids to the ribosome during translation
- **C.** They remove introns from pre-mRNA during splicing
- **D.** They base-pair with target messenger RNAs and block translation or trigger their degradation

**Correct Answer:** **D.** They base-pair with target messenger RNAs and block translation or trigger their degradation

**Why This Is Correct:** Mature microRNAs load into the RISC complex, which uses the microRNA as a guide to base-pair with target messenger RNAs and then block their translation or trigger their degradation. A describes a block at the level of transcription, which is not how microRNAs act. B describes tRNA, and C describes the spliceosome, both different molecules with different jobs.

> **High-Yield:** MicroRNAs silence genes after transcription by pairing with messenger RNA and blocking its use.

**ELI-10:** A microRNA is like a tiny note taped over a sentence in a cookbook. When the chef tries to read that page, the note covers the words, so no dish is made from that recipe. Sometimes the note also marks the page for shredding. Either way, the dish from that one recipe never appears.

rationales.whyCorrect: RNA polymerase transcribes a DNA template into RNA.
rationales.eli10: The cell copies one recipe onto a working note.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Where is an mRNA code converted into a polypeptide?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ribosomes translate codons and join amino acids.
rationales.eli10: A ribosome reads the note and builds the protein.

options.text: Each new molecule has one old and one new strand

rationales.whyCorrect: Each parental strand templates a complementary new strand.
rationales.eli10: Each new ladder keeps one old rail and builds one new rail.

rationales.whyCorrect: A codon is a three-nucleotide mRNA sequence.
rationales.eli10: The ribosome reads RNA letters in three-letter words.

rationales.whyCorrect: Messenger RNA conveys transcribed genetic information.
rationales.eli10: A working recipe note travels to the protein kitchen.

rationales.whyCorrect: A recessive trait appears only without a dominant allele.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term refers to the smallest unit that is considered to be alive?

rationales.whyCorrect: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; it is the smallest entity that can independently carry out all processes required for living, such as metabolism and reproduction. Molecules and atoms are chemical building blocks but are not themselves alive, while tissues and organs are higher levels of organization built from many cells.
rationales.eli10: Think of a brick wall. A single brick is the smallest piece you can still call 'part of the wall' and stack on its own. In living things, the cell is that single brick, the smallest piece that is still truly alive, while molecules are more like the tiny bits of clay that make up the brick.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes homeostasis?

options.text: The maintenance of stable internal conditions despite outside change
The gradual increase in an organism's overall size and total cell number
The production of new individual organisms from one existing parent
The conversion of food molecules into usable energy inside cells

rationales.whyCorrect: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions, such as temperature, pH, and fluid balance, to keep them within a narrow range even when the outside environment shifts. Option B describes growth, option C describes reproduction, and option D describes metabolism; each is a separate characteristic of life, while homeostasis specifically refers to internal stability.
rationales.eli10: Homeostasis is like a thermostat in your house. If it gets cold, the heater kicks on; if it gets hot, the AC turns on, all to keep the room comfortable. Your body does the same thing, sweating when hot and shivering when cold, to keep its insides just right.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is metabolism considered an essential characteristic of all living things?

options.text: It keeps an organism's DNA sequence from ever changing over time
It allows organisms to reproduce without inheriting any genetic material
It permanently prevents waste products from forming inside living cells
It supplies the energy and materials that sustain other life processes

rationales.whyCorrect: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in an organism, including those that release energy (catabolism) and those that build molecules (anabolism). Without a constant supply of energy and raw materials from metabolism, processes like growth, movement, and homeostasis could not occur. Metabolism does not freeze the DNA sequence, remove the need to inherit genetic material, or eliminate waste production; in fact, metabolic reactions generate wastes such as carbon dioxide.
rationales.eli10: Metabolism is like the kitchen and power plant of your body combined. It breaks down food to release energy and uses the pieces to build and repair you. Without that kitchen running, nothing else, like growing or moving, could happen because there would be no fuel.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does the characteristic of 'response to stimuli' differ from 'homeostasis'?

options.text: Response to stimuli occurs only in plants, while homeostasis occurs only in animal bodies
Response to stimuli answers outside signals, while homeostasis steadies internal conditions
Response to stimuli depends on reproduction, while homeostasis depends on continual growth
Response to stimuli and homeostasis are two different names for one identical internal process

rationales.whyCorrect: Response to stimuli is an organism's reaction to changes or signals in its surroundings, such as a plant bending toward light. Homeostasis is the internal regulation that keeps conditions stable. Although the two often work together, responding to a stimulus is an outward reaction, whereas homeostasis is inward balance.
rationales.eli10: Responding to stimuli is like jerking your hand away from a hot stove, a quick reaction to something outside. Homeostasis is like your body quietly keeping its temperature steady all day. One is reacting to the world; the other is keeping your insides calm and balanced.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between growth and reproduction as characteristics of life is accurate?

options.text: Growth produces new individuals, while reproduction increases an individual's size
Growth increases an individual's size or cell number, while reproduction produces new individuals
Both growth and reproduction always require two parents
Neither growth nor reproduction involves the use of DNA

rationales.whyCorrect: Growth is an increase in an organism's size, often through an increase in the number or size of cells, and it happens within one individual. Reproduction generates new, separate individuals and can be sexual (two parents) or asexual (one parent). Both rely on DNA, but they serve different roles: development versus continuation of the species.
rationales.eli10: Growth is you getting taller each year, one person becoming bigger. Reproduction is making a whole new person, like a plant dropping a seed that becomes a new plant. Getting bigger and making a new one are two different jobs, even though both use the body's instruction book, DNA.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the primary reason DNA (heredity) is included among the shared characteristics of living things?

options.text: It directly senses light and temperature changes in the surrounding environment
It is the only molecule cells can use to store and transfer chemical energy
It carries inherited instructions that direct an organism's form and function
It removes the need for cells to carry out their own metabolic reactions

rationales.whyCorrect: All living things use DNA (in some cases RNA in viruses, which are not considered fully alive) as hereditary material that stores the genetic instructions for building and operating the organism and is passed from parent to offspring. DNA itself does not act as a sensor (option A), ATP rather than DNA is the cell's main energy-transfer molecule (option B), and heredity does not substitute for metabolism (option D).
rationales.eli10: DNA is like a recipe book that parents hand down to their kids. It tells the body how to build itself and how to work, and copies get passed along when living things reproduce. Because every living thing uses this same kind of instruction book, we count it as a sign of life.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which example best illustrates an organism responding to a stimulus?

options.text: A bacterium copying its DNA and dividing into two identical daughter cells
A tree adding a new ring of woody tissue across an entire growing season
A touch-sensitive plant folding its leaves when a passing animal brushes it
A person's liver breaking down stored sugar molecules to release usable energy

rationales.whyCorrect: A touch-sensitive plant (such as Mimosa pudica) folding its leaves when an animal brushes it is a direct, rapid reaction to an external signal, which is the essence of responding to a stimulus. Each of the other options illustrates a different characteristic of life: in option A, a bacterium copying its DNA and dividing into two daughter cells is reproduction; in option B, a tree adding a ring of woody tissue over a season is growth; and in option D, the liver breaking down stored sugar to release energy is metabolism.
rationales.eli10: A stimulus is a signal that makes something react. When a touch-sensitive plant snaps its leaves shut the instant an animal brushes past, it is reacting to that touch, just like you flinch when something pokes you. The bacterium splitting into two daughter cells is making more of itself (reproduction), the new ring of wood is the tree getting bigger (growth), and the liver breaking down sugar is the body making energy (metabolism).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A student examines a structure made of several tissues that work together to perform digestion. At which level of biological organization is this structure best classified?

rationales.whyCorrect: An organ is a structure composed of two or more tissue types that function together to perform a specific task, such as the stomach carrying out part of digestion. A single tissue is a group of similar cells working together, while an organ system is multiple organs working together, so the described structure fits the organ level.
rationales.eli10: One kind of fabric is a tissue. Sew several kinds of fabric together into a working jacket with a zipper and pockets, and you have made an organ. The stomach is like that jacket, different tissues combined into one useful body part. Many such parts together would be a whole organ system.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A scientist observes an object that uses energy, grows, responds to its surroundings, maintains internal balance, and reproduces. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The object is living only if it can also survive without any energy
The object is nonliving because only cells can grow
The object cannot be classified without knowing its color
The object is a living organism because it shows the characteristics of life

rationales.whyCorrect: Biologists identify life by a shared set of characteristics, including organization, metabolism, growth, response to stimuli, homeostasis, and reproduction. An object displaying all of these is classified as living. The distractors misstate the criteria, since living things require energy rather than functioning without it.
rationales.eli10: Scientists use a checklist to decide if something is alive: does it use energy, grow, react, keep its insides balanced, and make more of itself? If it checks every box, it is alive. This object checks them all, so it counts as a living thing, no matter its color.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A virus contains genetic material and can evolve, yet most biologists do not classify it as fully living. Which feature best accounts for this?

options.text: They lack a nucleus, and only organisms with a nucleus are considered alive
They lack independent metabolism and cannot reproduce without hijacking a host cell
They carry RNA rather than DNA, and DNA is required for life
They consist of a single cell that lacks organelles

rationales.whyCorrect: Although viruses possess genetic material and evolve, they cannot perform metabolism or reproduce independently; they must commandeer a living host cell's machinery to make copies of themselves. Because they fail to meet key characteristics of life on their own, most biologists regard them as being at the border between living and nonliving. The other options misstate the criteria: lacking a nucleus (option A) does not disqualify something from being alive, since bacteria are alive without one; plenty of viruses carry DNA rather than RNA, and RNA can serve as hereditary material (option C); and viruses are not cells at all, so describing one as a cell without organelles (option D) is inaccurate.
rationales.eli10: A virus is like a USB stick with instructions but no computer. On its own it can't do anything, no growing, no making energy, no copying. It only works when it plugs into a real cell and borrows that cell's machinery. Since it can't live on its own, we don't count it as fully alive.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What would most likely happen to a multicellular organism if its cells completely lost the ability to maintain homeostasis?

options.text: Metabolic demand would fall to zero, letting the organism survive without energy
Reproduction rates would rise sharply to compensate for the unstable conditions
Internal conditions would drift beyond safe ranges, disrupting reactions and survival
The cells would immediately reorganize into a higher, more stable level of organization

rationales.whyCorrect: Homeostasis keeps variables like temperature, pH, and ion concentrations within the narrow ranges that enzymes and other cellular processes require. If cells could no longer regulate these conditions, biochemical reactions would fail, cellular function would collapse, and the organism's survival would be jeopardized. Losing regulation does not abolish the need for energy (option A), speed up reproduction (option B), or push cells into a higher level of organization (option D).
rationales.eli10: Your cells are like a fish tank that needs the water kept just right. Homeostasis is the filter and heater keeping it perfect. Turn those off and the water gets too hot, too dirty, or too acidic, and the fish get sick and die. Without homeostasis, a body's inside gets out of balance and stops working.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the cell membrane (plasma membrane)?

options.text: A rigid protein wall that gives the cell its fixed shape
A phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves the cell
A solid layer of carbohydrates that stores the cell's energy
A network of protein tubes that moves organelles around the cell

rationales.whyCorrect: The plasma membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that acts as a selectively permeable barrier, regulating the passage of substances into and out of the cell. This selective permeability maintains the internal environment (homeostasis) the cell needs to function. Option A is wrong on two counts: the membrane is flexible, not rigid, and the rigid outer layer some cells do have (the cell wall, absent in animal cells) is built from carbohydrates such as cellulose, not from protein. Option C describes storage molecules such as glycogen or starch, and option D describes the cytoskeleton.
rationales.eli10: Think of the cell membrane like a security fence with gates around a house. It is not solid and stiff; it is flexible, and the gates decide who gets in and who stays out. That gatekeeping is called being selectively permeable, and it keeps the inside of the cell just the way it needs to be.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell' because it produces most of the cell's ATP?

rationales.whyCorrect: The mitochondrion carries out cellular respiration, using oxygen and glucose breakdown products to generate most of the cell's ATP, the molecule that powers cellular work. This is why it is nicknamed the powerhouse of the cell. Ribosomes build proteins, the Golgi packages proteins, and lysosomes digest waste, so none of those are the main ATP producers.
rationales.eli10: The mitochondrion is like the power plant of a city. Just as a power plant turns fuel into electricity for everyone to use, the mitochondrion turns food energy into ATP, the tiny battery packs that run everything the cell does.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term refers to the gel-like fluid that fills the inside of a cell and surrounds the organelles?

rationales.whyCorrect: Cytoplasm is the semi-fluid substance (cytosol plus organelles) that fills the cell between the plasma membrane and the nucleus, providing the medium in which organelles sit and many metabolic reactions occur. Nucleoplasm is the fluid inside the nucleus specifically, the extracellular matrix is outside the cell, and the cell wall is an external structure found in plants, fungi, and some other organisms.
rationales.eli10: Cytoplasm is like the water inside a snow globe. The little figures floating inside are the organelles, and the fluid holds them in place and lets things move around. It fills up the space so the cell is not just an empty bag.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the nucleus in a eukaryotic cell?

options.text: To break down old organelles and cellular debris
To package and ship proteins to their destinations
To store the cell's DNA and direct protein synthesis
To generate energy through the breakdown of glucose

rationales.whyCorrect: The nucleus houses the cell's DNA and controls gene expression, transcribing DNA into messenger RNA that then directs protein synthesis at the ribosomes. Because proteins determine cell structure and function, the nucleus effectively acts as the cell's control center. The other options describe lysosomes, the Golgi apparatus, and mitochondria respectively.
rationales.eli10: The nucleus is like the manager's office that holds the master instruction manual (the DNA). The manager does not build things directly, but sends out copies of the instructions so the workers (ribosomes) know exactly what proteins to make. Control the instructions, and you control the whole cell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between rough endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER) and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (smooth ER) is accurate?

options.text: Rough ER synthesizes membrane lipids, while smooth ER folds and glycosylates proteins
Rough ER stores calcium ions, while smooth ER produces most of the cell's ATP
Both ER types are studded with ribosomes and differ only in their tubule diameter
Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER lacks them and makes lipids

rationales.whyCorrect: Rough ER appears rough because ribosomes stud its surface; these ribosomes synthesize proteins that are threaded into the ER for folding and modification. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and specializes in lipid synthesis, detoxification, and (in some cells) calcium storage. This division of labor is the key structural and functional difference between the two.
rationales.eli10: Picture two factory hallways. One hallway is covered in little machines (ribosomes) that snap together proteins, so it looks bumpy or rough. The other hallway has no bumps and instead mixes up fats and cleans up toxins. Same building, two different jobs, and the bumps tell you which is which.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change would most likely cause a cell to lose its ability to break down worn-out organelles and cellular waste?

options.text: A thicker layer of phospholipids in the cell membrane
An increase in the number of ribosomes
A larger, more folded mitochondrial inner membrane
A defect in the digestive enzymes inside lysosomes

rationales.whyCorrect: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes that break down damaged organelles, macromolecules, and cellular debris for recycling. If those enzymes are defective, the cell cannot digest waste, which is exactly what happens in lysosomal storage diseases. The other changes affect protein synthesis, energy production, or membrane thickness, not waste breakdown.
rationales.eli10: Lysosomes are the cell's recycling and garbage crew, and their tools are special enzymes that chop up junk. If the tools are broken, the trash just piles up inside the cell. That is why a problem with lysosome enzymes stops the clean-up, not a problem with the power plant or the fence.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells is accurate?

options.text: Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles, while prokaryotic cells do not
Prokaryotic cells enclose their DNA in a true nucleus, while eukaryotic cells do not
Only prokaryotic cells build ribosomes, while eukaryotic cells have none at all
Eukaryotic cells contain no DNA at all, while prokaryotic cells carry chromosomes

rationales.whyCorrect: The defining difference is that eukaryotic cells contain a true membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi), whereas prokaryotic cells lack these and keep their DNA in a nucleoid region. Both cell types have DNA and ribosomes, so those options are false, and it is eukaryotes, not prokaryotes, that have a nucleus.
rationales.eli10: Think of a prokaryotic cell as a studio apartment: everything is in one open room. A eukaryotic cell is like a house with separate rooms (organelles) that each have walls and doors. Both have people and stuff inside, but only the house divides the work into closed-off rooms.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher examines a cell and finds it contains an unusually large number of mitochondria. Which type of cell is this most likely to be?

options.text: A dead skin cell that no longer performs active functions
A muscle cell that must contract repeatedly and requires lots of energy
A cell whose main job is to store fat for insulation
A red blood cell that simply carries oxygen through the bloodstream

rationales.whyCorrect: Cells with high energy demands contain many mitochondria because these organelles produce the ATP needed to power their activity. Muscle cells contract frequently and therefore need abundant ATP, so they are packed with mitochondria. Dead skin cells are inactive, mature red blood cells actually lack mitochondria, and fat-storage cells are not especially energy-hungry.
rationales.eli10: The more work a cell does, the more power plants (mitochondria) it needs. A muscle cell is like a busy factory running all day, so it needs lots of power plants to keep the lights on. If you find tons of mitochondria, you have probably found a very hardworking, energy-hungry cell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a cell that secretes large amounts of protein hormones, which pathway correctly traces how a protein travels before it is released from the cell?

options.text: Ribosome on rough ER to Golgi apparatus to cell membrane
Mitochondrion to ribosome to nucleus to cell membrane
Golgi apparatus to ribosome to lysosome to cell membrane
Lysosome to smooth ER to nucleus to cell membrane

rationales.whyCorrect: Secreted proteins are synthesized by ribosomes on the rough ER, then transported in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus for modification, sorting, and packaging, and finally shipped in vesicles to the plasma membrane for release by exocytosis. This is the endomembrane secretory pathway. The other sequences scramble the order or include organelles (mitochondria, lysosomes) that are not part of the secretory route.
rationales.eli10: Making and shipping a protein is like an assembly line. The rough ER machines build it, the Golgi is the packaging and shipping department that labels and boxes it, and then the box travels to the cell membrane to be mailed out. The order matters: build, package, ship.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which example best illustrates the principle that a cell's structure is suited to its function?

options.text: A red blood cell has a nucleus that lets it divide rapidly in the bloodstream
A cheek cell has a thick cell wall that gives it a rigid shape
A nerve cell has long extensions that carry electrical signals over distances
A sperm cell is round and immobile to conserve its energy

rationales.whyCorrect: Structure-function relationships mean a cell's shape reflects its job. Neurons have long axons and dendrites precisely so they can transmit signals across long distances in the body, a clear match of form to function. The other options are factually wrong: mature red blood cells lack a nucleus, human cheek cells have no cell wall, and sperm cells are motile with a flagellum.
rationales.eli10: In biology, a cell's shape usually gives away its job, like how a fork looks different from a spoon because they do different things. A nerve cell is stretched out long like a wire because its job is to carry messages far across the body. The shape is the clue to the job.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What would happen if a cell's ribosomes were completely disabled?

options.text: The cell would continue functioning normally by using stored proteins forever
The cell would be unable to make new proteins, halting most of its activities
The cell would immediately swell and burst from water intake
The cell would switch to producing energy without needing enzymes

rationales.whyCorrect: Ribosomes translate messenger RNA into proteins, and proteins serve as enzymes, structural components, transporters, and signals essential to virtually all cellular processes. Without functioning ribosomes, no new proteins (including the enzymes that drive metabolism) could be made, so the cell's activities would grind to a halt and it could not sustain itself. Stored proteins are eventually degraded and cannot be replaced, so the cell cannot continue indefinitely.
rationales.eli10: Ribosomes are the builders that read the instructions and put proteins together, and proteins do almost every job in the cell, including speeding up reactions as enzymes. Turn off the builders and no new tools get made; as the old tools wear out, the whole cell slowly stops working. Nearly everything depends on that protein-building step.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A plant cell is placed in pure water and takes in water, yet it does not burst the way an animal cell in the same water would. Which structural difference best explains this outcome?

options.text: The plant cell uses extra mitochondria to actively pump the excess water back out
The plant cell's chloroplasts soak up and store all of the incoming water
The plant cell has no plasma membrane, so water flows straight through without building pressure
The plant cell's rigid cell wall limits swelling and pushes back against the incoming water

rationales.whyCorrect: As water enters by osmosis, the plant cell's rigid cell wall physically limits how much the cell can swell and generates turgor pressure that opposes further water entry, preventing rupture. An animal cell lacks a cell wall, so it keeps swelling and can lyse (burst). The other options are incorrect because mitochondria do not pump water, all cells have a plasma membrane, and chloroplasts do not store incoming water.
rationales.eli10: Imagine filling a water balloon inside a sturdy cardboard box. The balloon (the membrane) wants to keep growing, but the box (the cell wall) only lets it get so big before pushing back, so it never pops. An animal cell has no box around it, so it just keeps swelling until it bursts.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term describes the movement of a solute from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration without the direct use of cellular energy?

rationales.whyCorrect: Simple diffusion is the passive net movement of particles down their concentration gradient, driven by the kinetic energy of the molecules themselves rather than ATP. Because it moves substances from high to low concentration, no cellular energy input is required. Active transport, by contrast, requires ATP because it moves substances against their gradient.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a crowded room where people spread out into the empty hallway just because there is more space there. Nobody has to push them; they move on their own from the packed spot to the roomy spot. That natural spreading from crowded to empty is simple diffusion, and it costs the cell no energy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a membrane transport protein such as a channel or carrier protein?

options.text: To generate the cell's ATP supply by oxidizing glucose in the cytoplasm
To unwind and copy the cell's DNA strands before it divides in mitosis
To move specific solutes across the membrane's hydrophobic interior
To digest worn-out organelles and cellular debris inside the lysosome

rationales.whyCorrect: The phospholipid bilayer's hydrophobic core blocks charged ions and large polar molecules from passing freely. Transport proteins provide selective pathways or binding sites that allow these substances to cross, a process called facilitated transport. This selectivity is central to the membrane's role as a semipermeable barrier.
rationales.eli10: The cell membrane is like a wall with an oily middle that water-loving things cannot swim through. Transport proteins are like special doors built into the wall that let certain guests pass. Without those doors, ions and sugars would be stuck outside.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly defines osmosis?

options.text: The active pumping of ions across a membrane using ATP
The engulfing of large particles by the cell membrane
The diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane
The movement of glucose through a carrier protein

rationales.whyCorrect: Osmosis is specifically the passive movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of higher water concentration (lower solute) to lower water concentration (higher solute). It is a special case of diffusion involving the solvent, water, rather than a solute. No ATP is required because water moves down its own concentration gradient.
rationales.eli10: Osmosis is just water doing diffusion. If one side of a wall has lots of water and the other side is crowded with salt, water sneaks across to even things out. It is the water, not the salt, that does the traveling.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. Which change would most likely occur to the cell?

options.text: The cell will shrink and shrivel
The cell will swell and possibly burst
The cell will remain exactly the same size
The cell will actively pump water inward

rationales.whyCorrect: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration outside the cell than inside, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis to where solute is more concentrated. Losing water causes an animal cell to shrink or crenate. This illustrates how tonicity predicts the direction of net water movement.
rationales.eli10: Water always drifts toward the saltier side. Outside the cell is extra salty, so water leaves the cell to go there, and the cell dries up like a raisin. Hyper means the outside has more stuff dissolved in it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between active transport and facilitated diffusion is accurate?

options.text: Both carry solutes uphill against their gradients, and both hydrolyze ATP to do so
Active transport spends ATP to move solutes uphill; facilitated diffusion is passive
Facilitated diffusion hydrolyzes ATP, whereas active transport needs no energy source
Both move solutes straight through the lipid bilayer without any protein involvement

rationales.whyCorrect: Active transport uses energy, typically ATP, to move solutes from low to high concentration, working against the gradient. Facilitated diffusion is passive, using membrane proteins to move solutes down their gradient with no energy cost. Both rely on proteins, but only active transport requires an energy source.
rationales.eli10: Going downhill on a bike is free and easy, like facilitated diffusion following the gradient. Pedaling uphill takes effort and fuel, like active transport pushing against the gradient using ATP. Both use a path (a protein), but only the uphill trip needs energy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 sodium ions out of the cell and 2 potassium ions into the cell, both against their gradients. Why must this process use ATP?

options.text: Because water is following the ions by osmosis
Because the ions are too small to fit through channels
Because the ions are moving from low to high concentration

rationales.whyCorrect: Moving a solute against its electrochemical gradient, from lower to higher concentration, is energetically unfavorable and cannot happen spontaneously. The pump uses the energy released by ATP hydrolysis to drive this uphill movement. This is the defining feature of primary active transport.
rationales.eli10: Rolling a ball uphill never happens by itself; you have to spend energy to push it. The pump is shoving ions uphill to where they are already crowded, so it must burn ATP fuel to do it. If it were downhill, no fuel would be needed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which example best illustrates paracrine signaling?

options.text: A hormone released into the bloodstream that travels to a distant organ
A cell secreting a growth factor that diffuses a short distance to affect neighboring cells
A cell releasing a signal that binds receptors on the same cell that released it
Two cells communicating through direct membrane-to-membrane contact

rationales.whyCorrect: Paracrine signaling involves a signaling molecule that acts on target cells in the local vicinity of the releasing cell, diffusing only a short distance through the extracellular fluid. A secreted growth factor acting on nearby cells is a classic example. Endocrine signaling uses the bloodstream for long distances, autocrine signaling targets the releasing cell itself, and direct-contact signaling requires physical connection between cells.
rationales.eli10: Paracrine signaling is like whispering to the people sitting right next to you; only nearby cells hear the message. A cell releasing a chemical that drifts a tiny distance to its neighbors is that short whisper. Hormones carried in the blood are more like a loudspeaker heard far away.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A plant cell and an animal cell are both placed in pure distilled water. What would happen to each, and why?

options.text: Both burst, because neither cell can resist the inward rush of water
Both shrink, because water always exits cells placed in distilled water
The animal cell may burst, but the plant cell's wall resists bursting
Neither changes size, because distilled water is isotonic to the cytoplasm

rationales.whyCorrect: Distilled water is hypotonic to both cells, so water enters each by osmosis. The animal cell, lacking a wall, can swell and lyse (burst). The plant cell's rigid cell wall resists expansion, building turgor pressure that stops further water entry and keeps the cell intact.
rationales.eli10: Both cells drink in water because the outside is super watery. The animal cell is like a water balloon with no support, so it can pop. The plant cell wears a stiff jacket (the cell wall) that stops it from overfilling, so it just gets firm instead of bursting.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher observes that a cell takes in droplets of extracellular fluid along with dissolved substances by forming small vesicles from the plasma membrane. Which process is this cell using?

rationales.whyCorrect: Pinocytosis, or cell drinking, is a form of endocytosis in which the membrane invaginates to form vesicles containing extracellular fluid and its dissolved solutes. It brings material into the cell, unlike exocytosis, which expels material. It is nonselective and involves the formation of small vesicles.
rationales.eli10: Pinocytosis means the cell drinking. The membrane dips inward and pinches off a tiny bubble filled with the liquid around the cell, sipping it inside. Endo means in, exo means out, so this is the taking-in kind.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hormone binds to a receptor on the outer surface of a cell and triggers a chain of internal molecular changes that ultimately alters gene expression. What is the general name for this multi-step process?

rationales.whyCorrect: Signal transduction is the process by which an extracellular signal binding a receptor is converted into a cascade of intracellular events that produce a cellular response. It typically involves reception, transduction through relay molecules, and a response such as changed gene expression. This allows cells to respond to signals that cannot themselves enter the cell.
rationales.eli10: A signal outside the cell is like a doorbell being pushed; the person inside cannot see who is there but the ring sets off a chain of actions indoors. Signal transduction is that chain, turning the outside message into an inside response, step by step.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A drug blocks the ATP-binding site of a membrane pump that normally maintains a steep concentration gradient of an ion across the cell membrane. Over time, what would most likely happen to that gradient, and why?

options.text: The gradient would dissipate as the ion leaks downhill with no pump to restore it
The gradient would grow steeper because passive leakage through channels speeds up
The gradient would hold steady because osmosis of water preserves the imbalance
The gradient would reverse at once because the blocked pump now runs in reverse

rationales.whyCorrect: Active transport pumps continuously counteract the passive leakage of ions down their gradients. Blocking ATP binding disables the pump, so the ion slowly diffuses through channels and leaks toward equilibrium with nothing to restore the imbalance. Over time the concentration gradient collapses because maintaining it requires ongoing energy expenditure.
rationales.eli10: Keeping ions crowded on one side is like bailing water out of a leaky boat; you have to keep working or the water creeps back in. Stop the pump (stop bailing) and the ions slowly leak back until both sides are even. The gradient fades because nobody is doing the uphill work anymore.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cells lining the small intestine absorb glucose from the gut even when glucose is already more concentrated inside the cell than in the gut. This uphill glucose movement is powered by the simultaneous flow of sodium down its gradient into the cell. Which type of transport does this describe?

rationales.whyCorrect: Secondary active transport uses the energy stored in one substance's electrochemical gradient, here sodium moving downhill, to drive another substance, glucose, against its own gradient. The sodium gradient itself was established earlier by ATP-powered primary active transport, so the energy is indirect. This coupling of a downhill and an uphill movement through the same carrier is called cotransport.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a water wheel: rushing water flowing downhill turns the wheel, and the wheel lifts buckets uphill. Sodium rushing into the cell is the downhill water, and it drags glucose uphill along with it. The energy came earlier from a pump using ATP, so this indirect method is secondary active transport.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term describes a threadlike structure made of tightly coiled DNA and protein that carries genetic information?

rationales.whyCorrect: A chromosome is DNA wound around histone proteins and condensed into a compact, transportable structure that carries an organism's genes. Ribosomes build proteins, nucleotides are the individual building blocks of DNA, and centrioles help organize cell division, so none of those carry the genome. Recognizing this basic definition is the foundation for understanding how genetic disorders arise when chromosomes are altered.
rationales.eli10: Imagine your DNA is a super long shoelace of instructions. If you left it loose it would tangle everywhere, so the cell winds it up neatly around little spools of protein into a tidy bundle called a chromosome. That bundle is how the cell packs and carries all its instructions without making a mess.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many chromosomes are found in a typical human body (somatic) cell?

rationales.whyCorrect: Typical human somatic cells are diploid, containing 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs (22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes). The value 23 describes a haploid gamete (egg or sperm), and 44 refers only to the autosomes, ignoring the sex chromosomes. Knowing the normal chromosome number is essential for recognizing conditions caused by having too many or too few.
rationales.eli10: You got one full set of instruction bundles from your mom and one full set from your dad. Each parent gives 23, and 23 plus 23 makes 46. So almost every cell in your body carries 46 bundles, lined up as 23 matching pairs like socks.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies the sex chromosome combination typically associated with a biologically male human?

options.text: One X and one Y chromosome (XY)

rationales.whyCorrect: In humans, biological males typically carry one X and one Y sex chromosome, while biological females typically carry two X chromosomes. A single X (X only) describes Turner syndrome, and a viable human cannot survive with only a Y chromosome because the X carries essential genes. Understanding normal sex-chromosome patterns is the basis for understanding sex-chromosome disorders.
rationales.eli10: Think of the last pair of bundles as the ones that help set biological sex. Girls usually get a matching pair, X and X. Boys usually get a mismatched pair, one X and one Y. The little Y bundle is the one that tips development toward male.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the underlying cause of most cases of Down syndrome (trisomy 21)?

options.text: A single incorrect DNA base in the beta-globin gene
An extra copy of chromosome 21 due to nondisjunction
A missing piece deleted from the end of chromosome 21
Two X chromosomes present in a male cell

rationales.whyCorrect: Down syndrome most commonly results from nondisjunction, the failure of chromosome 21 to separate properly during meiosis, leaving a gamete with an extra copy so the resulting cell has three chromosome 21s. This is an aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number), not a single-base mutation or a simple deletion. A single-base change describes conditions like sickle cell disease, illustrating the difference between whole-chromosome and gene-level errors.
rationales.eli10: When sex cells are made, each pair of bundles is supposed to split so one goes each way, like fairly dealing cards. Sometimes a pair sticks together and both go into one cell. If that cell later joins another, the new person ends up with three copies of bundle number 21 instead of two, and that extra copy causes Down syndrome.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between autosomes and sex chromosomes is accurate?

options.text: Autosomes determine biological sex, while sex chromosomes do not
Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes
Sex chromosomes are always identical in every person
Autosomes are found only in gametes, not in body cells

rationales.whyCorrect: Of the 23 human chromosome pairs, 22 pairs are autosomes and 1 pair is the sex chromosomes, which are the pair that helps determine biological sex. Sex chromosomes are not always identical (XY males have two different ones), and autosomes are present in both body cells and gametes. This distinction matters because disorders are often classified by whether they involve autosomes or sex chromosomes.
rationales.eli10: Out of your 23 pairs of bundles, 22 pairs handle everyday body-building jobs; those are the autosomes. Only the last pair also carries the instructions that help decide biological sex. That last pair still does plenty of other everyday jobs too, like carrying genes for blood clotting and color vision. So it's 22 regular pairs plus 1 pair that adds the sex job on top.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A karyotype shows only 45 chromosomes with a single X and no second sex chromosome. This finding is characteristic of which condition?

rationales.whyCorrect: Turner syndrome is a monosomy caused by having a single X chromosome (45,X) with no second sex chromosome. Klinefelter syndrome is the opposite pattern (an extra X, 47,XXY), while Down and Edwards syndromes are autosomal trisomies (extra chromosome 21 and 18, respectively). Reading the sex-chromosome count on a karyotype lets you distinguish these conditions.
rationales.eli10: A karyotype is like a class photo where all the chromosome bundles line up so you can count them. If the picture shows just one X on the sex-chromosome team instead of the usual two, that missing partner points to Turner syndrome. One lonely X, no teammate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change would most likely produce a chromosomal (rather than a single-gene) disorder?

options.text: A substitution of one DNA base for another within a gene
The addition of a methyl group that turns a single gene off
The failure of a chromosome pair to separate during meiosis
A three-base deletion inside a single gene

rationales.whyCorrect: Chromosomal disorders involve changes in the number or large-scale structure of whole chromosomes, and nondisjunction during meiosis produces gametes with an abnormal chromosome number (aneuploidy). A base substitution, a three-base deletion inside one gene, and methylation of one gene are gene-level or epigenetic events affecting far smaller amounts of genetic material. This contrast highlights the scale difference between chromosomal and single-gene disorders.
rationales.eli10: Think of your genes as words and chromosomes as whole books. Changing one letter in a word, or dropping a few letters from it, is still a small gene-level change. But if an entire book gets copied twice or goes missing when cells split, that's a chromosome-level problem, and that whole-book mistake happens when a pair fails to separate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During meiosis, a chromosome 18 pair fails to separate, so one gamete receives an extra chromosome 18. If this gamete is fertilized by a normal gamete, what will the resulting cell contain?

options.text: A monosomy with only one copy of chromosome 18
A normal set with two copies of chromosome 18
A trisomy with three copies of chromosome 18

rationales.whyCorrect: The abnormal gamete carries two copies of chromosome 18, and the normal gamete adds one more, giving the zygote three copies, a trisomy (specifically trisomy 18, Edwards syndrome). Monosomy would result from the gamete that received no copy, and a normal outcome would require each gamete to contribute exactly one. This traces the direct consequence of nondisjunction to the offspring's chromosome number.
rationales.eli10: One parent's cell accidentally packed two copies of book 18 instead of one. The other parent's cell brought the normal single copy. Two plus one equals three copies of book 18 in the new cell, and having three of one book is called a trisomy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A karyotype report describes that a segment broke off the short arm of chromosome 5 and was lost. Which type of chromosomal change does this describe?

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Autosomal trisomies of chromosome 21 (Down syndrome) are compatible with survival, while trisomies of most other autosomes are usually not. Which explanation best accounts for why extra sex chromosomes (such as XXY) are also often survivable?

options.text: Extra X chromosomes are largely inactivated, reducing the gene-dosage imbalance
The Y chromosome silences all extra genes on additional X chromosomes
Sex chromosomes contain no genes, so extra copies have no effect
Sex chromosomes are always smaller than every autosome present

rationales.whyCorrect: In cells with more than one X chromosome, the extra X chromosomes are largely condensed and inactivated (forming Barr bodies), which greatly limits the excess gene expression, or dosage imbalance, that makes most other aneuploidies lethal. The Y is gene-poor rather than acting to silence Xs, and sex chromosomes certainly do carry genes. This explains why sex-chromosome aneuploidies are generally milder and more survivable than most autosomal trisomies.
rationales.eli10: Having extra copies of a busy book usually overwhelms the cell with too many instructions. But the body has a clever trick: when there are extra X books, it mostly shuts the spare ones down so only one stays open. With the extras turned off, the flood of duplicate instructions is much smaller, so the cell copes far better.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Most cases of Down syndrome result from nondisjunction, but a small percentage occur when a segment of chromosome 21 becomes attached to another chromosome (commonly chromosome 14) and can be passed down from a physically unaffected carrier parent. What type of chromosomal change does this describe?

rationales.whyCorrect: A translocation occurs when a segment of one chromosome breaks off and joins a different (nonhomologous) chromosome; in translocation Down syndrome, extra chromosome 21 material is fused to another chromosome such as 14. Because a parent can carry a balanced version with the normal amount of genetic material and no symptoms, this form can be inherited, unlike the random, age-related nondisjunction that causes most cases. Monosomy and nondisjunction change chromosome number rather than reattaching a segment, and a point mutation alters just one DNA base, far too small to describe this whole-segment rearrangement.
rationales.eli10: Usually Down syndrome happens by accident when chromosome bundle 21 fails to split evenly. But sometimes a chunk of book 21 gets glued onto a different book, like book 14. A parent can carry this glued-together arrangement without any problems and then pass the extra 21 material to a child. Moving a piece of one chromosome onto another is called a translocation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term best describes a specific segment of DNA that contains the instructions for making a functional product, such as a protein?

rationales.whyCorrect: A gene is the basic unit of heredity: a segment of DNA that codes for a functional product, typically a polypeptide or a functional RNA molecule. A chromosome is a much larger structure containing many genes, a nucleotide is the individual building block of DNA, and a ribosome is the cellular machine that builds proteins. Distinguishing these levels of organization is fundamental to understanding gene expression.
rationales.eli10: Think of your DNA as a whole shelf of cookbooks. A gene is one single recipe inside one of those books that tells the cell how to make one thing, like a specific protein. One entire book on the shelf is like a chromosome, a single letter on the page is like a nucleotide, and the cook following the recipe is like a ribosome. So the recipe itself is the gene.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In DNA, which base pairing rule is correct?

options.text: Adenine pairs with cytosine; guanine pairs with thymine
Adenine pairs with guanine; cytosine pairs with thymine
Adenine pairs with uracil; cytosine pairs with guanine
Adenine pairs with thymine; cytosine pairs with guanine

rationales.whyCorrect: In DNA, complementary base pairing follows the rule that adenine (A) bonds with thymine (T) and cytosine (C) bonds with guanine (G), held together by hydrogen bonds. This complementarity underlies accurate DNA replication and transcription. Uracil replaces thymine only in RNA, not DNA, which is why choice C is incorrect for DNA.
rationales.eli10: The two sides of the DNA ladder fit together like puzzle pieces that only match certain partners. A always holds hands with T, and C always holds hands with G. They never switch partners. Uracil (U) only shows up in RNA, not DNA, so it does not belong here.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the primary purpose of transcription in gene expression?

options.text: To copy the entire DNA molecule before cell division
To join amino acids together into a polypeptide chain
To make a messenger RNA copy of a gene's DNA sequence
To split a protein into its individual amino acids

rationales.whyCorrect: Transcription is the process in which the enzyme RNA polymerase synthesizes a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule using a gene's DNA as a template. This mRNA then carries the genetic message out to the ribosome. Copying the whole genome is DNA replication (choice A), and joining amino acids is translation (choice B), which are separate processes.
rationales.eli10: Imagine the master recipe book (DNA) is too precious to take out of the library. So you write down just the one recipe you need onto a sticky note (mRNA) and carry that copy to the kitchen. Transcription is the act of copying that one recipe from the book onto the note.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately compares transcription and translation?

options.text: Transcription makes protein from RNA; translation makes RNA from DNA
Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template; translation makes protein from an mRNA template
Both processes take place only inside the nucleus of the cell
Transcription requires ribosomes, while translation requires RNA polymerase

rationales.whyCorrect: Transcription uses DNA as a template to build RNA, while translation uses the mRNA as a template to assemble amino acids into a protein at the ribosome. In eukaryotes, transcription occurs in the nucleus and translation occurs in the cytoplasm, so they are not both nuclear (choice C). Choice D reverses the machinery: RNA polymerase drives transcription and ribosomes drive translation.
rationales.eli10: These are two steps in a relay race. First, transcription copies the DNA recipe into an RNA note. Second, translation reads that RNA note and builds the actual protein, one amino acid at a time. The order matters: the usual direction of information flow is DNA to RNA to protein.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A codon is a sequence of three mRNA bases. What does each codon specify during translation?

options.text: One amino acid (or a start/stop signal)
One nucleotide to add to the DNA
One gene to be transcribed next

rationales.whyCorrect: The genetic code is read in triplets called codons, and each codon corresponds to one amino acid or to a start/stop signal that controls where translation begins and ends. This triplet code allows 64 possible codons to specify the 20 standard amino acids plus punctuation. A codon does not specify an entire protein or a whole gene, which are far larger units.
rationales.eli10: The RNA message is read three letters at a time, like reading a word made of exactly three letters. Each little three-letter word tells the cell which single building block (amino acid) to add next. Some words mean start here or stop now, like punctuation in a sentence.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change to a gene's DNA sequence would most likely have NO effect on the resulting protein?

options.text: A substitution that changes a codon into a stop codon
A deletion of a single base near the start of the coding region
A substitution that changes a codon to one specifying the same amino acid
An insertion of two bases in the middle of the coding region

rationales.whyCorrect: Because the genetic code is redundant (degenerate), several codons can specify the same amino acid, so a substitution that produces a synonymous codon is a silent mutation with no change to the protein. In contrast, single-base deletions or two-base insertions cause frameshifts that scramble all downstream codons, and changing a codon to a stop codon truncates the protein. This illustrates why not all mutations alter the protein product.
rationales.eli10: The code has backup spellings for the same building block, kind of like how color and colour mean the same thing. If a DNA change just swaps one spelling for another spelling of the same amino acid, the protein comes out exactly the same. That is called a silent change.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Every cell in your body contains the same genes, yet a nerve cell and a muscle cell look and act very differently. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Different genes are expressed (turned on or off) in different cell types
Nerve and muscle cells contain completely different sets of genes
Muscle cells lose the genes they do not need during development
Nerve cells replace their DNA with RNA as they mature

rationales.whyCorrect: Nearly all body cells carry the same complete genome, but each cell type selectively expresses only a subset of its genes through gene regulation. This differential gene expression produces the specialized proteins that make a neuron a neuron and a muscle cell a muscle cell. Cells do not delete or lose the genes they are not using; those genes are simply not transcribed.
rationales.eli10: Every cell has the same full cookbook, but each cell only cooks certain recipes. A muscle cell cooks the muscle recipes and leaves the nerve recipes closed, while a nerve cell does the opposite. The book is identical; the difference is which pages they choose to use. That choosing is called gene expression.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A DNA template strand reads 3'-TAC-GGA-5'. Which mRNA sequence would be produced from this template during transcription?

rationales.whyCorrect: RNA polymerase reads the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction and builds the new RNA antiparallel to it, in the 5' to 3' direction, using uracil wherever the template has adenine. Reading the template 3'-T A C G G A-5' and pairing each base (T with A, A with U, C with G, G with C, G with C, A with U) gives the mRNA 5'-AUG-CCU-3', choice D. Choice B is the complementary sequence written with thymine, which makes it DNA rather than RNA. Choice C simply copies the template's bases unchanged, ignoring both complementary pairing and the T-to-U substitution. Choice A converts only the first base and then copies the rest of the template verbatim, leaving a G-G-A block that was never complemented.
rationales.eli10: Think of the template strand as a row of puzzle pieces read from its 3' end toward its 5' end. The cell snaps in the matching partner for each piece to build the RNA, and that new RNA grows in the opposite direction, from its own 5' end to its 3' end. The partners are T with A, A with U, C with G, and G with C, because RNA uses U instead of T. Matching T-A-C-G-G-A one at a time gives A-U-G-C-C-U. If your answer still has a T in it, it is DNA, not RNA, so it cannot be right.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which example best illustrates a point mutation causing a change in a protein?

options.text: An entire chromosome is duplicated during cell division
A single base change causes the codon for glutamic acid to code for valine
Two homologous chromosomes exchange large segments during meiosis
A cell fails to divide and ends up with twice the normal DNA

rationales.whyCorrect: A point mutation is a change in a single nucleotide base, and when it alters the amino acid specified (as in the sickle cell mutation, glutamic acid to valine), it is a missense mutation that changes the protein. The other choices describe chromosome-level events (duplication, crossing over, and failed division) that involve large amounts of DNA rather than a single base. This distinguishes small-scale from large-scale genetic changes.
rationales.eli10: A point mutation is like a single typo in one word of a recipe, changing salt to silt. Just that one wrong letter can change what gets made. The famous sickle cell example is exactly this: one letter swap turns one building block into a different one, changing the protein.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher finds that a gene is transcribed into mRNA normally, but no protein is produced. Which step of gene expression is most likely disrupted?

rationales.whyCorrect: Since mRNA is being made normally, transcription is working; the failure to produce protein points to translation, the step where ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids. DNA replication and DNA base pairing are not part of expressing an already-transcribed gene into protein. Isolating which step fails requires knowing what product is and is not being made.
rationales.eli10: If the recipe note (mRNA) got copied fine but no dish (protein) ever came out of the kitchen, then the copying step worked and the cooking step is the problem. Cooking the note into the actual protein is translation, so that is where the breakdown is.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What would happen to the reading of a gene if a single base were inserted near the beginning of its coding region?

options.text: Only the codon at the insertion site would change; the rest would be normal
The reading frame would shift, altering most downstream codons and likely the whole protein
The gene would simply be skipped and not transcribed at all
The inserted base would be automatically removed before translation

rationales.whyCorrect: Because the genetic code is read in nonoverlapping triplets, inserting a single base shifts the reading frame for every codon downstream of the insertion, a frameshift mutation. This typically produces an entirely different and usually nonfunctional amino acid sequence and often introduces a premature stop codon. A single insertion is far more disruptive than a single substitution precisely because it displaces the frame rather than changing one codon.
rationales.eli10: Imagine reading a sentence three letters at a time: THE-CAT-ATE. Now stick one extra letter at the front: XTH-ECA-TAT-E. Every group after the insert is now nonsense. Adding one letter bumps everything over, so the cell reads the wrong three-letter words from that point on. That is a frameshift.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between DNA and RNA is accurate?

options.text: DNA carries out translation at the ribosome; RNA stores genetic information in the nucleus
DNA is usually single-stranded and uses uracil; RNA is usually double-stranded and uses thymine
Both DNA and RNA contain the sugar deoxyribose and are always double-stranded
DNA is usually double-stranded and uses thymine; RNA is usually single-stranded and uses uracil

rationales.whyCorrect: DNA is typically a double-stranded helix containing the sugar deoxyribose and the base thymine, serving as long-term information storage. RNA is typically single-stranded, contains ribose, and uses uracil in place of thymine, and it carries out roles like transferring the message to the ribosome. Choice A also reverses their functions: DNA stores information while RNA (as mRNA) participates directly in translation.
rationales.eli10: DNA is like the sturdy two-sided master book kept safe, spelled with the letter T. RNA is like a lightweight one-sided working copy sent out to do jobs, and it swaps in the letter U for T. Two strands and T means DNA; one strand and U means RNA.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term best describes a permanent change in the nucleotide sequence of an organism's DNA?

rationales.whyCorrect: A mutation is any permanent alteration in the DNA nucleotide sequence, which may arise spontaneously or from mutagens. Translation, transcription, and replication are normal cellular processes that read or copy DNA rather than permanently changing its sequence. Recognizing this definition is the foundation for understanding how genetic variation and genetic disease arise.
rationales.eli10: Think of DNA as a recipe written out in letters. A mutation is like a typo that gets permanently saved into the recipe, so every future copy has the same mistake. Translation, transcription, and replication are just steps where the kitchen reads or photocopies the recipe, not where the typo happens.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly defines epigenetics?

options.text: The study of how ribosomes assemble amino acids into complete functional proteins
The study of permanent deletions and insertions within the DNA nucleotide sequence
The study of heritable changes in gene activity that do not involve changes to the DNA sequence
The study of how duplicated chromosomes are pulled apart during cell division

rationales.whyCorrect: Epigenetics examines changes in gene expression that can be inherited by daughter cells but that do not alter the underlying DNA nucleotide sequence. Mechanisms such as DNA methylation and histone modification turn genes on or off without editing the genetic code itself. This distinguishes epigenetics from mutation, which does change the sequence.
rationales.eli10: Imagine the DNA is a book, and every word is spelled exactly right. Epigenetics is like putting sticky notes or bookmarks on certain pages that say 'skip this' or 'read this a lot.' The words never change, but which parts get read does, and those notes can even be passed to the next copy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a point mutation?

options.text: A single base pair is substituted for a different base pair
An entire chromosome fails to separate during cell division
A long segment of a chromosome is duplicated
A whole gene is transferred to another chromosome

rationales.whyCorrect: A point mutation is a change affecting a single nucleotide (base pair), most commonly a substitution of one base for another. Larger-scale events such as chromosomal nondisjunction, segment duplications, or translocations involve much more DNA and are classified as chromosomal mutations. Point mutations underlie many single-gene disorders such as sickle cell disease.
rationales.eli10: A point mutation is like changing just one letter in a word, turning 'cat' into 'cot.' The other choices are like moving whole sentences or copying entire paragraphs, which are much bigger changes than a single letter swap.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A single nucleotide is inserted near the beginning of a protein-coding gene. Why does this frameshift mutation often have severe effects?

options.text: It changes only the very last amino acid in the protein
It prevents the DNA from ever being replicated again
It shifts the reading frame so most downstream codons are misread
It adds a chemical mark that silences the gene without changing the code

rationales.whyCorrect: Because the genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets (codons), inserting or deleting a number of bases that is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame. Every codon downstream of the insertion is regrouped incorrectly, usually producing a completely different amino acid sequence and often a premature stop codon. This is why frameshifts are typically more damaging than a single substitution.
rationales.eli10: The cell reads DNA three letters at a time, like 'THE-CAT-ATE.' If you jam an extra letter near the front, everything reshuffles into nonsense: 'THX-ECA-TAT-E.' One added letter wrecks every word after it, which is why a frameshift can ruin the whole protein.
