subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does DNA methylation typically affect the gene it acts upon?

options.text: It changes the DNA base sequence of the gene
It deletes the promoter region of the gene
It always increases production of the gene's protein
It usually reduces or silences expression of the gene

rationales.whyCorrect: DNA methylation adds methyl groups to cytosine bases, commonly in promoter regions, which tends to make the chromatin less accessible and represses transcription. This is an epigenetic change: gene activity is turned down without altering the DNA sequence itself. It is a key mechanism cells use to control which genes are active in different tissues.
rationales.eli10: Methylation is like slapping a 'do not read' sticker on a gene. The words underneath are untouched, but the sticker makes the cell skip over that gene, so it makes little or none of that protein. That is why methylation usually quiets a gene down.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between a silent mutation and a nonsense mutation is accurate?

options.text: A silent mutation changes one amino acid, while a nonsense mutation leaves the protein unchanged
A silent mutation keeps the same amino acid, while a nonsense mutation adds an early stop codon
Both mutations lengthen the protein by adding extra amino acids past the normal stop codon
A silent mutation deletes one base pair, while a nonsense mutation inserts an extra base pair

rationales.whyCorrect: Because the genetic code is redundant, a silent mutation changes a codon to another codon that specifies the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged. A nonsense mutation instead changes a codon into a stop codon, prematurely halting translation and usually producing a shortened, nonfunctional protein. Both are single-base substitutions rather than insertions or deletions, and neither lengthens the protein.
rationales.eli10: A silent mutation is like spelling 'color' as 'colour'—it looks different but means the same thing, so nothing changes. A nonsense mutation is like sticking a big STOP sign in the middle of a sentence, so the protein gets cut off early and usually doesn't work.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change would most likely cause a mutation to be passed on to an organism's offspring?

options.text: A mutation occurring in a skin cell after sun exposure
A mutation occurring in a liver cell during adulthood
A mutation occurring in a sperm or egg cell
A mutation occurring in a muscle cell during exercise

rationales.whyCorrect: Only mutations in the germ line (sperm or egg cells) can be transmitted to offspring, because these cells form the next generation. Mutations in somatic cells such as skin, liver, or muscle affect only that individual and are not inherited. This distinction between germ-line and somatic mutations is central to understanding inherited genetic disease.
rationales.eli10: Your body cells (skin, liver, muscle) are like workers who never have kids of their own—a change in them stays with you. But egg and sperm cells are the ones that actually become a baby, so a change there gets copied into the next generation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher finds that two people have identical DNA sequences for a certain gene, yet one produces the protein and the other does not. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: An epigenetic mark such as methylation silences the gene in one person
A frameshift insertion in one person shifts the gene's reading frame
A nonsense mutation in one person ends translation of the gene too early
A large deletion has removed the whole gene from one person's genome

rationales.whyCorrect: Since the DNA sequences are identical, the difference in expression cannot come from a mutation, which by definition would change the sequence: a frameshift insertion, a nonsense substitution, or a deletion would each show up as a sequence difference. An epigenetic modification such as DNA methylation can silence a gene without altering its sequence, explaining why one person makes the protein and the other does not. This scenario highlights how gene expression can differ even with the same genotype.
rationales.eli10: If both cookbooks have the exact same recipe printed, but one cook never makes the dish, the recipe itself isn't the problem—someone put a 'skip this page' sticky note in one book. That sticky note is epigenetics, changing what gets used without changing the words.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In sickle cell disease, a single DNA base change swaps one amino acid (glutamic acid) for another (valine) in the hemoglobin protein. Which type of mutation does this represent?

rationales.whyCorrect: A missense mutation is a point mutation that changes one codon so it codes for a different amino acid, exactly as seen in sickle cell disease where glutamic acid is replaced by valine. This single amino acid change alters hemoglobin's shape and function. It contrasts with a silent mutation (no amino acid change) and a nonsense mutation (a new stop codon).
rationales.eli10: A missense mutation is like changing one letter so a word turns into a different real word—'bat' becomes 'cat.' In sickle cell, one changed letter swaps one building block of the protein for another, and that small swap changes how the blood cells are shaped.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which example best illustrates a mutagen contributing to mutation?

options.text: A ribosome reading a messenger RNA strand to build a protein
Ultraviolet light from the sun damaging DNA in skin cells
A cell copying its DNA accurately before dividing
A methyl group being removed from a promoter region

rationales.whyCorrect: A mutagen is a physical or chemical agent that increases the frequency of mutations by damaging DNA, and ultraviolet radiation is a classic example that causes damage such as thymine dimers in skin cells. Accurate DNA copying and normal translation do not cause mutations, and removing a methyl group is an epigenetic change rather than a sequence change. Recognizing mutagens connects to real-world cancer risk.
rationales.eli10: A mutagen is anything that scrambles the DNA letters, and sunlight's UV rays are a common one—too much sun can create typos in your skin cells' DNA. That's why sunburns matter and why sunscreen helps protect the recipe inside your cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Studies show that identical twins, who share the same DNA sequence, can develop different diseases over their lifetimes partly because their patterns of DNA methylation drift apart. What does this finding best demonstrate?

options.text: New point mutations must have altered one twin's DNA sequence over their lifetime
Environmental factors can alter gene expression epigenetically, leaving DNA intact
Epigenetic marks are set at conception and can never change during a person's life
Identical twins never truly share a genome, which is why their disease risks differ

rationales.whyCorrect: Identical twins begin with the same DNA sequence, so differing disease outcomes linked to methylation differences show that gene expression can change through epigenetic mechanisms rather than sequence mutations. This illustrates the dynamic, environmentally responsive nature of the epigenome.
rationales.eli10: Twins start with the exact same instruction book, but as they live different lives, they end up putting different sticky notes on their pages—some genes get louder, some get quieted. The words never changed, but the notes did, which is why twins can turn out differently even with matching DNA.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What would happen if a mutation occurred in a body's DNA repair genes, and why would this be significant?

options.text: Cells would stop making any proteins at all immediately
All epigenetic marks would be erased from the genome
The DNA sequence would become permanently locked and unable to change
Mutations would accumulate faster because damaged DNA is corrected less effectively

rationales.whyCorrect: DNA repair genes encode proteins that detect and fix errors and damage in DNA, keeping the mutation rate low. If these genes are mutated and lose function, errors go uncorrected and mutations accumulate more rapidly, increasing the risk of conditions such as cancer. This shows how a single mutation in a maintenance system can amplify overall genetic instability.
rationales.eli10: DNA repair genes are like the spell-checkers of the cell, catching typos before they stick. If the spell-checker itself breaks, typos pile up everywhere because nobody is fixing them. That's why damage to repair genes is dangerous—the whole recipe collection gets sloppier over time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which term best describes the process by which organisms with heritable traits that improve survival and reproduction tend to leave more offspring than organisms lacking those traits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Natural selection is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals based on heritable traits that affect fitness. Over generations, advantageous alleles become more common in the population. This is the core mechanism Darwin proposed to explain adaptation, and it requires variation, heritability, and differential reproductive success.
rationales.eli10: Imagine rabbits where a few happen to run a little faster. Foxes catch the slow ones more often, so the fast ones live to have babies who are also fast. Nature is 'picking' the runners without anyone deciding it on purpose. That natural 'picking' by survival and having babies is called natural selection.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In evolutionary biology, what does the term 'adaptation' most accurately refer to?

options.text: A change an individual makes to its body during its lifetime to survive better
The total number of offspring an individual produces in its lifetime
The random shuffling of alleles during the formation of gametes
A heritable trait shaped by natural selection that improves an organism's fit to its environment

rationales.whyCorrect: An adaptation is an inherited characteristic that has become common in a population because it enhanced survival and reproduction in a particular environment. It must be heritable and the product of natural selection over generations. This distinguishes it from acclimation, which is a reversible individual adjustment, and from fitness, which measures reproductive success.
rationales.eli10: An adaptation is a built-in feature you were born with that helps you survive, like a polar bear's thick fur. It is passed down from parents to babies, not something the bear grew just because it got cold one afternoon. If it helps the animal live and have babies, and it gets passed on, it is an adaptation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies the ultimate source of the new genetic variation on which evolution depends?

options.text: Use and disuse of body parts

rationales.whyCorrect: Mutation is the original source of new alleles because it changes the DNA sequence, creating genetic variants that did not exist before. Other processes such as recombination reshuffle existing variation, and gene flow moves it between populations, but only mutation generates entirely new alleles. Natural selection then acts on this variation rather than creating it.
rationales.eli10: Think of DNA like a recipe book copied over and over. Sometimes a tiny copying mistake changes a word in a recipe, and that mistake is a mutation. Those mistakes create brand-new versions of instructions that never existed before. Everything else just reshuffles recipes that already exist, so mutation is where truly new variety starts.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Bacteria in a hospital become increasingly resistant to an antibiotic after repeated exposure. Which explanation is most consistent with natural selection?

options.text: Resistant bacteria already existed by chance and survived to reproduce while susceptible ones died
The antibiotic directly rewrote bacterial DNA to make every cell resistant
Exposure to the antibiotic made all bacteria stronger over their individual lifetimes
Each bacterium sensed the antibiotic and deliberately developed resistance to survive

rationales.whyCorrect: Antibiotic resistance arises because random mutations produce resistant variants before or independent of exposure; the antibiotic then selectively kills susceptible cells, leaving resistant ones to multiply. The environment selects among pre-existing variation rather than creating the needed trait on demand. This illustrates that selection acts on variation but does not direct which mutations occur.
rationales.eli10: Before the medicine even shows up, a few bacteria happen to have a lucky feature that shrugs it off. When the medicine arrives, it wipes out the ordinary ones but not the lucky few, and those lucky ones multiply into a whole crowd. The medicine did not teach them to resist; it just cleared the way for the ones that already could.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between natural selection and genetic drift is accurate?

options.text: Natural selection introduces new alleles, whereas genetic drift removes all variation instantly
Natural selection is random, whereas genetic drift consistently favors the fittest alleles
Both processes require large populations to have any effect on allele frequencies
Natural selection changes allele frequencies based on fitness, whereas genetic drift changes them by random chance

rationales.whyCorrect: Natural selection is a non-random process in which allele frequencies shift according to how traits affect survival and reproduction. Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies due to chance sampling of who reproduces, and its effects are strongest in small populations. Neither process creates new alleles; that is the role of mutation.
rationales.eli10: Natural selection is like a fair race where faster runners win more often, so speed spreads for a reason. Genetic drift is like drawing marbles from a bag with your eyes closed, where which colors you grab is just luck. In a small bag, luck can wipe out a color entirely, which is why drift matters most in small populations.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The wing of a bird and the wing of a bat share a similar underlying bone structure inherited from a common ancestor. What term describes these structures?

rationales.whyCorrect: Homologous structures share the same basic anatomical plan because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if their current functions differ. Analogous structures, by contrast, look similar because of convergent evolution but do not share ancestry. The shared limb-bone arrangement in bird and bat wings reflects common descent, which is evidence for evolution.
rationales.eli10: A bird wing and a bat wing are built from the same set of arm bones, just rearranged, like two houses built from the same box of Lego passed down from grandma. Because the parts came from the same source, we call them homologous. If two animals looked alike but got their parts from totally different toolkits, that would be a different story.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the primary reason that a trait must be heritable for it to drive evolutionary change by natural selection?

options.text: Heritable traits are always more beneficial than traits acquired during life
Non-heritable traits cannot vary among individuals in a population
Only traits passed to offspring can accumulate and shift a population's makeup over generations
Natural selection can only act on traits that never change once an organism is born

rationales.whyCorrect: Evolution is a change in heritable trait frequencies across generations, so selection can only produce lasting change if the favored trait is transmitted genetically to offspring. A beneficial trait acquired during an individual's life (such as bigger muscles from exercise) dies with that individual and cannot spread. Heritability links an individual's reproductive success to the next generation's composition.
rationales.eli10: If a weightlifter builds huge muscles, their baby is not born with huge muscles, because muscles from the gym are not written into the DNA passed on. For a trait to spread through a whole group over time, it has to ride along in the DNA to the kids. No DNA ticket, no trip to the next generation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A population of moths lives on tree bark that becomes darkened by soot from a nearby factory. Which change would most likely occur over many generations?

options.text: Individual light moths gradually turn dark to blend in with the sooty bark
Dark-colored moths become more common because they are better camouflaged from predators
The moth population evolves the ability to fly only at night to escape the change
All moths become dark within a single generation to avoid being seen

rationales.whyCorrect: On darkened bark, dark moths are harder for predators to spot, so they survive and reproduce more often, increasing the frequency of dark alleles over generations. This is the classic case of directional selection in peppered moths driven by an environmental change. Evolution acts on the population across generations, not by transforming individuals within their lifetimes.
rationales.eli10: On dark, sooty trees, a dark moth is like wearing camouflage while a light moth is like wearing a bright white shirt in the dark. Birds easily grab the easy-to-see light ones, so more dark moths survive to have babies. Over many generations the forest fills up with dark moths, not because any one moth changed color, but because the well-hidden ones kept winning.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A small group of birds is blown by a storm onto a remote island and starts a new population. By chance, this founding group happens to lack several alleles common in the mainland population. Which process does this scenario best illustrate?

options.text: Directional natural selection for island survival
The founder effect, a form of genetic drift
Gene flow between the island and mainland populations

rationales.whyCorrect: The founder effect occurs when a new population is started by a small number of individuals whose alleles are, by chance, not representative of the original population. This is a type of genetic drift because the change in allele frequency results from random sampling rather than differential fitness. Small founding groups often show reduced genetic diversity as a result.
rationales.eli10: Imagine grabbing just a tiny handful of jellybeans from a giant jar and moving them to a new jar; that small handful probably won't include every color the big jar had. The few birds that landed on the island are that handful, and the whole island population grows from just their limited set of genes. This lucky, unrepresentative start is called the founder effect.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which example best illustrates convergent evolution producing analogous structures?

options.text: The forelimb bones of a human, cat, and whale, which share a common ancestral pattern
The nearly identical DNA sequences shared by chimpanzees and other close primate relatives
The tiny pelvic bones found in whales, which no longer support any functional hind limbs
The streamlined body and fins of a dolphin and a shark, which are only distant relatives

rationales.whyCorrect: Convergent evolution occurs when distantly related organisms independently evolve similar features because they face similar environmental pressures. Dolphins (mammals) and sharks (fish) evolved streamlined bodies separately as adaptations to fast swimming, making these analogous structures. The shared forelimb pattern is homology, the whale pelvis is vestigial, and shared DNA reflects common ancestry.
rationales.eli10: A dolphin and a shark are only distant relatives, but both chase food and dodge danger in water. In each group, the individuals that happened to be born a little sleeker tended to catch more food and escape more often, so sleek bodies and fins spread separately in both groups. Nobody planned it; water pushes back the same way on every swimmer, so the same shape kept winning twice. Same solution, separate origins, is called convergent evolution.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What would most likely happen to a population if natural selection consistently favored individuals with average trait values while selecting against both extremes?

options.text: The population would split into two distinct groups at opposite extremes of the trait
The population would show reduced variation as intermediate phenotypes become more common
The average value of the trait would steadily shift toward one extreme over time
The population would gain new alleles that had never existed before

rationales.whyCorrect: This describes stabilizing selection, which favors intermediate phenotypes and selects against both extremes, narrowing the range of variation around the mean. A classic example is human birth weight, where very small and very large babies historically had lower survival. Directional selection shifts the mean toward one extreme, and disruptive selection favors both extremes, so those are not the expected outcomes.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a class where being too short or too tall both get you picked last, but average height is just right, so over time almost everyone ends up around the middle height. Nothing new gets added; the extremes just get trimmed away, making the group more alike. That trimming toward the middle is called stabilizing selection.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A biologist observes that two populations of the same fish species, separated by a new dam for many generations, can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring even when placed together. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The two populations have undergone identical adaptations due to gene flow
Genetic drift has been eliminated because the populations are now separate
Reproductive isolation has led to speciation between the two populations
The dam caused directed mutations that made the fish deliberately incompatible

rationales.whyCorrect: When populations are separated and accumulate enough genetic differences that they can no longer produce fertile offspring, reproductive isolation has occurred and they are considered separate species under the biological species concept. The dam acted as a geographic barrier, an example of allopatric speciation. Gene flow is actually blocked by the barrier, drift continues in each population, and mutations are random rather than purposefully directed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The **octet rule** says atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons so that their outermost **electron shell** holds eight electrons. Oxygen has six valence electrons. Which statement correctly applies the octet rule to oxygen?

options.text: Oxygen will lose six electrons to empty its outer shell.
Oxygen will gain six electrons to fill its outer shell.
Oxygen will gain two electrons to complete its outer shell.
Oxygen will gain two neutrons to stabilize its nucleus.

rationales.whyCorrect: With six valence electrons, oxygen needs two more to reach the stable octet of eight, whether by gaining electrons or by sharing them in bonds. rationales.eli10: Picture a school bus with exactly eight seats along its side. Oxygen's bus has six kids already seated, and it feels restless until all eight seats are full. To fix that, it can accept two kids from another atom, or it can agree to share two of its seats with a neighbor atom's kids. Either way, the bus ends up with eight kids in eight seats, which is what the octet rule describes.
rationales.highYield: Oxygen has six valence electrons and needs two more to complete its octet.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: **Electronegativity** is the measure of an atom's pull on shared electrons, and oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen. Which statement best describes the bond between hydrogen and oxygen in a water molecule?

options.text: A polar covalent bond, because the shared electrons are pulled closer to the oxygen atom.
A nonpolar covalent bond, because both atoms pull equally on the electrons.
An ionic bond, because oxygen completely strips the electrons away from hydrogen.
A hydrogen bond, because the oxygen atom attracts the hydrogen atom.

rationales.whyCorrect: The large electronegativity difference makes the shared electrons sit nearer oxygen, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge, which is the definition of a polar covalent bond. B requires equal pulls that do not exist here. C overstates the shift, which is a partial pull rather than a full transfer. D misnames the bond, since hydrogen bonds form between molecules, not between the hydrogen and oxygen within one molecule.
rationales.eli10: Picture a tug-of-war with one rope held by a strong grown-up and a small child. The rope stands for the pair of shared electrons, and the grown-up, oxygen, pulls it much closer to its own side. The rope is never fully handed over, but it sits nearer to the strong puller. The two ends of the rope develop tiny charges, one slightly negative and one slightly positive, which is why the bond is called polar.
rationales.highYield: A large electronegativity difference means unequal sharing of electrons, which produces a polar covalent bond with partial charges.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Water molecules cling to one another through **hydrogen bonds**, a behavior called **cohesion**, and they also cling to other polar surfaces, a behavior called **adhesion**. Which statement correctly explains both behaviors?

options.text: High specific heat makes water sticky at any temperature.
Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules and between water molecules and polar surfaces, so water sticks to itself and to those surfaces.
Water dissolves ionic compounds, which makes it cling to everything it touches.
The low density of ice pushes water molecules against the walls of their container.

rationales.whyCorrect: Cohesion is the hydrogen-bond attraction between water molecules, and adhesion is the same attraction toward other polar surfaces, so one interaction explains both behaviors. When enough of them grip the wall, the whole chain of hand-holders climbs up it against gravity, which is why water rises in narrow tubes.
rationales.highYield: Cohesion and adhesion are both hydrogen-bond attractions, one between water molecules and one toward other polar surfaces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Liquid water freezes into **ice**, and unlike most substances, ice is less dense than the liquid water it floats in. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Frozen water molecules move faster, spreading themselves farther apart.
Ice contains no hydrogen bonds, so its molecules pack tightly together.
Hydrogen bonds lock water molecules into a fixed, open lattice that takes up more space than liquid water does.
Ice is filled with trapped air bubbles that always make it lighter than water.

rationales.whyCorrect: In ice every water molecule forms a full set of hydrogen bonds that hold it in a spacious crystal lattice, whereas in liquid water the bonds constantly break and reform, letting molecules pack more closely. A reverses the physics, since freezing slows molecules down. B is wrong because ice is packed with hydrogen bonds. D describes an accidental feature of some ice, not the general mechanism.
rationales.eli10: Picture a dance floor full of people moving around. Liquid water molecules are like those dancers, always shifting and slipping between each other, so they fit together tightly. When the music stops and they freeze into ice, every dancer locks hands with four fixed neighbors in a wide, open pattern. That open pattern leaves empty spaces, so the frozen crowd takes up more room than the moving crowd did. The same number of dancers spread over more room means lighter per box of space, so ice floats.
rationales.highYield: Ice floats because its hydrogen-bond lattice holds water molecules farther apart, making ice less dense than liquid water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Water has a high **specific heat**, which means it must absorb a relatively large amount of energy for each degree its temperature rises. Which real-world observation is a direct consequence?

options.text: Water evaporates quickly from a hot sidewalk.
Coastal cities swing between much hotter summers and colder winters than inland cities.
Ice sinks to the bottom of lakes in winter.
Lakes and oceans warm up and cool down slowly, moderating the climate of nearby land.

rationales.whyCorrect: High specific heat lets large bodies of water take in or release great amounts of heat with only small temperature changes, so they smooth out the temperature swings near coasts. A is a consequence of high heat of vaporization, not specific heat. B reverses the moderating effect. C is a consequence of ice being less dense than liquid water.
rationales.eli10: Think of water as a giant sponge for heat energy. When the summer sun pours down, the sponge soaks up a huge amount of that energy without getting much hotter itself. A coastal city sits next to this sponge, so its air never heats up very fast, and in winter the sponge gives the stored heat back slowly. The city ends up with mild weather because the watery sponge evens everything out.
rationales.highYield: High specific heat means water changes temperature slowly, which is why oceans stabilize coastal climates.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The **pH scale** describes hydrogen ion concentration in powers of ten, and lower pH means more hydrogen ions. A solution with a pH of 6 has how many times more hydrogen ions than a solution with a pH of 8?

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Water has a high **heat of vaporization**, meaning a large amount of energy must be absorbed to turn liquid water into vapor. Which real-world observation is a direct consequence of this property?

Table salt dissolves easily in water.
Sweating cools the body because evaporating water carries a large amount of heat away from the skin.

rationales.whyCorrect: Each water molecule that leaves the skin as vapor takes a large amount of heat with it, and the high heat of vaporization is what makes that cooling so effective. A shows cohesion and surface tension. B follows from ice being less dense than liquid water. C shows solvent power, a real water property but unrelated to evaporation.
rationales.eli10: Imagine kids at a pool who can only leave the water by paying a toll of heat energy. When sweat evaporates off your skin, every escaping water molecule pays that toll from your skin, so your skin loses heat and feels cooler. Because water charges a very large toll, this trick works incredibly well, and it is the same reason you feel cold when you step out of a pool into the wind.
rationales.highYield: The high heat of vaporization is why evaporation, such as sweating, removes a large amount of heat from a surface.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cell needs to import a large polar molecule, but the molecule cannot pass through the **plasma membrane** by simple diffusion. Which feature of the membrane explains this barrier?

options.text: The membrane is too thick for any molecule to cross without a protein channel.
The hydrophobic interior of the bilayer repels large polar molecules.
The phosphate heads of the phospholipids block all molecules except water.
The membrane lacks the enzymes needed to pull the molecule inside.

rationales.whyCorrect: The phospholipid bilayer has a hydrophobic core of fatty acid tails, and large polar molecules and ions cannot dissolve through it. A fails because small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen cross the bilayer easily. C fails because small polar molecules like water do pass, and the heads do not act as a universal filter. D fails because import depends on transport proteins, not on membrane enzymes.
rationales.eli10: Think of the membrane as a greasy wall between two rooms. Small oily things slip right through the grease, but a big water-loving soccer ball cannot get through a grease wall. It needs a special door, which is a transport protein. The molecule in the question is the soccer ball, and without a door it stays out.
rationales.highYield: Membrane permeability follows chemistry: small nonpolar molecules cross the bilayer freely, while large polar molecules need transport proteins.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher adds a drug that blocks all transport through the **nuclear envelope**. Which cellular process would be disrupted most immediately?

options.text: Production of ATP in the mitochondria.
Synthesis of phospholipids in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
Translation of messenger RNA in the cytoplasm.
Replication of DNA during the S phase of the cell cycle.

rationales.whyCorrect: The nuclear envelope controls traffic between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, and messenger RNA must pass through a pore to reach the ribosomes in the cytoplasm. D fails because DNA replication occurs inside the nucleus and needs no pore transport. A fails because mitochondria make ATP without exchanging anything with the nucleus. B fails because smooth endoplasmic reticulum lipid synthesis does not depend on nuclear export.
rationales.eli10: The nucleus is like a castle with a single gate. The castle holds the instruction books, and copies of the instructions must pass through the gate to reach the workers outside. If you bolt the gate shut, the workers outside run out of orders and stop building. That is why blocking the pores stops the making of proteins in the cytoplasm.
rationales.highYield: The nuclear envelope is not a seal; pores move messenger RNA out and proteins in, so blocking them halts cytoplasmic translation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A pancreatic cell is actively secreting digestive enzymes into the bloodstream. Which statement correctly describes the role of the **rough endoplasmic reticulum** and its ribosomes in making these enzymes?

options.text: Free ribosomes in the cytosol translate the enzymes, which then diffuse to the plasma membrane on their own.
Ribosomes inside the nucleus translate the enzymes, and the nuclear pores release them.
Mitochondrial ribosomes translate the enzymes and ship them to the cell surface.
Ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum translate the enzymes and feed them into the ER lumen.

rationales.whyCorrect: Proteins destined for secretion are made by ribosomes docked on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and the growing chain enters the ER lumen directly. A fails because free ribosomes make proteins that stay in the cytosol. B fails because translation never occurs inside the nucleus. C fails because mitochondrial ribosomes make only mitochondrial proteins.
rationales.eli10: Think of ribosomes as two kinds of workers in a factory. Free workers build things for use right there on the factory floor. Bound workers stand at the conveyor belt of a wrapping station, so everything they build drops straight onto the belt and gets packaged for shipping. Secreted proteins are made by the workers at the wrapping station, which is the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
rationales.highYield: Destination is set at the ribosome: free ribosomes make cytosolic proteins, while bound ribosomes feed secreted proteins into the ER lumen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cell makes a protein that it will release into the bloodstream. After synthesis on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which sequence of structures does the protein follow on its way out of the cell?

options.text: Rough endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi apparatus to secretory vesicle to plasma membrane.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum to lysosome to Golgi apparatus to plasma membrane.
Golgi apparatus to rough endoplasmic reticulum to peroxisome to plasma membrane.
Nucleus to rough endoplasmic reticulum to cytoplasm to plasma membrane.

rationales.whyCorrect: The secretory pathway runs from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus, where proteins are modified and sorted, then into a secretory vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane to release the protein. B fails because the smooth ER does not handle secreted proteins and lysosomes do not deliver cargo outward. C fails because the Golgi acts after the rough ER, not before it. D fails because proteins are not made in the nucleus.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a mail-order package moving through a factory. Workers at the packing station, the rough endoplasmic reticulum, make the item and box it. Then it rolls down the sorting belt, the Golgi apparatus, where workers add labels and addresses. Finally, it rides a delivery van, a secretory vesicle, to the loading dock, the plasma membrane, where it leaves the factory.
rationales.highYield: The secretory pathway is one-directional: rough ER to Golgi apparatus to secretory vesicle to plasma membrane.

rationales.highYield: The rigid cell wall lets plant cells build turgor pressure that would lyse an animal cell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A single cell cannot grow without limit. Which physical constraint involving the **surface-area-to-volume ratio** sets the maximum size a cell can reach?

options.text: A very large cell would need more DNA than a single nucleus can hold.
A very large cell would have a cell wall too thick to absorb nutrients.
A very large cell could not divide its ribosomes fast enough.
Surface area grows more slowly than volume, so exchange across the membrane cannot keep up with the cell's needs.

rationales.whyCorrect: As a cell grows, volume increases as the cube of its size while surface area increases only as the square, so beyond a limit the membrane cannot supply the cytoplasm fast enough. A fails because DNA content does not set the size limit. B fails because most cells have no wall at all. C fails because ribosome numbers grow along with the cell and are not the constraint.
rationales.eli10: Think of a growing ice cube in a drink. The bigger the cube, the more frozen drink it has inside, but the outside surface where it melts grows much more slowly than the inside. rationales.highYield: Surface area scales with the square of size while volume scales with the cube, capping how large any cell can grow.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A student must draw the **phospholipid bilayer** that forms the framework of the plasma membrane. Which arrangement of the phospholipids is correct?

options.text: Hydrophilic heads face outward toward water on both sides, and hydrophobic tails point inward away from water.
Hydrophobic tails face outward toward water, and hydrophilic heads point inward toward each other.
Both heads and tails face outward, leaving the interior of the bilayer empty of lipid.
The phospholipids form a single layer with all heads on one side and all tails on the other.

rationales.whyCorrect: Each phospholipid is amphipathic, so the hydrophilic phosphate heads face the watery surroundings on both surfaces while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails cluster in the interior away from water. B reverses the arrangement and would put water-fearing tails into water. C leaves the bilayer empty in the middle, and D describes a single layer, not a bilayer.
rationales.eli10: Think of a crowd of tadpoles, each with a round head and a long tail. When they line up in two rows, all the round heads point toward the outside water and all the tails point inward, away from the water. The tails squeeze together in the middle like a greasy oil layer. This double row of tadpoles is how phospholipids build the bilayer.
rationales.highYield: Phospholipids are amphipathic, so heads face the water and tails hide in the bilayer interior.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In the laboratory, washing a plasma membrane with a salt solution releases one type of **membrane protein** while leaving the lipid bilayer intact, but detergent is required to release the other type. What does the easy release by salt wash tell you about the first protein?

options.text: It is a transmembrane channel that spans the whole bilayer.
It is covalently anchored to the cytoskeleton inside the cell.
It is a peripheral protein attached only to the surface of the membrane.
It is an integral protein embedded deep in the hydrophobic core.

rationales.whyCorrect: Peripheral proteins sit on the membrane surface and are held by weak electrostatic interactions, so a mild salt wash releases them without harming the bilayer. Integral proteins, including transmembrane channels, are embedded in the hydrophobic core and need detergent, so A and D are wrong. The salt wash gives no evidence of a cytoskeleton anchor, so B is unsupported.
rationales.eli10: Imagine painted stickers on the outside of a lunchbox. A gentle wipe with a damp cloth lifts the stickers right off, and the lunchbox is unharmed. Now imagine a spoon stuck all the way through the lunchbox from one side to the other. No wipe will pull that spoon out, because it passes through the wall. Peripheral proteins are like the stickers, and integral proteins are like the spoon.
rationales.highYield: Peripheral proteins come off with a gentle salt wash, while integral proteins need detergent because they are embedded in the bilayer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two molecules are compared: oxygen, which is small and nonpolar, and glucose, which is large and polar. Which statement best predicts how each crosses the plasma membrane, given the membrane's **selective permeability**?

options.text: Both molecules cross the lipid bilayer directly because both are uncharged.
Both molecules require carrier proteins and ATP because neither can cross the lipids.
Glucose crosses the lipid bilayer directly, while oxygen requires a channel protein.
Oxygen crosses the lipid bilayer directly by simple diffusion with no energy cost, while glucose needs a transport protein.

rationales.whyCorrect: The membrane is selectively permeable, so the small nonpolar oxygen dissolves in the hydrophobic core and diffuses freely, while the large polar glucose needs a transport protein. rationales.highYield: Small nonpolar molecules cross the bilayer by simple diffusion with no energy cost, but large polar molecules need transport proteins.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a beaker of pure water. Which statement best predicts what will happen to the cell, based on **osmosis** and tonicity?

options.text: The cell shrinks because water leaves the cell to dilute the beaker.
The cell swells and may burst because water enters by osmosis, moving from the higher water concentration outside to the lower concentration inside.
The cell stays the same size because the membrane stops water movement in both directions.
The cell shrinks because salts leak out of the cell into the pure water.

rationales.whyCorrect: Pure water is hypotonic relative to the cell interior, so osmosis moves water from the higher water concentration outside to the lower concentration inside, swelling the cell until it may burst. A has the gradient reversed, since water leaves cells in hypertonic conditions. C ignores that the membrane is permeable to water, and D confuses the moving species, because water moves and salts do not leak here.
rationales.eli10: Picture a water balloon with a little juice inside, dropped into a bowl of pure water. The outside water is thin and watery, while the inside juice is thicker and more crowded. Water loves to even things out, so outside water pushes through the balloon wall to join the crowd inside. The balloon swells and pops if too much gets in.
rationales.highYield: Osmosis moves water toward the side with more solute, so a hypotonic environment makes a cell swell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a study of **facilitated diffusion** of glucose, the rate of glucose entry stops increasing at high extracellular glucose concentrations even though more glucose keeps arriving outside. What best explains this ceiling?

options.text: The concentration gradient for glucose has reversed direction.
Glucose becomes insoluble at high concentrations.
The carrier proteins become saturated because every binding site is occupied.
The membrane becomes impermeable to glucose above a threshold.

rationales.whyCorrect: Facilitated diffusion depends on carrier proteins with a finite number of binding sites, so when every carrier is busy the rate cannot rise further, producing the plateau. The gradient still points inward and glucose stays soluble, so A and B cannot explain the ceiling, and D invents a change in the membrane that does not occur.
rationales.eli10: Think of a toll bridge with ten booths and exactly ten ticket collectors. No matter how many cars line up, only ten can cross at a time because the collectors cannot work faster. If hundreds of cars show up, the extra ones just wait. The crossing rate has hit its ceiling, and adding more cars does not help. That ceiling is what scientists call saturation.
rationales.highYield: Saturation of carrier binding sites is the signature of facilitated diffusion, while simple diffusion never plateaus.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The **sodium-potassium pump** in a neuron moves ions against their concentration gradients. Which statement correctly describes the pump's action?

options.text: It pumps two sodium ions in and three potassium ions out, using ATP.
It moves three sodium ions in and two potassium ions out, powered by the gradient itself.
It lets sodium and potassium flow down their gradients to restore the resting potential.
It pumps three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, hydrolyzing ATP each cycle.

rationales.whyCorrect: The sodium-potassium pump is a primary active transporter that hydrolyzes ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, both against their gradients. rationales.eli10: Imagine a bouncer who only works when he is paid a coin of energy. Each time he is paid, he pushes three heavy boxes out of a room and lets two smaller boxes in. This always goes against the crowd, so it never happens by itself. The bouncer is the pump and the coin is the energy from ATP.
rationales.highYield: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to push three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An intestinal cell absorbs glucose against its concentration gradient using the downhill movement of sodium into the cell as its energy source. What is the name of this **cotransport** mechanism?

options.text: Secondary active transport by a cotransporter that couples sodium movement to glucose movement.
Primary active transport that hydrolyzes ATP to move glucose directly.
Simple diffusion of glucose through the lipid bilayer.
Facilitated diffusion through a glucose carrier protein.

rationales.whyCorrect: When the downhill flow of one ion drives another substance uphill, the coupled mechanism is secondary active transport, also called cotransport, and it uses the sodium gradient instead of ATP. B is wrong because no ATP is hydrolyzed in this step, and C and D are passive processes that can only move glucose down its gradient, not against it.
rationales.eli10: Picture an airport moving sidewalk full of people riding forward. A tired worker wants to move backward, against the flow, which normally takes a lot of effort. But if the riders grab the worker's hand, the crowd moving forward drags the worker along with them. That is exactly how sodium drags glucose into the cell.
rationales.highYield: Cotransport uses one ion moving down its gradient to pull another substance up its gradient without ATP.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cell is moved from a warm environment to a cold one. How does **membrane fluidity** change, and what role does **cholesterol** play?

The membrane is unchanged because temperature cannot alter membranes.
The membrane becomes less fluid as lipid tails pack more tightly, while cholesterol keeps the membrane from becoming too rigid.
The membrane dissolves because cholesterol melts at low temperature.

rationales.whyCorrect: Lower temperature slows phospholipid movement, so the membrane becomes less fluid as the lipid tails pack more tightly, and cholesterol inserts between the tails to limit that packing. A describes the temperature effect backward. B ignores the documented response of membranes to cold, and D invents a melting behavior cholesterol does not have.
rationales.eli10: Think of a bowl of oil left in a cold garage, and imagine tiny balls mixed into it. In the cold the oil thickens, and the balls make sure it does not turn into a solid block by getting in the way of the oil molecules clinging together. In warm weather the oil thins out, and the same balls hold it together so it does not fall apart. The balls act like cholesterol in the membrane.
rationales.highYield: Cold stiffens membranes, and cholesterol buffers the membrane so it does not become too rigid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a cell, glucose is oxidized to carbon dioxide and water during cellular respiration, releasing energy that the cell captures. Which statement best describes the **first law of thermodynamics** as it applies to this process?

The energy released comes from the creation of new energy during the formation of product bonds.

rationales.whyCorrect: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed, so the total energy of the universe stays constant while energy from glucose is converted into heat and ATP. rationales.highYield: Energy is conserved in every cellular reaction, never created and never destroyed.

B violates the law by claiming that new energy is created, and C violates it by claiming that energy is destroyed as heat. D is wrong because the cell converts energy from glucose into ATP, it does not create it.

**ELI-10:** Think of a piggy bank that can never be filled from outside or emptied for good. When you move coins from one hand to another, the total number of coins stays the same. subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction inside a cell has a negative change in **free energy** and is therefore **exergonic**. Which statement about this reaction is correct?

options.text: It is endergonic and requires an input of energy to proceed.
It is spontaneous, meaning it releases free energy and can proceed without added energy.
It can only proceed when the activation energy is very large.
It stores free energy in its products for later use.

rationales.whyCorrect: A negative change in free energy means the reaction is exergonic and spontaneous, releasing free energy that can do work. C confuses the kinetic barrier of activation energy with the thermodynamic direction of the reaction, and D describes the opposite situation, energy being stored in the products.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a ball resting on top of a hill with a clear path down. If nothing blocks it, the ball rolls downhill by itself and gives up its stored height. rationales.highYield: A negative free energy change marks an exergonic, spontaneous reaction that releases energy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: **ATP** consists of an adenine base, a ribose sugar, and three phosphate groups. Which part of the molecule stores the energy released during **hydrolysis**?

options.text: The bond between adenine and ribose, which is the weakest link in the molecule.
The bonds that join the sugar to the base.
The hydrogen bonds between the phosphate groups and surrounding water.
The bonds between the phosphate groups, especially the terminal phosphate bond, which releases energy when hydrolyzed.

rationales.whyCorrect: The energy that powers cellular work is stored in the bonds between the phosphate groups, and hydrolysis of the terminal phosphate bond releases it, leaving ADP and an inorganic phosphate. A and B point to bonds in the base and sugar, which do not carry the transferable energy. C is wrong because the energy lives in the molecule's own bonds, not in hydrogen bonds with water.
rationales.eli10: Think of the cell's energy packet as a rolled-up party popper with a spring loaded inside. The last phosphate group is the tab that holds the spring shut. When the cell pops the tab, the spring snaps and releases a burst of energy to do work. The empty popper can be reloaded so the cell can use it again.
rationales.highYield: ATP hydrolysis splits off the terminal phosphate group and releases the energy stored between the phosphates.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Even a highly exergonic reaction proceeds only when reactant molecules collide with enough energy to reach the **transition state**. What does the **activation energy** of a reaction represent?

options.text: The energy barrier that must be overcome for reactants to reach the transition state.
The total free energy released by the reaction.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products.
The energy stored in the bonds of the product molecules.

rationales.whyCorrect: Activation energy is the energy input required to bring reactants up to the transition state, the peak of the energy hill. B and C describe the free energy change, which is the difference between reactants and products, not the barrier. D mistakes the energy content of the products for the energy needed to start the reaction.
rationales.eli10: Picture a match that only lights when you strike it hard against a rough strip. The bump of the strike is the push needed to start the flame. The energy of that push is the activation energy, and once it is paid, the flame burns on its own. Even a reaction that gives off energy needs this small push to get started.
rationales.highYield: Activation energy is the hill to the transition state, while the free energy change is the height difference between reactants and products.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: **Enzymes** speed up reactions that would otherwise be far too slow for the cell. What exactly does an enzyme change about a reaction?

options.text: It raises the activation energy so that only very energetic collisions can react.
It lowers the activation energy by stabilizing the transition state, so more collisions are effective.
It changes the free energy change of the reaction, making it more negative.
It increases the temperature inside the active site to speed up molecular collisions.

rationales.whyCorrect: Enzymes speed reactions by lowering the activation energy, typically by stabilizing the transition state so that more collisions reach the required energy. Enzymes never change the free energy change or the equilibrium of a reaction, which rules out C. A describes the opposite of enzyme action, and D is false because enzymes do not act by raising temperature.
rationales.eli10: Think of rolling a boulder over a hill to reach the other side. A rough dirt trail needs a huge push, but a paved road with a gentler slope needs only a small push. The enzyme is the road builder, it flattens the slope so the boulder crosses with less effort. It does not change where the boulder ends up, only how easy the trip is.
rationales.highYield: Enzymes lower the activation energy without changing the free energy change or the equilibrium.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher measures the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction across a range of temperatures. At temperatures far above the optimum, the reaction rate drops sharply even though more thermal energy is available. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The substrate is destroyed by the heat and can no longer bind the enzyme.
The activation energy of the reaction increases as the temperature rises.
The enzyme denatures, losing its three-dimensional shape and the function of its active site.
The heat makes the reaction endergonic, so it can no longer proceed.

rationales.whyCorrect: Above the optimum temperature, heat breaks the weak interactions that hold the enzyme in its folded shape, so the enzyme denatures and the active site stops working. The substrate is generally stable at these temperatures, ruling out A. Activation energy does not rise with temperature, and the free energy change does not switch sign, ruling out B and D.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a pair of mittens knitted with careful loops that hold their shape. Boiling water loosens the knots and the mittens flop into a shapeless mess. A heated enzyme is like those mittens, its folds fall apart and the pocket that grabbed the substrate disappears. Once unfolded, the enzyme cannot do its job anymore.
rationales.highYield: High temperatures denature enzymes by destroying the weak interactions that hold their three-dimensional shape.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At low substrate concentration, doubling the substrate doubles the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction. When substrate is present in great excess, doubling it again barely changes the rate. What best explains this plateau?

options.text: The excess substrate destroys the enzyme, so fewer active sites remain.
The activation energy rises when substrate becomes more abundant.
The product builds up and inhibits the reaction through feedback inhibition.
The enzyme molecules are already saturated, so all active sites are occupied and extra substrate cannot speed things up.

rationales.whyCorrect: At high substrate concentration all active sites are occupied, so the rate is limited by the number of enzyme molecules and adding more substrate has no effect. Excess substrate does not destroy the enzyme (A), and the activation energy does not rise with substrate abundance (B). Product accumulation can inhibit an enzyme (C), but it does not explain the plateau in the initial rate at saturation.
rationales.eli10: Picture a taxi stand with ten taxis and a long line of waiting riders. When the line is short, every new rider is picked up almost instantly. Once all ten taxis are full, more riders arriving cannot speed up the stand at all. The enzyme is like the taxis, each one can carry only one passenger at a time.
rationales.highYield: At saturation the enzyme, not the substrate, becomes the limiting factor for reaction rate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A drug molecule resembles the substrate of an enzyme and binds at the enzyme's **active site**, blocking the true substrate. Which description of this kind of inhibition is accurate?

options.text: It is competitive inhibition, and increasing the substrate concentration can overcome it.
It is competitive inhibition, and increasing the substrate concentration cannot overcome it.
It is noncompetitive inhibition, and it permanently changes the shape of the active site.
It is allosteric inhibition, and it binds far from the active site.

rationales.whyCorrect: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and occupies the active site, so raising the substrate concentration gives the true substrate an advantage and overcomes the inhibition. B states the opposite prediction. C describes noncompetitive inhibition, and D describes allosteric binding away from the active site, neither of which matches a drug that blocks the active site itself.
rationales.eli10: Think of a parking lot with one spot reserved for a delivery van. A look-alike car that fits the same spot can sneak in first and block the van. The more vans that arrive, the better their chance of grabbing the spot before the look-alike. Adding more genuine vans is how the cell beats this kind of blocker.
rationales.highYield: Competitive inhibitors lose the race when substrate concentration rises because both fight for the same active site.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A toxin binds to an enzyme at a site away from the active site and reduces the reaction's maximum rate without changing the substrate concentration needed for half that maximum rate. What kind of inhibitor is this?

options.text: A competitive inhibitor that blocks substrate binding at the active site.
A noncompetitive inhibitor that lowers the number of functional enzyme molecules.
A competitive inhibitor that reduces the enzyme's affinity for its substrate.
An irreversible inhibitor that destroys the substrate molecule.

rationales.whyCorrect: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds at a site away from the active site and lowers the maximum rate by reducing the number of functioning enzyme molecules, without changing the substrate concentration needed for half the maximum rate. Bringing more balls cannot help because the setter is the bottleneck.
rationales.highYield: Noncompetitive inhibitors lower the maximum rate but leave the substrate concentration for half the maximum rate unchanged.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a metabolic pathway, the final product binds to an enzyme that catalyzes an early step, at a site distinct from the active site, and shuts the pathway down when the product is abundant. What is this kind of regulation called, and why is it useful to the cell?

options.text: Competitive inhibition, because the product competes with the substrate for the active site.
Enzyme saturation, because the product fills all the active sites.
Feedback inhibition via allosteric regulation, because it prevents wasteful overproduction of the product.
Denaturation, because the product unfolds the enzyme when it is abundant.

rationales.whyCorrect: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway binds to an early enzyme at an allosteric site and shuts the pathway down, preventing wasteful overproduction. D is wrong because the enzyme stays folded, it is not denatured.
rationales.eli10: Think of a faucet that fills a bathtub, with a floating ball watching the water level. When the tub is full, the float pushes the handle and stops the flow. The finished product of the pathway is like the float, it reaches back and closes the early step that made it. This way the cell never makes more product than it needs.
rationales.highYield: Feedback inhibition lets the end product of a pathway shut down an early enzyme through allosteric binding.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Pepsin, an enzyme in the stomach, works best at a strongly acidic **pH** near 2, while most cellular enzymes work best near neutral pH. Why does pH change how well an enzyme works?

options.text: pH changes the free energy released by the reaction.
pH changes the activation energy of the uncatalyzed reaction.
pH changes the temperature optimum of the enzyme.
pH alters the charges on amino acid side chains, which can disrupt the shape of the active site and the binding of substrate.

rationales.whyCorrect: pH alters the ionization of amino acid side chains, and the ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's folded shape depend on those charges, so an unfavorable pH distorts the active site and weakens substrate binding. A is wrong because pH does not change the free energy released. B is wrong because the activation energy of the uncatalyzed reaction is not what the enzyme alters, and C is wrong because pH and temperature are independent variables.
rationales.eli10: Think of a lock that opens only when the key slides in at just the right angle. If the lock frame warps, the key still fits but cannot turn. Strong acid or base changes the charges on an enzyme's parts, and those charges were holding the shape in place. A warped enzyme cannot catch its substrate well, so the reaction slows down.
rationales.highYield: Each enzyme has an optimal pH because hydrogen ion concentration controls the charges that hold its folded shape.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hormone binds a **G protein-coupled receptor**, and the activated receptor in turn activates a G protein. What happens immediately after the G protein is activated?

options.text: The G protein phosphorylates a protein kinase that then travels into the nucleus.
The G protein splits into two fragments that diffuse in opposite directions.
The G protein exchanges its GDP for GTP, and the GTP-bound subunit binds and activates an effector enzyme such as adenylyl cyclase.
The receptor itself opens a channel that lets calcium ions enter the cytosol.

rationales.whyCorrect: A G protein is active only while it carries GTP, and the receptor acts as an exchange factor that prompts the swap of GDP for GTP. The GTP-bound subunit then binds and activates an effector enzyme such as adenylyl cyclase. A misassigns the kinase work of the cascade to the G protein itself, B confuses activation with cleavage, and D describes a ligand-gated ion channel rather than a GPCR.
rationales.eli10: Think of the G protein as a worker holding a nearly dead battery. While the battery is low, which is the GDP, the worker stands around doing nothing. When a signal arrives, the receptor swaps in a fresh battery, the GTP. Now the worker jumps up and switches on a machine that makes the cell's internal message.
rationales.highYield: The G protein is the pathway's switch: GDP means off, and GTP means on.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A single epinephrine molecule can ultimately cause a liver cell to release millions of glucose molecules from stored glycogen. Which property of **signal amplification** explains how one molecule produces such a large effect?

options.text: One receptor can bind many epinephrine molecules at the same time.
Epinephrine is hydrophobic and passes through the membrane, so it can activate many receptors.
At each step of the cascade, one activated molecule switches on many molecules of the next type, multiplying the message at every level.
The same epinephrine molecule is reused many times by the response machinery.

rationales.whyCorrect: Amplification works because every cascade step activates multiple copies of the next component, so the effect multiplies geometrically from one receptor to many enzymes and finally to a flood of product molecules. A is backwards, because each receptor binds one ligand at a time. B misidentifies epinephrine, which is hydrophilic and acts at the surface, and D misstates the ligand's role, since epinephrine is not reused by the response machinery.
rationales.eli10: Think of the signal like one coin dropped into a row of machines. The first machine takes the coin and spits out ten coins. The next machine takes those ten and spits out ten for each one, and the pile keeps growing. That is how one tiny signal can end up releasing thousands of stored sugars.
rationales.highYield: Amplification is geometric multiplication: one receptor, many relays, and a flood of product at the end.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: After a cell responds to a signal, the pathway must be turned off so the cell can reset. Which of the following is a genuine mechanism of **signal termination**?

options.text: The G protein hydrolyzes its bound GTP to GDP, which returns the G protein to its inactive state.
The receptor binds the ligand permanently, locking the pathway in the on position.
Phosphatases are destroyed, so every phosphorylated protein stays active.
Second messengers such as cyclic AMP are sealed inside the cell forever.

rationales.whyCorrect: Terminating a pathway means reversing its steps: the G protein inactivates itself by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP, and phosphatases erase the phosphates that kinases added. B and D do the opposite by locking the pathway on. C also keeps the pathway active, because without phosphatases the phosphorylated proteins stay switched on.
rationales.eli10: Think of a signaling pathway as a faucet with a timer. The G protein is like a spring that unwinds on its own. Once the spring unwinds, the water stops, and the pathway turns off. The cell resets every switch so it is ready for the next signal.
rationales.highYield: Signal termination is the pathway in reverse: GTP hydrolysis and phosphate removal reset every switch.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During tadpole development, the tail is removed as the animal becomes a frog, and the tail cells die in an orderly way without spilling their contents into the surrounding tissue. What is this form of **programmed cell death**, and what signaling event typically triggers it?

options.text: Necrosis, which is triggered when the cells are damaged by an injury.
Apoptosis, which is triggered by a death signal such as a ligand binding a death receptor on the cell surface.
Autolysis, in which the cell's own lysosomes burst and digest it.
Senescence, in which the cell stops dividing but stays alive.

rationales.whyCorrect: Apoptosis is controlled cell death in which the cell is dismantled without leaking its contents, so no inflammation follows, and it is triggered by signals such as a ligand binding a death receptor. A describes necrosis, which is accidental and inflammatory. C describes lysosomal rupture, not the programmed pathway, and D describes cell-cycle arrest, in which the cell survives.
rationales.eli10: Think of apoptosis as a building that is demolished on purpose because the city no longer needs it. Workers follow a careful plan, taking the building apart piece by piece and cleaning up the rubble. Nothing spills onto the street, and the neighbors are not bothered. Necrosis, by contrast, is like a building that collapses by accident and leaves dangerous debris everywhere.
rationales.highYield: Apoptosis is tidy, programmed demolition, while necrosis is messy, accidental destruction.

rationales.highYield: Hydrophobic steroid hormones act inside the cell on gene expression, which is why their effects appear slowly.

options.text: Homologous chromosomes carry versions of the same genes, one from each parent, while sister chromatids are identical copies of a single chromosome joined at the centromere.
Sister chromatids come one from each parent, while homologous chromosomes are identical copies of one chromosome.
Homologous chromosomes separate from each other in meiosis II, while sister chromatids separate from each other in meiosis I.
A tetrad contains two chromatids in total, one from each homologous chromosome.

rationales.whyCorrect: After replication, each of the 46 chromosomes exists as two sister chromatids, and the cell also carries 23 pairs of homologous chromosomes inherited one from each parent. rationales.eli10: Think of a pair of socks from the same package: the two socks are sister chromatids, identical copies. rationales.highYield: Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome; homologous chromosomes are the matched pair inherited from the two parents.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Meiosis has two divisions with different jobs. Which statement correctly matches each division to its role?

options.text: Meiosis I is equational because it splits replicated chromosomes into two cells without changing the chromosome number.
Meiosis I is the reductional division because homologous chromosomes separate, halving the chromosome number; meiosis II is the equational division because sister chromatids separate.
Both meiotic divisions reduce the chromosome number by half, first from 46 to 23 and then from 23 to about 12.

rationales.whyCorrect: The chromosome count drops from diploid to haploid in meiosis I, when homologs separate, so meiosis I is called the reductional division. rationales.eli10: Picture a wallet holding pairs of dollar bills, one bill from each of two relatives. Only the first division is a true reduction, and that is why it gets the name reductional division.
rationales.highYield: The chromosome number is cut exactly once, in meiosis I; meiosis II only splits chromatids.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During prophase I, **synapsis** brings homologous chromosomes together into **tetrads**, and **crossing over** can occur. Which statement best describes what crossing over does?

options.text: It swaps entire chromosomes between the two daughter cells.
It joins sister chromatids of a single chromosome into one structure.
It exchanges corresponding segments between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, creating new combinations of alleles.
It occurs during meiosis II while the sister chromatids are being pulled apart.

rationales.whyCorrect: Crossing over physically breaks and rejoins segments of nonsister chromatids, so a chromatid ends up carrying some alleles from each homolog, which is genetic recombination. A confuses whole-chromosome movement with segment exchange. B misidentifies the partners, since sister chromatids carry identical alleles and swapping between them would create nothing new. D places the event in the wrong division, because crossing over happens in prophase I.
rationales.eli10: Imagine two matching storybooks, one from your mom and one from your dad, with different endings. Crossing over swaps a few pages between the two books. Each book now has a mixture of both endings, so every child gets a slightly different story. That mixing of pages is genetic recombination.
rationales.highYield: Crossing over swaps segments between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I, never between sister chromatids.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A diploid cell with 2n = 4 has two pairs of homologous chromosomes. Assuming no crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can **independent assortment** produce in the gametes of this cell?

options.text: 2, because only one orientation of the chromosome pairs is possible per cell.
6, because the two pairs can form six possible arrangements at the metaphase plate.
8, because each of the four chromosomes can assort independently into either daughter cell.
4, because each of the two chromosome pairs can orient in either of two ways, giving 2 times 2 possible combinations.

rationales.whyCorrect: Each pair of homologous chromosomes aligns independently at metaphase I, so the number of possible gamete types from a cell with n chromosome pairs is 2 to the power of n, and here n = 2, giving 4. A and B offer numbers that match no formula for this case. C would require four independently assorting units, but only two pairs are present. With 2n = 4 the real count is 4, and humans with 23 pairs can produce over 8 million combinations by this mechanism alone.
rationales.eli10: Think of a lunch line where each child picks one fork from a pair of forks and one spoon from a pair of spoons. rationales.highYield: Independent assortment yields 2 to the power of the haploid number possible gamete types, with no crossing over counted.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During **anaphase I** of meiosis in a diploid cell, a student observes chromosomes moving toward opposite poles. Which description matches what is actually separating at this stage?

rationales.whyCorrect: In anaphase I the spindle separates the members of each homologous pair, so each pole receives one duplicated chromosome, and sister chromatids remain attached. subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts **mitosis** and meiosis in a diploid organism?

options.text: Mitosis produces four genetically unique haploid cells, while meiosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, while meiosis produces four genetically distinct haploid cells.
Both processes include synapsis and crossing over during prophase.
Both processes reduce the chromosome number by half in each division.

rationales.whyCorrect: Mitosis copies the genome once and divides once, preserving the diploid number and genetic identity, while meiosis divides twice and produces four haploid cells that differ by crossing over and independent assortment. A swaps the outcomes of the two processes. C and D describe features unique to meiosis, since mitosis never pairs homologs and never reduces the chromosome number.
rationales.eli10: Think of photocopying a worksheet versus shuffling a deck of cards. Mitosis makes an exact copy of the worksheet, same pages in the same order. Meiosis shuffles the deck and deals out new hands, so every hand is different. Both processes start from the same original material but end with very different results.
rationales.highYield: Mitosis makes identical diploid copies; meiosis makes four distinct haploid cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: **Spermatogenesis** and **oogenesis** are the processes of gamete formation in animals. Which statement correctly describes how they differ?

options.text: Spermatogenesis yields one large functional gamete and three polar bodies, while oogenesis yields four equal-sized sperm.
Oogenesis begins at puberty, while spermatogenesis begins before birth.
Oogenesis produces one large ovum that keeps most of the cytoplasm, while spermatogenesis produces four small, equal-sized sperm.
Both processes produce four functional gametes from every primary sex cell.

rationales.whyCorrect: In oogenesis the cytoplasm is distributed unevenly so one ovum receives nearly all of it and the polar bodies receive very little, which supplies the future embryo with stored materials. In spermatogenesis meiosis produces four small motile gametes of roughly equal size, all of them functional. A swaps the two descriptions, B reverses when each process starts, and D ignores the polar bodies that limit oogenesis to one functional gamete per primary oocyte.
rationales.eli10: Think of a pie being shared. In spermatogenesis the pie is cut into four equal slices, so everyone gets a full meal. In oogenesis the pie is cut very unevenly: one huge slice for the egg and three tiny crumbs that are later thrown away. The big slice is the ovum, and the crumbs are the polar bodies. The egg needs all that food because it may grow into a whole new organism.
rationales.highYield: Oogenesis funnels nearly all the cytoplasm into one ovum; spermatogenesis produces four equal sperm.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A couple has a child with **Down syndrome**, which results from trisomy 21. Which of the following events most directly explains how a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21 arose?

options.text: Crossing over exchanged a segment between chromosome 21 and a different chromosome.
Independent assortment placed both copies of chromosome 21 into one daughter cell.
A single gene on chromosome 21 duplicated itself during DNA replication.
Nondisjunction occurred, so homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids failed to separate and both copies of chromosome 21 went into one gamete.

rationales.whyCorrect: Trisomy 21 requires a gamete that carries an extra chromosome 21, and the only way that forms is nondisjunction, a failure of homologs in meiosis I or of sister chromatids in meiosis II to separate. When such a gamete fuses with a normal gamete, the zygote has three copies of the chromosome. A and C cannot add a whole chromosome, and B mislabels the normal process of independent assortment as the cause.
rationales.eli10: Picture a train station where pairs of travelers must split onto two trains. Normally one traveler of each pair boards each train. If the ticket inspector forgets to split one pair, both travelers board the same train and the other train gets none. That missed split is nondisjunction. When the overloaded train joins with a train from the other parent, the child gets three copies instead of two.
rationales.highYield: Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis, and trisomy 21 is its most famous result.
