subjectWideQuestions.stem: A girl is diagnosed with **Turner syndrome**, having one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome, a condition written as 45, X. Which statement best explains how this **aneuploidy** arises?

options.text: Nondisjunction in a parent produced a gamete with no sex chromosome, and fertilization with a normal gamete carrying one X produced a zygote with a single X.
The father's Y chromosome was deleted from the zygote shortly after fertilization.
An egg that received two X chromosomes fused with a sperm carrying a Y chromosome, producing a zygote with three sex chromosomes.
Crossing over transferred the X chromosome genes onto an autosome, replacing the missing sex chromosome.

rationales.whyCorrect: Turner syndrome is a monosomy, a form of aneuploidy in which one sex chromosome is missing, and the usual cause is nondisjunction in either parent producing a sperm or egg without a sex chromosome. B describes a post-fertilization event that is not the established cause. C would produce a zygote with three sex chromosomes, which is a different condition. D invents an exchange between non-homologous chromosomes, which crossing over does not normally perform.
rationales.eli10: Think of a bakery that packs cakes in pairs, one from each baker. If one baker's tray accidentally ships empty, the customer receives a cake with only one half. In the same way, a gamete without a sex chromosome joins with a normal one, and the baby ends up with a single X. The missing half is what doctors call monosomy. Turner syndrome is one of the results when that empty tray leaves the bakery.
rationales.highYield: Aneuploidy is a wrong chromosome count, and a missing sex chromosome is the hallmark of Turner syndrome.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: **Sexual reproduction** is costly because it requires finding a mate and passes on only half of each parent's genes. Which of the following best explains why sexual reproduction remains so widespread?

options.text: It doubles the chromosome number of the species in every generation.
Recombination and independent assortment generate new combinations of alleles, and the resulting genetic variation gives populations more material for natural selection.
It produces offspring that are genetic clones, preserving beneficial gene combinations exactly.
It prevents mutations from ever being passed on to offspring.

rationales.whyCorrect: The main evolutionary payoff of sex is variation: crossing over and independent assortment reshuffle alleles, and the variety of offspring increases the chance that some will survive environmental change. A is false because meiosis keeps the chromosome number constant across generations. C describes the benefit of asexual reproduction, which cannot reshuffle genes. D is false because mutations are still inherited, but their reshuffled combinations change the fate of the population.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a clothing shop that sells identical shirts in one size. If everyone wears the same shirt, one cold winter leaves the whole town cold. Now imagine a shop that mixes sizes, colors, and fabrics randomly. When the weather changes, at least some people will have a coat that fits. Sexual reproduction is that mixing shop, keeping populations ready for surprises.
rationales.highYield: Sexual reproduction wins because recombination creates variation that natural selection can act on.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher cuts a circular **plasmid** with a **restriction enzyme** that produces **sticky ends**, then cuts a gene of interest with the same enzyme. Which statement best explains why sticky ends make it easy to join the gene into the plasmid?

options.text: The single-stranded overhangs base-pair with the complementary overhangs on the other DNA piece, aligning the gene with the plasmid.
The double-stranded overhangs are chemically labeled, so the gene can be detected wherever it lands.
The overhangs are short RNA segments that recruit enzymes to splice the gene into the plasmid.
The enzyme leaves blunt ends that DNA ligase cannot seal, so the gene stays separate and safe.

rationales.whyCorrect: Restriction enzymes such as EcoRI cut at specific palindromic sequences and leave short single-stranded overhangs, called sticky ends, that base-pair with complementary overhangs on another DNA molecule. Cutting the insert and the plasmid with the same enzyme produces matching overhangs, so the gene aligns with the plasmid and DNA ligase seals the strands together. B describes chemically labeled ends, C invokes RNA guides, which are a feature of CRISPR rather than restriction enzymes, and D is wrong because this enzyme produces sticky overhangs and ligase can seal the aligned ends.
rationales.eli10: Picture a strip of paper with zigzag cut edges on both ends. Two strips cut with the same zigzag tool fit together perfectly, like puzzle pieces. The zigzag is the sticky end, made of unpaired bases waiting for their partners. That is why scientists use the same cutting enzyme on the gene and on the plasmid, so the two pieces click together.
rationales.highYield: Sticky ends pair by the same complementary base-pairing that holds DNA strands together, so matching cuts make the insert and vector click together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During **gel electrophoresis**, a mixture of DNA fragments is loaded into wells at one end of an **agarose gel** and an electric current is applied. How does the gel separate the fragments?

options.text: Larger fragments carry a stronger negative charge and race to the far end first.
Smaller fragments slip through the gel matrix more easily and travel farthest from the well.
Fragments rich in guanine and cytosine form stronger bonds and move farthest.
All fragments travel the same distance because the charge per molecule is identical.

rationales.whyCorrect: DNA is negatively charged, so fragments move toward the positive electrode, but the agarose matrix sieves them by size and smaller molecules slip through the pores fastest and travel farthest. A reverses the size rule, C invokes base composition, which does not affect migration through agarose, and D ignores the sieving effect of the gel matrix.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a forest of tree roots acting as a sieve for wiggly objects of different sizes. The small jelly worm slips between the roots quickly, while the big jelly blob gets stuck and crawls slowly. Electricity pulls the DNA through the roots, so the smallest pieces reach the far end first. Scientists measure how far each piece traveled to learn its size.
rationales.highYield: Gel electrophoresis sorts DNA by size, and smaller fragments always travel farther through the gel.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The **polymerase chain reaction** (PCR) amplifies a target DNA segment through repeated temperature cycles. What is the correct order of the three main steps in each cycle?

rationales.whyCorrect: Each cycle begins with denaturation, heating the double-stranded DNA near 95 degrees Celsius so the strands separate, followed by annealing, when the temperature drops and primers bind to their complementary sequences, and then extension, when a heat-stable polymerase builds new strands. Only D lists the steps in that order, and the other options scramble the cycle.
rationales.eli10: Think of copying a sentence with a photocopier that doubles every time it runs. First, heat unzips the DNA like pulling the two sides of a zipper apart. Then cooler temperatures let short primers stick to each side, marking where copying starts. Finally, the machine fills in the missing letters to make two complete double strands. Each round doubles the copies, so one copy quickly becomes many.
rationales.highYield: Every PCR cycle doubles the target by melting, annealing, and extending, and heat-stable polymerases survive the melting step.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A forensic lab receives a tiny bloodstain containing very little DNA and runs PCR with **primers** designed for a specific region of the genome. What does the reaction actually amplify?

options.text: Only the target segment flanked by the primers, copied repeatedly from the original DNA strands.
The complete genome of the organism, copied in a single cycle.
All of the RNA in the sample, reverse-transcribed into DNA each cycle.
The primers themselves, which the polymerase copies instead of the DNA.

rationales.whyCorrect: The primers flank the target region, and the polymerase copies only the DNA between them, using the original strands and then the newly made strands as templates, so the number of copies doubles each cycle. B overstates the product, C describes reverse transcription of RNA, which PCR does not perform, and D is wrong because primers are short synthetic starting sequences that define the product rather than being amplified themselves.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a photocopier that only copies the middle paragraph of a page, marked by two bookends. The bookends are the primers, and they tell the machine exactly which paragraph to copy. Every pass makes a fresh copy of just that paragraph, never the whole page. After many passes, one page has become a huge stack of identical paragraphs.
rationales.highYield: PCR amplifies only the segment between the primers, which is why primers are designed specifically for the region of interest.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In **Sanger sequencing**, the reaction contains normal nucleotides plus a small amount of **dideoxy nucleotides** that lack the 3-prime hydroxyl group. What happens when the polymerase inserts a dideoxy nucleotide?

options.text: The strand grows faster because the dideoxy nucleotide carries extra energy.
Chain elongation stops at that position, so the mix produces fragments of different lengths that reveal the sequence.
The double helix denatures, allowing the fragments to be weighed on a scale.
The dideoxy nucleotide is converted to a normal nucleotide and the chain continues.

rationales.whyCorrect: A dideoxy nucleotide lacks the 3-prime hydroxyl group, so when the polymerase inserts one, no bond can form for the next nucleotide and synthesis stops at that position. Because the reaction mixes normal and dideoxy nucleotides, the products are fragments that stop at every possible position, and their lengths reveal the sequence one base at a time. A and D describe effects that dideoxy nucleotides do not have, and C confuses denaturation with the chain-termination readout.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a typewriter where some keys jam the machine when pressed. Every time the typewriter hits a jammed key, it stops, leaving a partial sentence. If you run the machine many times with different keys jammed, you collect partial sentences that end at every position. Lining them up reads the full message, just as the stopped fragments reveal the DNA sequence.
rationales.highYield: Dideoxy nucleotides stop DNA synthesis at every base, and the lengths of the stopped fragments spell out the sequence.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: **Next-generation sequencing** produces millions of short DNA sequence reads at once. How do researchers assemble a complete genome from these short reads?

options.text: They translate every read into protein and infer the genome from the amino acid sequences.
They sort the reads by chromosome number and count them at each position.
They align overlapping reads and merge them into longer contiguous sequences, then order those sequences.
They insert each read into a plasmid and let bacteria recombine them into a genome.

rationales.whyCorrect: Short reads from next-generation sequencing overlap with one another, so researchers align the overlapping ends and merge them into longer contiguous sequences called contigs, then order the contigs into scaffolds and chromosomes. Deep coverage ensures that most positions appear in many reads, which makes the overlaps reliable. A assumes the reads map to known proteins, B ignores the sequence information, and D describes no real assembly method.
rationales.eli10: Think of a long book that was shredded into millions of tiny strips of paper, each with a few words. To rebuild the book, you look for strips that share the same last words and first words and glue them together. Piece by piece the strips form longer passages, and eventually the whole book is restored. That is how scientists rebuild a genome from short reads.
rationales.highYield: Short reads are assembled by matching overlapping ends, like rebuilding a torn book from strips of paper.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In **CRISPR-Cas9** gene editing, the Cas9 protein cuts DNA at a specific location guided by a **guide RNA**. What makes the guide RNA pick that location?

options.text: The protein folds its own shape to match the sequence it edits.
The target sequence must contain a start codon that Cas9 recognizes.
Cas9 cuts randomly, and the guide RNA repairs the damage afterward.
The guide RNA carries a sequence complementary to the target, so it base-pairs with the genomic DNA and steers Cas9 to that site.

rationales.whyCorrect: The guide RNA carries a sequence complementary to the target, so it base-pairs with the genomic DNA and positions the Cas9 nuclease to cut at that exact site, next to a short motif called a protospacer adjacent motif. Changing the guide RNA changes the cut site, which is why CRISPR can be programmed for different genes. A and B describe targeting mechanisms that do not exist, and C is wrong because the cut is guided rather than random.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a pair of molecular scissors that need an address before they cut. The guide RNA is the address card, with a sequence that matches the spot in the genome. When the card finds its matching spot, it sticks there and the scissors snip right at that address. Change the card and the scissors cut somewhere else.
rationales.highYield: The guide RNA programs Cas9 by base-pairing with the target, so changing the guide changes where the cut lands.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A **transgenic organism** carries a foreign gene introduced through **recombinant DNA** technology. Which example best fits this definition?

options.text: Corn plants carrying a bacterial gene that produces a protein toxic to insect pests.
A yeast strain whose own genes make ethanol during fermentation.
A person with a mutation that changes one amino acid in hemoglobin.
A bacterium that picks up a new plasmid from another bacterium in pond water.

rationales.whyCorrect: A transgenic organism carries a foreign gene deliberately inserted into its genome with recombinant DNA techniques, and corn carrying a bacterial insect-toxin gene is a textbook example. B describes genes that yeast already has, C is a mutation in an existing human gene, and D is a natural gene transfer that does not involve deliberate engineering.
rationales.eli10: Think of a car that comes from the factory with a GPS built in from another company. The GPS is a foreign part that was deliberately installed, and now the car can do something new. A transgenic organism is like that car, carrying a gene from another species that was installed on purpose. That new gene gives the crop or animal a new ability, such as resisting insects.
rationales.highYield: Transgenic organisms carry a foreign gene deliberately inserted with recombinant DNA tools, as in Bt crops.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Forensic labs use **DNA fingerprinting** to compare a crime-scene sample with a suspect's DNA. What does the analysis actually compare, and why does it identify individuals so powerfully?

options.text: The complete DNA sequence of every chromosome, compared base by base.
The lengths of short tandem repeat regions at several locations across the genome.
The number of chromosomes present in each cell sample.
The protein sequence of a single gene shared by everyone.

rationales.whyCorrect: DNA fingerprinting compares the lengths of short tandem repeat regions at several loci, and because the number of repeats at each locus varies widely among people, the combined pattern is effectively unique to an individual. PCR amplifies the repeat regions and gel or capillary electrophoresis measures their lengths. A is unnecessary, C ignores that chromosome number is the same in every person, and D is wrong because a gene shared by everyone reveals little about identity.
rationales.eli10: Think of a DNA fingerprint as a barcode built from several short repeating patterns. At each spot on the barcode, a person has a pattern repeated a certain number of times, and people differ in how many repeats they have. Matching several of these patterns across many spots is like comparing the whole barcode. A full match is so rare that it points to one person almost beyond doubt.
rationales.highYield: Short tandem repeats at many loci make each person's DNA fingerprint effectively unique.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a **paternity test**, DNA fingerprinting is performed on a child, the mother, and a man alleged to be the father. Which pattern of results supports paternity?

options.text: The child matches the mother at every location and shares no bands with the man.
The man's profile is an exact copy of the child's profile.
Every band in the child that does not come from the mother matches a band in the man.
The man and the mother share identical profiles, so the child matches both.

rationales.whyCorrect: A child inherits one copy of each chromosome from each parent, so every band in the child's fingerprint must trace to the mother or the father, and paternity is supported when the bands that do not match the mother match the alleged father. A would rule the man out, B is impossible because the child also carries maternal bands, and D confuses the parents' profiles with the child's inheritance.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a child's sock collection where every sock came from one of two stores. The mother's shopping bag tells you which socks came from her store, and the rest must have come from the father's bag. If the man's bag holds every remaining sock, he is almost certainly the father. If his bag is missing any sock, someone else must have bought it.
rationales.highYield: A child inherits one copy from each parent, so every band must trace to the mother or the father.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The **Human Genome Project** produced a reference sequence of the human genome. Which statement correctly describes both the project's result and an ethical issue it raised?

options.text: Humans have about one million genes, and genetic data is fully private.
Only a single chromosome was sequenced, and the project was abandoned.
All human genomes are identical, so genetic testing has no value.
The project produced a reference genome of about three billion base pairs and raised concerns about genetic privacy and discrimination.

rationales.whyCorrect: The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, produced a reference sequence of about three billion base pairs and identified roughly 20000 to 25000 genes, and it sparked wide debate about genetic privacy and the risk of discrimination by insurers or employers. A gives a false gene count and dismisses privacy concerns, and B and C are factually wrong about what was sequenced and how much genomes vary between people.
rationales.eli10: The project was like writing down a library of instructions with about three billion letters, the complete operating manual of a human. Finishing the manual let doctors read genes and find disease-causing typos. But the manual is personal, so the project also started a big conversation about who gets to read it. Today the rules about keeping genetic information private are still being written.
rationales.highYield: The Human Genome Project delivered a three-billion-base-pair reference genome and opened the debate on genetic privacy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a population of beetles, some individuals are dark colored and some are light colored. Birds catch more light-colored beetles, so dark beetles survive and produce more offspring. Which condition must also be present for **natural selection** to change the population's average color over generations?

options.text: Dark color must be passed from parents to offspring.
The population must be very small.
The birds must leave the area.
Every beetle must produce the same number of offspring.

rationales.whyCorrect: Natural selection requires variation, differential survival and reproduction, and heritability, and without inheritance a favored trait dies with the individual that carried it. B describes a situation where drift, not selection, dominates. C removes the selective pressure, and D cancels the differential reproduction described in the stem.
rationales.eli10: Think of a bowl of mixed candy where kids always grab the red pieces first. The red pieces disappear, but if the candy machine keeps making the same mix, the bowl never truly changes. For the mix to change for good, the machine must copy whatever pieces survive best. Passing the winning trait to the next generation is the part scientists call heritability.
rationales.highYield: For a trait to evolve by natural selection, it must be heritable, because selection acts on individuals but evolution needs the trait passed to offspring.

### Q14-01 Natural selection and heritability

In a population of beetles, some individuals are dark colored and some are light colored. Birds catch more light-colored beetles, so dark beetles survive and produce more offspring. Which condition must also be present for **natural selection** to change the population's average color over generations?

- **A.** Dark color must be passed from parents to offspring.
- **B.** The population must be very small.
- **C.** The birds must leave the area.
- **D.** Every beetle must produce the same number of offspring.

**Correct Answer:** **A.** Dark color must be passed from parents to offspring.

**Why This Is Correct:** Natural selection requires variation, differential survival and reproduction, and heritability, and without inheritance a favored trait dies with the individual that carried it. B describes a situation where drift, not selection, dominates. C removes the selective pressure, and D cancels the differential reproduction described in the stem.

> **High-Yield:** For a trait to evolve by natural selection, it must be heritable, because selection acts on individuals but evolution needs the trait passed to offspring.

**ELI-10:** Think of a bowl of mixed candy where kids always grab the red pieces first. The red pieces disappear, but if the candy machine keeps making the same mix, the bowl never truly changes. For the mix to change for good, the machine must copy whatever pieces survive best. Passing the winning trait to the next generation is the part scientists call heritability.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement best defines an **adaptation** in the context of evolution?

options.text: Any physical change an organism undergoes during its lifetime.
A heritable trait that improves an organism's fitness in its environment.
Any trait that makes an organism look different from its parents.
A structure that an organism no longer uses.

rationales.whyCorrect: An adaptation is a heritable trait that raises fitness, which is an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment, and this definition sits at the core of the modern synthesis. A describes acquired changes that are not inherited. C describes mere variation, and D describes a vestigial structure.
rationales.eli10: Picture a winter jacket that fits you well while a neighbor owns one that is too thin. The good jacket helps you survive cold weather, much like a helpful trait helps an animal survive. A helpful inborn trait that helps an animal survive and raise young in its home is called an adaptation. The key part is that the animal is born with the trait and passes it to its offspring.
rationales.highYield: An adaptation is always a heritable trait that raises fitness, never a change acquired during an individual's lifetime.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The flipper of a whale and the wing of a bat look different on the outside, yet both contain the same arrangement of bones. Which pair of structures would biologists classify as **homologous**?

options.text: The wings of a bird and the wings of a butterfly.
The wing of a butterfly and the wing of a bat.
The flipper of a whale and the wing of a bat.
The eye of a squid and the eye of a human.

rationales.whyCorrect: Homologous structures share an underlying bone pattern inherited from a common ancestor, and both the whale flipper and the bat wing are modified mammalian forelimbs. The other three pairs serve similar functions but evolved independently, so they are analogous structures rather than homologous ones.
rationales.eli10: Think of two families that each own a dresser built by their great-grandfather. The dressers share the same inner plan even if one now holds tools and the other holds clothes. The same is true of a whale flipper and a bat wing, which both come from the forelimb of an ancient mammal. Structures with a shared inner plan from a shared relative are homologous.
rationales.highYield: Homologous structures share a common ancestor, while analogous structures share only a function.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Whales carry small pelvic bones that do not attach to any hind limbs, and fossils of early whale ancestors show larger hind limbs. Which statement best explains why the pelvic bones are described as **vestigial structures**?

options.text: They help whales balance and steer while swimming.
They first evolved in whales as a new feature.
They show that whales are descended from fish with backbones.
They are reduced remnants of hind limbs that were functional in four-legged ancestors.

rationales.whyCorrect: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of organs that were functional in ancestors, and the whale pelvic bones fit this definition. The fossil series of whale ancestors, from four-legged land mammals to modern swimmers, shows hind limbs shrinking over time. A misreads the bones' function, B reverses the evolutionary direction, and C misidentifies the ancestral group.
rationales.eli10: Imagine you own an old coat with sleeves that were once full length but were shortened over time until only stubs remain. The stubs are leftovers, not new features. Whales carry small leftover bones that were once legs, and the fossil record shows those leg bones shrinking. Leftovers from ancestors are called vestigial structures.
rationales.highYield: A vestigial structure is a reduced leftover of a trait that was functional in an ancestor, and fossils often reveal the intermediate stages.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Researchers find that humans and chimpanzees share very similar DNA sequences, and that early embryos of many vertebrates pass through similar stages. Which conclusion is best supported by these two lines of evidence from **molecular biology** and **embryology**?

options.text: Similar environments produce similar DNA and similar embryos.
Shared DNA sequences and shared embryonic patterns point to descent from a common ancestor.
Embryo similarities prove that DNA is not inherited.
DNA comparisons work only for species that look alike.

rationales.whyCorrect: Molecular comparisons show that closely related species share more DNA, and embryology shows that related groups pass through similar early stages, so both lines of evidence independently support common ancestry. A treats convergent similarity as an explanation for deeply shared patterns. C contradicts inheritance, and D wrongly limits DNA evidence.
rationales.eli10: Two cousins may have different faces but very similar baby pictures. Species that share a common relative show it in their early development and in their DNA recipes. DNA holds the instructions for building a body, so similar instructions suggest a shared author. When separate clues point the same way, scientists trust the conclusion.
rationales.highYield: DNA sequence comparisons and embryo comparisons are independent lines of evidence that both point to common ancestry.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The finches of the Galapagos Islands resemble finches on the nearby South American mainland more than they resemble birds on distant Pacific islands, even though some distant islands have similar climates. This pattern is a classic example from the study of **biogeography**. Which idea does it support?

options.text: Island species are most closely related to species in the nearest source region, not to similar-looking species far away.
Similar climates always produce identical species.
Each island's species arose independently with no link to other regions.
Birds on distant islands are always unrelated to birds on nearby islands.

rationales.whyCorrect: Biogeography predicts that closely related species appear near one another because they share recent ancestors, which is exactly what the Galapagos finches show with their mainland relatives. Climatic similarity can produce look-alike but unrelated species, so B fails. C ignores shared ancestry, and D overstates the general pattern.
rationales.eli10: If your family moved to a new town, your relatives nearby would resemble you more than strangers across the country who share your hair color. Animals spread outward from a home region, so species near that home look like their relatives there. Where an animal lives is a clue about who its family is. That is the idea of biogeography.
rationales.highYield: In biogeography questions, geographic closeness with shared ancestry beats climatic similarity every time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which list correctly states the five conditions that keep a population in **Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium**?

options.text: No mutations, random mating, no natural selection, small population, no gene flow.
High mutation rate, nonrandom mating, no natural selection, large population, no gene flow.
No mutations, random mating, no natural selection, a very large population, and no gene flow.
No mutations, random mating, strong natural selection, a very large population, and no gene flow.

rationales.whyCorrect: The five Hardy-Weinberg conditions are no mutation, random mating, no natural selection, a very large population, and no gene flow, and together they keep allele frequencies constant. A fails on population size, B fails on mutation and mating, and D fails on selection and gene flow.
rationales.eli10: Think of a jar of colored beads that nobody touches. The mix of colors stays the same if nobody adds beads, nobody removes beads, and nobody picks favorites. Each rule protects the bead mix from changing. When every rule holds, the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
rationales.highYield: Memorize the five Hardy-Weinberg conditions: no mutation, random mating, no selection, a very large population, and no gene flow.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a population of 1000 frogs, 90 frogs show a **recessive phenotype**. If the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of the **dominant allele**?

rationales.whyCorrect: The recessive phenotype frequency is 90 divided by 1000, or 0.09, which equals q squared, so q is 0.30. Since p plus q equals one, the dominant allele frequency p is 1 minus 0.30, or 0.70. Option B reports the phenotype frequency, C reports the recessive allele frequency, and D is a miscalculation.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a jar of one hundred beads where nine are red, and a red bead can only show when a bead carries two red genes. When genes pair randomly, about three of every ten genes in the jar are red, so seven of every ten are the other color. Scientists use numbers like these to predict how genes spread through a population.
rationales.highYield: To convert a recessive phenotype frequency into an allele frequency, take the square root and subtract from one.

### Q14-08 Hardy-Weinberg allele frequency calculation

In a population of 1000 frogs, 90 frogs show a **recessive phenotype**. If the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of the **dominant allele**?

- **A.** 0.70
- **B.** 0.09
- **C.** 0.30
- **D.** 0.03

**Correct Answer:** **A.** 0.70

**Why This Is Correct:** The recessive phenotype frequency is 90 divided by 1000, or 0.09, which equals q squared, so q is 0.30. Since p plus q equals one, the dominant allele frequency p is 1 minus 0.30, or 0.70. Option B reports the phenotype frequency, C reports the recessive allele frequency, and D is a miscalculation.

> **High-Yield:** To convert a recessive phenotype frequency into an allele frequency, take the square root and subtract from one.

**ELI-10:** Imagine a jar of one hundred beads where nine are red, and a red bead can only show when a bead carries two red genes. When genes pair randomly, about three of every ten genes in the jar are red, so seven of every ten are the other color. Scientists use numbers like these to predict how genes spread through a population.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A meadow holds a population of only 20 flowers, while a nearby field holds 20,000 flowers of the same species. A storm kills most individuals in both places, and the survivors repopulate each area. Why does **genetic drift** alter allele frequencies much more strongly in the small population?

options.text: Small populations mutate faster than large populations.
Natural selection is weaker in large populations.
Gene flow always increases in small populations.
The survivors of a small population are a small random sample, so chance alone can swing allele frequencies widely.

rationales.whyCorrect: Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies caused by sampling error, and sampling error is largest when very few individuals pass on their genes. In a population of 20,000, chance deviations from the expected mix largely cancel out. A confuses drift with mutation, B misstates the role of selection, and C misstates gene flow.
rationales.eli10: Flip a coin ten times and you might get eight heads, but flip it ten thousand times and the count stays near half and half. A tiny group of survivors is like a short series of coin flips, so pure luck can change the mix. Bigger populations average out the luck. That random sway is called genetic drift.
rationales.highYield: Genetic drift is pure chance, so it has its strongest effect on small populations.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hurricane carries a small group of beetles from the mainland to a distant island, where they establish a new population that carries only part of the mainland's **gene pool**. Which term best describes this event?

options.text: Gene flow, because alleles travel between established populations.
Founder effect, because a few individuals start a new population from a small sample of the source gene pool.
Bottleneck effect, because the population shrank for one generation.
Nonrandom mating, because the survivors paired with specific mates.

rationales.whyCorrect: The founder effect occurs when a small group colonizes a new area and carries only a subset of the source population's alleles into the new gene pool. A bottleneck, by contrast, shrinks an existing population to a few survivors, so C mislabels the scenario. Gene flow describes ongoing allele exchange between established populations, and D is unrelated to this event.
rationales.eli10: If a club picks five members at random to start a new club, the new club only has the habits of those five people. The new group may look very different from the big club even though it started from it. When a small group founds a new population in a new place, the result is the founder effect.
rationales.highYield: The founder effect starts a new population with a few colonizers, while the bottleneck effect shrinks an existing population to a few survivors.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a population of seed-eating birds, individuals with very small beaks and individuals with very large beaks both survive and reproduce well, while medium-beaked birds survive poorly because they handle both seed types slowly. Which statement correctly describes **disruptive selection** acting on beak size?

options.text: It favors the middle beak size, pushing the population toward the average.
It favors one extreme, shifting the average beak size over generations.
It favors both extremes, acting against the intermediate beak size.
It eliminates all beak variation by chance in small populations.

rationales.whyCorrect: Disruptive selection favors both extreme phenotypes and acts against the intermediate phenotype, which is exactly what the stem describes. A describes stabilizing selection, B describes directional selection, and D describes genetic drift rather than selection on beak size.
rationales.eli10: Picture a game where only very tall people and very short people can reach the prizes, while people of middle height get nothing. Over time the crowd splits into two groups, the tall and the short. Selection that favors both ends and squeezes the middle is called disruptive selection.
rationales.highYield: Extremes favored over the middle is disruptive selection, the middle favored is stabilizing selection, and one end favored is directional selection.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A river divides a single population of small rodents into two groups that can no longer meet. Over many generations, the two groups diverge until they cannot interbreed. Which term best describes this pattern of **speciation**?

options.text: Sympatric speciation, because the two groups diverged without a physical barrier.
Genetic drift, because allele frequencies changed randomly.
Gene flow, because genes moved between the two groups.
Allopatric speciation, because a physical barrier separated the two groups and stopped gene flow.

rationales.whyCorrect: Allopatric speciation begins when a physical barrier such as a river separates one population, stopping gene flow so the two groups diverge into separate species. A mislabels the event as sympatric, which requires speciation without a barrier. B names one process within the divergence rather than the speciation pattern, and C is the opposite of what the barrier causes.
rationales.eli10: Two friends move to opposite ends of a huge city and stop visiting each other. They slowly pick up different habits until they seem like different people. When a river or mountain blocks two groups from meeting, they slowly change until they become separate species. That kind of separation is called allopatric speciation.
rationales.highYield: Allopatric speciation requires a physical barrier; sympatric speciation happens without one.
